lawyer:
Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed with Mahmudul Islam, Advocates ------- For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, Addl. AG with QA Hossain, AAG ------- For the Respondents.
parties:
National Engineers Ltd., a Private Limited Company  ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Director, Military Lands and Cantonment Directorate and others  ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
AM Mahmudur Rahman, J. : By this Rule issued under Article 102 of our Constitution the petitioner asks us to declare that the order dated 15.6.1988 as contained in Memo. No. 6/ML & C/ME0/40-3/Sha-3/70. Annexure-A issued by Respondent 1 and the order dated 18.6.1988 as contained in Memo. No. BD/LC/375/86/70. Annexure-B issued by respondent 2 has been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect.

2. The aforesaid rule has been issued upon a voluminous application annexing to it a large number of documents and papers and respondents have equally put in affidavits-in-opposition annexing plethora of documents and papers. However we in a nut-shell. narrate the relevant facts of the cases of both the petitioner and the respondents M/s. Allenberry & Co. some time in 1942-43 for setting up a factory for manufacturing of drums got lease of 12.50 acres of land from the then Ministry of Defence and set up a factory on the lease-hold land and subsequently sold the industry to M/s. Drums Metal Limited. The share-holders and the Directors of M/s. Drums Metal Limited were Pakistani nationals. On emergence of Bangladesh the said company was declared abandoned one under President's Order No.16 of 1972 and was taken over by the Government of Bangladesh with all its assets and liabilities and was placed under the management of the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation. Pursuant to the decision of the Government of Bangladesh to disinvest M/s Drums Metal Ltd. an advertisement was published in the newspaper on June 20.1976 for the sale of the said industrial undertaking in auction to the highest bidder. The petitioner along with others participated in the bid on May 20.1976 and offered Tk. 91 lacs towards the price of the lands, machineries, equipments and buildings and undertook to pay the debt of the said company payable to the Commercial Banks. The petitioner paid Tk. 91.000.00 as earnest money for submitting the bid. The petitioner alleged that at the time of advertisement respondent 2 did not disclose that the lands underneath the factory were lease-hold property. Rather it gave an impression that the said lands were absolutely held by M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. On August 9.1976 in a meeting the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Industry agreed that out of the total lands in occupation of M/s Drums Metal Ltd. 4.65 acres would be taken away and be given to the Bangladesh Air Force and the company would retain its possession of 3.28 acres for running its business. Thereafter, on June 7, 1977 respondent 3 issued a letter of intent indicating that instead of 7.93 acres they would sell 3.28 acres of land. On receiving the said letter the petitioner made representation to the Government to reduce price for shrinkage of the land. But that not being accepted the petitioner agreed to purchase 3.28 acres of land and made down payment of Tk. 22 lacs to the Government as required by the letter of intent. Thereafter, the Ministry of Industry and the petitioner entered into an agreement on September 13,1977 Annexure-D, for sale of the undertaking of M/s Drums Metal Ltd. together with 3.28 acres of land on which the building, factory, etc. of the said Company situated and delivered possession to the petitioner. According to the terms of the said agreement, the petitioner was to pay Tk. 69 lacs in 9 equal annual instalments on execution of the said agreement. After execution of the aforesaid agreement the petitioner learnt that the lands were within Dhaka Cantonment and under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence. It also came to learn that the President of the People's Republic of Bangladesh through the Military Estate Officer entered into an agreement, Annexure-E, on July 13,1977 with the said M/s Drums Metal Ltd. to lease out 3.28 acres of land for 20 years from April 1,1963 to March 31,1983. It is further stated that the Disinvestment Board took a decision, Annexure-E (1), in a meeting held on 20.5.1977 that the matter of extension of lease would be taken up between the Ministry of Industry and the Ministry of Defence in 1983, the year of expiry of the lease. The petitioner states that in terms of Annexure-D, the Government was to execute and register the sale deed within 3 months from the payment of the last installment and the petitioner was always ready and willing to pay the balance Tk.8,91,479.00 as soon as Ministry of Industry is willing to accept the amount and is able to execute and register the sale deed. But the Government took no step for executing the sale deed in spite of the letter dated 18.9.1986, Annexure-G' intimating willingness of the petitioner to deposit the balance amount on hearing that the Ministry of Defence is ready to execute the deed of sale. The petitioner further states that it had to spend Tk. 6.5 crores for repair and renovation of the equirments of the factory for carrying on business on the representation of the Government that it would do its parts in terms of the contract. And on such impression given to it the respondents are estopped to deny the right of the petitioner to use and occupy the land in which it had acquired "indefeasible right, title and interest in the Drum Factory and the lands underneath the said factory." The petitioner further states that for execution of the deed of sale by the Ministry of Industries the petitioner has no obligation. And the Ministry of Industry being fully aware of its obligation made a request on March 7,1983, Annexure-H, to the Ministry of Defence to extented lease for a period of 20 years. But the lease was extended for 5 years only from 31st March, 1983 by an order dated February 18,1984 as per Annexure-1'. The petitioner in order to avoid further conflict requested for extension of lease for 20 years. But the lease was extended upto 31st March, 1986 by Respondent 1 by a letter dated 9.3.1986 subject to payment of premium of Tk. 1,48,30,562.00 and annual rent of Tk. 14,83,055.20 contrary to the terms of Agreement, Annexure—'D' and disproportionate to the rent and premium previously charged for the said land which is arbitrary, illegal and malafide. The petitioner on March 27,1986 approached the President against such demand in vain. The Ministry of Industries by its Memo dated 18.10.86, Annexure-'K', pointed out to the Principal Staff Officer to the Chief Martial Law Administrator that a contractual obligation arises for sale of the land on the part of the Government in view of the Agreement, Annexure-'D'. And the Ministry of Industries also requested to hold a meeting with the Ministry of Defence to resolve the matter. The petitioner asserts that the Ministry of Industry failed to resolve the matter contrary to its assurance, promise and representation and its obligation arising out of the agreement of sale inspite of petitioner's willingness to perform its own obligation and readiness to pay the last instalment as per terms of the said agreement. The petitioner further states that as it refused to pay illegal demand the Military Estate Officer started certificate case under Public Demands Recovery Act, 1913 for recovery of the demand which on contest failed on 20.8.87 on the ground that claim was not recoverable under the said Act, Annexure-'L'. It is further alleged that having failed to realise the demand the impugned notices were issued. Prior to issuance of these notices the Managing Director of the petitioner company made correspondences with the Adjutant General to resolve the problem which are marked Annexure-'o'(1)'o(2), P & P(1) to this petition but got no favourable reply from that end. On the other hand, Respondent 1 issued impugned notices under Annexure-'A' to hand over 2.26 acres of land by June 22,1988 to the Administrator of Military Lands, Central Circle, Dhaka and Respondent 2. issued notice under section 3 of the Central Government Lands and Building (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance, 1965 Annexure-'B' on 18.6.1988 intimating the petitioner that 2.26 acres of land had already been taken possession by Military Estate Officer and directed the petitioner to vacate 1.02 acres by June 22, 1988 on the ground that the petitioner was in unauthorised occupation in the said land on expiry of lease period. The petitioner states that it had no knowledge earlier about taking over of 2.26 acres of land by Military Estate Officer in which still the petitioner is in physical possession.

3. This Rule is resisted by the respondents 1 and 2 by filing a joint affidavit-in-opposition and by Respondent 3 by a separate affidavit-in-opposition. In short, case of respondent 1 and 2 is, that the lands belong to the Armed Forces of Bangladesh and are managed by the Directorate of Military Lands and Cantonment. As 3.28 acres of land arc required for the purpose of parking space for International Conference Centre and as it was necessary to resume it accordingly, the petitioner was directed to deliver vacant possession of 3.28 acres of land on expiry of extended lease on 31.3.1986 by two notices dated 10.3.86 and 2.4.86. As the petitioner did not comply with the direction of the said notices possession was taken of the vacant land covering 2.26 acres on 7.4.86 by Respondent 2 and on that date physical possession was handed over to Bangladesh Army Notice as per Annexure—'A' was issued on June 15,1988 to the Cantonment Head Quarter to hand over the vacant possession of the said 2.26 acres in their possession by 22.6.88 to the respondent 2 so that delivery of possession of that land may be made to the Ministry of Public Works. As the plants, machineries and structures situate on the rest 1.02 acres of land the possession thereof could not be taken over. To resume the said land Respondent 2 issued notice on 18.6.88, Annexure-'B' to the petition to deliver vacant possession to him by June 22,1988. There notices were issued on expiry of extension of lease on 31st March, 1986. The respondents also denied the statement of the petitioner that it was in possession of entire 3.38 acres of land. The lease to M/s. Allenberry and Co. was sanctioned by the Government of Pakistan under Memo. No. 7/M/51/891-L/D-5/59, Annexure-1, issued by the Director, Military Lands and Cantonments on 27th November, 1959 covering an area of 12.50 acres which, however, subsequently was reduced to 7.93 acres by the Ministry of Defence by Memo. No. 18/285/L/SO(A)/63/1178/D-5/69. Annexure-2 on 3rd May, 1969. And lease to M/s. Durms Metal Ltd. was granted for 20 years with effect from April, 1963. After emergence of Bangladesh in pursuance to the decision of the Government on 9.8.1976 out of 7.93 acres of land 4.65 acres was resumed for Bangladesh Air Force. Thereafter, a new agreement, Annexure-E, was executed between the President of Bangladesh and the M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. on July 13, 1977 for lease of 3.28 acres of land for 20 years with effect from 1.4.63 to 31.8.83. The respondents state that M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. only had lease-hold interest in the land for a limited period M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. was declared as an abandoned industry under President's Order No.16 of 1972. But on subsequent decision of the Government to disinvest the said industrial undertaking notices dated 21.4.76 was published in "The Dainik Bangla" for sale of the unit. The Respondent 2 in view of the said notice brought the matter to the notice of Respondent 1. Thereafter, the Ministry of Defence by letter dated 12.5.76, Annexure-4, requested the Ministry of Industry not to take any step in respect of Military land leased out to M/s. Drums Metal ltd. Respondents state that the petitioner has no enforceable contractual right arising out of the tender for sale of the unit so far as it relates to the land in question. Respondents further state that the petitioner had full knowledge on 17.8.1976 that the land belong to the Ministry of Defence and he has entered into agreement for sale of industrial unit and took over the lease-hold interest for a limited period and as such question of sale of 3.28 acres of Military land does not arise. They further state that the petitioner had full knowledge about the character of land when it purchased tender document with "enterprise profile". And under Annexure-'D' no right, title and interest accrued to the petitioner in respect of the land and the lease having had expired on March 31, 1983 Respondent 2 had the legal sanction to issue the impugned notices. The respondents also categorically deny the statement of the petitioner that at the time of advertisement the respondents gave an impression that the lands absolutely belonged to M/s. Drum Metals Factory. The Respondents further state that the petitioner cannot acquire the land in excess of the right, title and interest of the M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. They denied the statements of the petitioner that the President and Chief Martial Law Administrator on 16.2.84 extended the lease for 5 years from 31.3.83. Rather the office of the Commander-in-Chief merely recommended for extension of lease for 5 years by memo dated February 16, 1984, Annexure-5. The Respondents further denied that truth of the allegation that the premium and rent are arbitrarily fixed and that it was malafide and states that the same was assessed by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka at the prevailing market price. The Ministry of Industry by a letter dated 7.3.83 requested the Secretary, Ministry of Defence to extend the lease of 3.20 acres of land for 20 years with effect from 1.4.83 which was sent to the Commander of Services who, however, recommended for renewal of lease for a further period of 5 years on conditions of resumption of land by the Military Land and Cantonment Directorate after expiry of the extended period and to shift the Drum Metals Factory to Industrial Area. Accordingly, the petitioner was advised to submit a proposal in Schedule-5 of the Cantonment Land Administration Rules for lease of 3.28 acres of land for 5 years with effect from 1.4.83 by a letter dated April 8, 1984, Annexure-6, addressed to the Managing Director of the petitioner Company. But the petitioner refused to accept said terms and insisted on extension for further period of 20 years. On 17.9.85 the Chief Martial Law Administrator, Secretariat communicated to the Respondent 1 that the lease may be extended upto 31.3.86 and Tk. 1,92,79,717.60 as assessed as premium and rent on the basis of current valuation of the land supplied by the Deputy Commissioner Dhaka for the extended period of lease under the Cantonment Land Administration Rules, 1937 and the petitioner was to pay the premium and rent for such period. But the petitioner did not pay the said amount which was condition precedent for renewal of lease upto 31.3.1986 and as such no lease deed for the extended period could be executed and on expiry of the lease period the petitioner is found to be in unauthorised possession of 1.02 acres of land. Annexure 13, 14, 16, 17 are the documents showing resumption of 2.26 acres of land and taking over the same. The respondents denied the statement of the petitioner the Government made representation to the petitioner that the title in the land would be transferred to the petitioner. Memorandum dated 18.10.86 is merely recommendatory one and does not create any right, title and interest in favour of the petitioner in the land. It is further stated that physical possession has already been handed over to the Bangladesh Army on 7.4.86 and the plants, machineries and structure are situated on the rest 1.02 acres. As the possession was already taken over the Respondent 1 by a letter dated 15.6.88, Annexure-A, requested Quarter Master General to hand over the possession of the vacant land to the Respondent 2 by 22.6.1988 for subsequent transfer to the Ministry of Public Works for necessary development for parking space and the remaining 1.02 acres of land which was under unauthorised occupation of the petitioner, the Respondent 2 issued the notice dated 18.6.88 legally for taking vacant possession.

4. The Respondent 3 denied the statement of the petitioner that Respondent 3 gave an impression that said land was absolutely held by M/s. Drums Metal Limited. The further case of Respondent 3 was that as the petitioner as a prospective bidder procured the application form, terms of bidding and a printed "enterprise profile" Annexure-1-B, containing the particulars and details of enterprise wherein it was specifically stated that the lease deed for 20 years which was available with them was to expire in 1984. It further states that on 19.5.77 the Chairman, Working Group on Disinvestment held a meeting for negotiation to increase the price quoted during the bid as it was low and the petitioner attended the meeting and raised his offer to Tk. 91 lacs from Tk. 76 lacs and during negotiation the petitioner again posted with the fact that the interest in the land was lease-hold right. The minutes of the said meeting Annexure-VII was also signed by the Managing Director of the petitioner company with the knowledge about the nature of the land whereupon the factory situates as there is reference in the minute that lease will expire in 1983. Respondent 3 also denied the truth of the statement made in paragraph No. 8 of the petition and also denied the statement of the petitioner that by issuing the letter of intent respondent proposed to sell title in the land. On the other hand, it is slated that by accepting the terms of letter of intent the petitioner excepted the legal position that he could not acquire any title in the land and is estopped from claiming any title in the land. As the petitioner failed to pay the installment the Respondent 3 could not execute the sale deed and the petitioner acquired only the plants and machineries of the unit and lease-hold interest in the land for the unexpired period of lease. The Government also did not make any representation as alleged in the petition in paragraph 15 and there is no question of any estoppel against the Government. The Respondent 3 states that it made efforts for extension of lease for a further period of 20 years not out of any legal obligation but only to resolve the problem and the recommendation of Respondent 3 does not create any right in favour of the petitioner in order to get such extension of the period of lease. Respondent 3 emphatically states that it was deliberate misrepresentation on the part of the petitioner that the Respondent 3 represented that the land was offered for sale and the Government intended to sell the land to the petitioner. Respondent 3 also states that the Government is not estopped from resuming possession of the land after expiry of the lease on 31st March, 1986. It further asserts that the petitioner has been approaching various offices in the Ministry of Defence for renewal of lease which conclusively shows that he was fully aware that the lands underneath the Factory was lease-hold interest of M/s Drums Metal Ltd. Thus, Respondent 3 states that as no right accrued to the petitioner under agreements, Annexure-D, the petition under Article 102 is not maintainable.

5. The petitioner also filed affidavit-in-reply. In substance in reply the petitioner reiterated the statements and submission made in the petition itself. So we do not propose to narrate the same to burden the judgment any further.

<u>6. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed extraneously urgued that in view of the agreement for sale of M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. with its assets and liabilities including 3.28 acres of land and the petitioner having had paid huge amount of money to the Commercial Bank in liquidation of debt of the company it has acquired a right to use and occupy the said land and as the petitioner is willing to fulfill its obligation under the agreement, the impugned notices issued have been issued without lawful authority and are of no legal effect. He contends that in view of the agreement the petitioner was not a lessee, nor a purchaser or an unauthorized occupant but he has been in possession of the land on the strength of the aforesaid agreement and his legal right to continue to possess the said land cannot be invaded by an illegal invasion by issuance of the impugned notices. He contends that the Annexure-D is to be read as a whole to discover intention of the parties from the expression they have used in the document itself. Mr. Ahmed referred us to Rule 1 from Chapter 3 of Odger's " Construction of Deeds and Statutes, 5th Edn." wherein it has been stated that the meaning of the document or of a particular part of it is to be sought for in the document itself. Mr. Addl. Attorney-General does not dispute the above Rule of construction. But he refers us to a passage from the decision of House of Lords in the case of Butterley Co. Ltd. Vs. New Hucknal Colliery Co. Ltd. reported in (1910) AC 381 wherein it has been observed "In construing a document in all cases the object is to see what is the intention expressed by the words used. But from the imperfection of language it is impossible to know what that intention is without inquiring further, and seeing what the circumstances were with reference to which the words were used and what was the object appearing from those circumstances which the person using them had in view, for the meaning of words varies according to the circumstances with respect to which they were used." Inviting our attention to the above observation the learned Addl, Attorney-General contends that in the instant case mere reading of the Agreement of sale is not enough to discover the intention of the parties. He says that intention of the Government was to disinvest the industrial unit which was placed under the Ministry of Industries although the Ministry of Industries was aware that the unit was set up on a lease-hold land which belongs to the Ministry of Defence and from "Enterprise profile" the petitioner also was able to gather for what purpose the agreement for sale was executed. On facts and attending circumstance of the instant case we are of the opinion that from reading the Agreement as a whole the intention of the parties cannot be discovered and in order to do so the circumstances under which the said Agreement was executed has to be taken into consideration. Looking from this angle we hold that although the Agreement was for sale the object for executing the agreement was to sell the industrial undertaking which was an abandoned property and not the land underneath it which belonged to the Ministry of Defence and was not and could not be declared as abandoned land under PO 16 of 1972.</u>

7. Mr. Ahmed submits that on representation of the Government through Respondent 3 the petitioner has acquired an 'indefeasible right' to use and occupy the land in that on such representation and assurance as reflected in Annexure D the petitioner has invested huge amount of money to its great detriment and as such the respondents are estopped from denying the right of the petitioner to use and occupy the land. In continuation of his argument Mr. Ahmed urged before us that as the deed of agreement was executed on behalf of the President by the Ministry of Industries it was responsibility of the Government to act pursuant to the terms as contained in the said agreement of sale. In support of his contentions Mr. Ahmed relied on a number of decisions including the decision in the case of A.K. Thangadurai and others Vs. District Forest Officer, Madura and others, 1985 Mad. 104, the case of Collector of Customs, Chittagong and others. Vs. A. Hannan. 42 DLR (AD) 167, Secretary, Ministry of Industries Vs. Nationalised Industries Textile Mills Corporation 1981 BLD (AD) 91, Sharpping Matshajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh and others 1987 BLD (AD) 106, M/s. Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh and others, 1979 (SC) 621, the case of Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions, (1948) 2 All E.R 767 and the case of State of U.P. Vs. Zahoor Ahmed and others, AIR 1973 (SC) 2520.

8. The learned Addl. Attorney-General repelled the contention of the petitioner saying that the theory of promissory estoppel has no role to play in the instant case. He cites the decision in the cases of M/s. fit Ram Shiv Kumar and others Vs. The State of Haryana and another, 1980 (SC) 1285, the case of Federal Crop Insurance Corporation Vs. A.A. Merril and N.D. Merril, 332 US 379, Howell Vs. Falmouth Boat Construction Co. Ltd. (1951) A.C. 837, Excise Commissioner U.P. Allahabad Vs. Ram Kumar, (1976) (supp) SCR 532.

9. Now we are required to examine whether the Government is estopped to deny the right of the petitioner to occupy the land on the facts of the instant case on the doctrine of promissory estoppel as contended at the Bar. This leads us to examine then authorities cited by Mr. Ahmed and the learned Addl. Attorney-General. In A.K. Thangadurai the State Government leased out forest land for cardamom cultivation to private individuals who applied for renewal of lease on payment of renewal fee and premium as demanded and were in possession of lease-hold land and incurred substantial expenses for improving the land. Long thereafter on 9.2.1979 the State Government issued GO No. Ms. 84 Forest & Fisheries and GO No. Ms. 1220 on 7.11.79 adopting the policy that lease of two hectares each will be granted for cardamom cultivation to small farmers, tribals, landless poor etc. and in pursuance of the policy the lease of the petitioner was not renewed. The court held, on facts of that case, that although they did not pay the full amount of fee and premium but on the principle of equitable estoppel the Government was resisted to act against the interest of the petitioners in that lessees continued to possess the lease-hold land on the basis of lease but the Department officers who delayed the issue of formal grant of renewal could not take advantage of those GOMs which came into existence long subsequently and say that the petitioners have no right of renewal under the said two Government Orders. In that case there was no lack of power of the State Government to keep its promise. That case rests on different contexts and distinguishable from the facts of the present case. In the present case the petitioner impugner the notices on the ground of lack of authority. On facts as we have stated earlier that the lease subsequently extended by the Chief Martial Law Administrator expired on 31st March, 1986 but action was taken in issuing the impugned notices in 1988 on expiry of the lease-hold interest. On a reference to the material placed by the respondents it also appears that the petitioner was requested to obtain form to apply for extension of lease but the petitioner did not do so on the ground that it was unreasonable to do so on the face of the agreement for sale. The case Collector of Customs Vs. A. Hannan 42 DLR 167, is also distinguishable. The facts of that case was that in 1984 there was acute scarcity of sugar in the country and Government gave concession with regard to customs duty and sales tax which was announced under section 19 of the Customs Act and under section 4(1) of the Sales Tax Ordinance. In that case concessional rate was withdrawn after the importer acted on the basis of earlier concession of custom duty and sales tax granted by the same authorities. And the learned Judges held that the importers having acted upon the assurance given, the Government cannot retrace its step and ask for duty mentioned in the subsequent notification as the Government is estopped to do so on the doctrine of promissory estoppel. We find that the case stands on different footing in that the same authorities which granted the concession subsequently withdrew the same after the importers acted on the basis of earlier concession granted to them for import of sugar so far as the customs duty and sales tax are concerned. And as such the principle laid down therein has little application to the facts of the instant case. In Sharpping case the lease of fishery was for a term of 6 years and the lease was cancelled on the ground for non-payment of installment before expiry of the lease period. But in the instant case there was no occasion to cancel the lease as at the time of issuance of the impugned notices the lease period expired. Instead of cancellation of lease the notices have been issued for taking possession under the Central Government Lands and Building (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance; 1965. Thus, on facts of the instant case the principle laid down in Sharpping case has also no application in this case.

10. In M/s. Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh and others, 1979 (SC) 621. the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India observed : "The true principle of promissory estoppel, therefore, seems to be that one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or affect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not." The aforesaid observation was made by the Supreme Court after reviewing a large number of decisions both Indian and English as well as American jurisdiction. In the said decision the Supreme Court again observed as follows:-

"The courts in America for a long time took the view that the doctrine of promissory estoppel does not apply to the Government but more recently the courts have started retreating from that position to a sounder one, namely, that the doctrine of promissory estoppel may apply to the Government when justice so requires. The second edition of American Jurisprudence brought out in 1966 in paragraph 123 points out that "equitable estoppel will be invoked against the State when justified by the facts", though it does warn that this doctrine "Should not be lightly invoked against the State," Later in the same paragraph it is stated that "as a general rule, the doctrine of estoppel will not be applied against the State in its governmental, public or sovereign capacity", but a qualification is introduced that promissory estoppel may be applied against the State even to its governmental, public or sovereign capacity if "its application is necessary to prevent fraud or manifest injustice."

Mr. Ahmed inviting our attention to the aforesaid passage of the report put emphasis that the doctrine of promissory estoppel has got every manner of application in the instant case. But on a careful reading of the decision we are unable to agree with the learned counsel for the petitioner. The Supreme Court in the aforesaid observation as quoted above also noted the abundant caution given in the American Jurisprudence that the doctrine " should not be lightly invoked against the State" and also stated that the doctrine may be applied against the State even in its governmental, public or sovereign capacity if its application is necessary" to prevent fraud or manifest injustice." In the case before us we do not find any fraud or manifest injustice has been caused by issuing the impugned notices nor do we find that Ministry of Industry ever acted fraudulently in its dealing with the petitioner so far the transfer of the land underneath the factory of M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. is concerned. On the other hand, we, on facts, find that from the side of the Respondent 3 there was offer to obtain forms for extension of lease which the petitioner did not do. Thus, on the facts of the instant case we are of the opinion that the aforesaid observation made by the Supreme Court rather helps the respondents inasmuch as it has said that equitable estoppel will be invoked against the State when justifying by facts and should not be lightly invoked against the State in its governmental, public or sovereign capacity unless the application of the doctrine is necessary to prevent fraud or manifest injustice. In this case there being no fraud or manifest injustice done to the petitioner the doctrine should not be invoked against the respondents.

11. The decision made in the case of Robertson V. Minister of Pensions, (1948) 2 All E.R. 767 relied upon by Mr. Ahmed was given with reference to different context the facts of which are distinguishable from the facts in the instant case before us. In Robertson in December, 1939 the claimant was injured in an accident while on military service, and on examination by a medical board, found unfit for general service, and graded in Category B. In March, 1941, he wrote to War Office, requesting that the question of attributability in regard to the disability should be settled. The War Office without consulting the Minister of Pensions replied that the claimant's disability had been accepted as attributable to military service. On the faith of that assurance the claimant took no steps to obtain independent medical opinion or to secure possession of X-ray plates relating to his accident. In the case the question fell for consideration before the King's Bench Division as to whether the Crown was bound by the letter of the War Office, an agent of the Crown and whether the assurance contained in the letter from the War Office was binding on the Minister of Pensions. The learned Judge held that the letter from the War Office was on the face of it an authoritative decision intended to be binding and to be acted on, and the fact that the claimant had, as a result of that letter, forborne from getting a medical opinion was sufficient to have made the letter binding. It further held that the letter being clear and explicit the doctrine of executive necessity could not be implied therein, so as to entitle the Crown to revoke the decision without cause. According to our opinion, the principle laid down therein equally has application in the facts of the present case inasmuch as we do not find that the Ministry of Defence gave any assurance to transfer the land nor the Ministry of Industry gave such assurance. On facts we find that the impugned notices were issued after expiry of the lease period.

12. In M/s. Jit Ram Shiv Kumar and others, relied upon by the learned Additional Attorney-General, the fact is that the Municipal Committee of Bahadurgarh established Mandi Fateh with a view to improve trade in the areas. The Committee decided that the purchasers of the plots in the Mandi would be exempted from payment of octroi duty on the goods imported within the Mandi and the Mandi shall remain immune from payment of octroi duty forever and on 2.3.84 by resolution it took a decision that Mandi will remain free from octroi duty according to proclamation relating to sale of plots which was confirmed by the Punjab State. But later on 8.5.84 it resolved that octroi duty should also be levied on the goods imported into Fateh Mandi but acting under section 236 of the Punjab Municipal Act the Punjab Government annulled the said resolution. Again the Municipal Committee passed a resolution on 21.7.1985 and requested the Government to cancel resolution dated 2.3.84 and the State of Haryana, which came into existence on 1.11.1964 under Punjab Re-organisation Act, approved the resolution of the Municipal Committee dated 21.7. 1965 by its memo dated 30.10.1967 and cancelled resolution of date 2.3.84. Thereafter, the Municipal Committee started charging octroi duty on the goods imported into the Mandi. The appellants impugned in Writ Petitions before the High Court the order dated 21.7.65 and the order dated 30.10.67 as illegal, ultra vires and without jurisdiction and pleaded that both the Municipal Committee and State Government are estopped to charge octroi duty on the doctrine of promissory estoppel. A Full Bench of the High Court rejected the petitions leading to filing appeals before the Supreme Court of India by the petitioners. The question that arose for consideration before the Supreme Court was whether the proclamation of sale which notified that there would be no octroi levy in the Mandi relying on which the petitioners bid at auction would estop the Municipality on the doctrine of promissory estoppel from recommending to the Government to cancel the resolution No.1 dated 2.3.1954 and the government levying octroi duty under section 61 of the Punjab Municipalities Act. The learned judges of the Supreme Court after reviewing a large number of its decisions as well as of English and American jurisdiction expressed their view about applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel. The Supreme Court following its earlier decision in the case of Excise Commissioner UP Allahabad Vs. Ram Kumar (1976) Suppl SCR 532 wherein it was held that "it is now well settled by a catena of decisions that "there can be no question of estoppel against the Government on exercise of its legislative, sovereign or executive powers" came to the conclusion that the principle of estoppel is not available against the Government in exercise of legislative, sovereign or executive power. Their Lordships while discussing the doctrine of promissory estoppel as propounded by Denning, J. in the Central London Property Trust Vs. High Tress House Ltd. (1956)1All ER 256 commented that the " doctrine of promissory estoppel burst into sudden blaze in 1946 when Denning, J. sitting in the Court of King's Bench delivered the judgment ..... .''Their Lordships also referred to the judgment of Lord Denning, J. in Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions case. The correctness of the case of Robertson came up for consideration before the House of Lords in Howell Vs. Falmouth Boat Construction Co Ltd. Lord Simonds commented on the view taken by Denning, J. in the Robertson case as" My Lords, I know of no such principle in our law nor any authority". The Supreme Court of India further held at page 1298 of the report that the decisions of the English courts did. not accept the view of Denning, J. in Robertson case. The House of Lords in Howell's case disagreed with the view of Lord Denning, J. holding that there could not be an estoppel against express provisions of the law nor could the State by its action waive its rights to exercise powers entrusted to it for the public good. 'The view taken in Howell's case was accepted as correct by the Supreme Court of India in Excise Commissioners UP Allahabad. The facts in the case of Excise Commissioner was that the respondents before the Supreme Court were highest bidder in auction for exclusive manufacture and selling of liquor in the State of UP Before holding the auction, the rates of excise duty and prices of country liquor and the conditions of licence were announced but no announcement was made as to whether the exemption from sales tax in respect of sale of country liquor granted by the notification dated 6.4.1959 was or was not likely to be withdrawn. After the licences were granted the government of UP issued a notification under sections 31 and 4 of UP Sales Tax Act. 1948, superseding the earlier notification by which payment of the sales tax was exempted, imposing sales tax on the turnover in respect of country liquor. The said notification was challenged on the ground that the State Government did not announce at the time of the earlier auction that the earlier notification was likely to be withdrawn. The Supreme Court held that the State Government is not estopped or precluded from subjecting the sales of liquor to tax if it felt impelled to do so in the interest of revenue of the State. On facts, the cases before the Supreme Court of India were stronger than the present case before us inasmuch as in the instant case we could not find any assurasnce, promise, and impression given to the petitioner for sale of land underneath M/s. Drum Metal Ltd. In M/s. Jit Ram the Supreme Court of India also referred to the decision in the case of Motilal Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. and observed "The doctrine cannot be invoked for preventing the Government from acting in discharge of his duty under the law. The Government would not be bound by the acts of its officers and agents, who act beyond the scope of their authority. A person dealing as an agent of the Government must be held to have noticed all the limitations of his authority."

13. In the case of Federal Crop Insurance Corporation Vs. A.A. Merrill and N.D. Merrill, (332 US 380-388) relied upon by the learned Additional Attorney-General it was observed:

"Whatever the form in which the Government functions, anyone entering into an arrangement with the Government takes the risk of having accurately ascertained that he who purports to act for the Government stays within the bounds of his authority."

Therefore, in the light of the aforesaid observations of the Supreme Court of the United States and the Supreme Court of India we are of the opinion that even the Ministry of Industry giving assurance as alleged by the petitioner it was the duty of the petitioner to ascertain as to whether the Ministry of Industry acted for the Government within its bounds of authority. In the case before us on facts it has conclusively been proved that the lands underneath M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. belongs to Ministry of Defence and the petitioner had knowledge about it from Annexure-E. Mr. Ahmed contended that both the Ministries of the Defence and the Industry represent the Government and as such it was the duty of the Ministry of Defence to give effect to the agreement for sale (Annexure-D) We are afraid to accept this contention not only in view of the observations of the Supreme Court of United States and Supreme Court of India but as well as on the ground that the impugned notices were issued on expiry of the lease period. Although on facts in Federal Crop Insurance Corporation stands on a much stronger footing yet court made the aforesaid observation. As Supreme Court of India in M/s. Jit Shiv Kumar has already considered Howell's case to which we have already referred we need not further discuss the same except that therein it was held that the government officer in his dealings with any subject may have assumed an authority, which he did not possess, to grant a licence, does not debar the Crown from enforcing a statutory prohibition. The question raised before us as to whether the Annexure 'A' and 'B' were issued without any lawful authority on facts, we find, that Ministry of Industry acquired under P.O. 16n2 the industrial undertaking of M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. who acquired the right, title and interest of Allenberry & Co. Thus, in our opinion although the Ministry of Industry entered into an agreement and made certain correspondence with the Ministry of Defence in order to extend the period of lease that cannot be pleaded as promise or representation or an impression given to the petitioner to sell the land. From "Enterprise Profile" Annexure-l-B to the affidavit-in-opposition of the Respondent 3 the petitioner was sufficiently posted with the knowledge that the lease was for 20 years to expire in 1984. Thus, it cannot be said that the petitioner had no knowledge about the character of the land and the petitioner acted on the assurance, representation or impression given to it by the Respondent 3 that M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. had absolute title in the land. The lease having had expired prior to the issuance of notices the petitioners were served with the impugned notices to deliver possession in favour of the respondents by Annexure-'A' &'B' and as such we do not find that there was want of jurisdiction on the part of Respondents 1 and 2 to issue such notices. Second so far as the action of the Respondent 3 is concerned can it be said that it is bound by representation made by it as is now urged? It requires seeing that for what purpose on the representation the petitioner invested the huge money. The Annexure-'D' is subsequent to obtaining the information for holding the bid and the information contained in the "Enterprise Profile" is itself sufficient to indicate that the land belonged to Ministry of Defence. In view of our discussion hereinbefore on doctrine of promissory estoppel taking into consideration the principle laid down therein we have no hesitation to say that agreement executed by the Ministry of Industry cannot bind the Government on the doctrine of promissory estoppel more so when the petitioner had knowledge that the said belonged to Ministry of Defence.

14. The learned Additional Attorney-General also with reference to Articles 56(3), 56(5) and 145 (1) of the Constitution contends that all executive action of the Government shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President under Article 56 (3) and under Article 56(5) the President is authorised to make rules for allocation and transaction of the business of the Government. And under Article 145(1) all contracts and deeds made in exercise of the executed authority of the Republic shall be expressed to be made by the President by such person and in such manner as he may direct or authorise. He also placed before us the Rules of Business, 1975 (revised up to 1989). Hecantends that the assurance given by the Ministry of Industry as alleged contravened Article 56(5) and the Rules of Business in that according to Rule 3(ii) of the Rules the business of the Government shall be distributed among the Ministries as indicated in Schedule-I to the Rules. Under Schedule-l the Military Lands and Cantonments were allocated to the Ministry of Defence which is to deal with the same. He also refers us to Annexure- 'E' which was executed by the Military Estate Officer. According to Rule 31 of the Cantonment Lands Administration Rules, 1937, he continues to say, that a lease for a building site for a period not exceeding 30 years or a lease in perpetuity, may be granted by the Military Estates ' Officer in the forms prescribed in Schedule -IX for special reasons where such a course appear to be advantageous to the Government He also refers us to Rule 15 of the said Rules to show that sale of Military and Cantonment Land for any purpose without definite orders of the Government is prohibited. And from Annexure-I, it appears that the Central Government accorded sanction to lease of 12.50 acres of land at Tejgaon, Dhaka Cantonment to M/s. Allenberry Co. Ltd. for 30 years with effect from April 1,1953 and it appears that the lease was executed in form prescribed in Schedule -IX as per Rule 31(1). Thus, the learned Additional Attorney-General contends that there is no scope to say that the land underneath the Industrial Unit of M/s. Drums Metal Ltd. does not belong to the Ministry of Defence. Therefore, in view of our above discussions on the decision cited at the Bar and in view of the provisions of Articles 56(3), 56(5) and 145(1) of the Constitution and the aforesaid Rules of Business our irresistible conclusion is that the petitioner cannot on the strength of Annexure-'D' acquire any right in the land on the alleged assurance of Respondent 3, as we find the Respondent 3 did not give any assurance, promise or impression that Annexure- 'D' was executed for sale of the land. Even assuming that Respondent 3 made such representation that will not at all bind the Government in that such assurance even if given it is beyond the limits of the authority of Respondent 3 and as such the Government is not estopped on the doctrine of promissory estoppel from issuing the impugned notices and the contention of Mr. Ahmed that 'Ext. D will float as oil over the vast sheet of water, the document produced by the respondents does not impress us.

<u>15. The learned Additional Attorney-General raised the question of maintainability of the rule on the ground of want of legal right. We have already held that on expiry of the period of lease-hold interest the petitioner had no legal right to maintain the Writ Petition in that under Annexure-'D' to the petition no right accrued to the petitioner in the land. We find that as the petitioner was an unauthorised occupant of the land it is not entitled to have a declaration as sought for in this Writ Petition. We are of the opinion that where a petitioner has no legal right he cannot maintain an application under Article 102 of the Constitution. We find support from the case of Taleakhal Progressive Fishermen's Cooperative Society Ltd. VS. Bangladesh and others, 1981 B.L.D. (AD) 103. The learned Addl. Attorney-General also referred us to the case of Dr. Umakant Saran Vs. State of Bihar and others to argue that an aggrieved party must have a legal right and the authority must have legal duty to entitle the party to obtain relief in Writ jurisdiction. In Umakant the learned Judges of the Supreme Court of India held that in order to issue mandamus to compel the authority to do something it must be shown that the statute imposes a legal duty and the aggrieved party had a legal right under the statute to enforce its performance. Annexure- 'D' upon which the contention of the petitioner was made that it had indefeasible right in the land and as such the notices- Annexure-A' and 'B' have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect has no leg to stand. In Radha Krish Agarwal Vs. State of Bihar, 1977 (SC) 1496 Beg, C.J. observed:</u>

<u>"We do not think that any of these cases could assist the appellants or is at all relevant. None of these cases lays down that, when the State or its officers support to operate within the contractual field and the only grievance of the citizen could be that contract between the parties is broken by the action complained of, the appropriate remedy is by way of a petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution and not an ordinary suit. There is a formidable array of authority against any such a proposition."</u>

<u>The learned Chief Justice in his judgment also referred to the case of Lekhraj Satramdas -Vs- M. M. Shah 1966 (SC) 334 wherein it has been held that duty or obligation falling upon a public servant out of a contract entered into by him as such public servant cannot be enforced by the machinery of a writ under Art. 226 of the Constitution. The learned C.J. also referred the case of Bachhanidhi Rath V. State of Orissa, 1972 (SC) 843 wherein the Supreme Court of India declared:</u>

<u>If a right is claimed in terms of a contract such a right cannot be enforced in a writ petition.</u>

<u>In view of the facts of this case before us we are also of the opinion that the petitioner is not entitled to invoke Article 102 of our Constitution on the ground of breach of terms of contract as contained in clause V of the deed of agreement for sale (Annexure-D) as contended by Mr. Ahmed. Under Article 102 of the Constitution this court only can declare that an act done by person in connection with the affairs of the Republic has been done without jurisdiction or malafide or refrain from doing the act which he is required to do so under a law the High Court can declare either the act done without jurisdiction or can issue writ of mandamus upon that person to do the act which he refrained from doing but this court under Article 102 cannot give order for enforcement of a right but a violation of a legal right by an authority can be declared without jurisdiction. We are also of the view if there is a breach of any terms of the agreement for sale as contained in Annexure-D the remedy lies in a properly constituted suit for damages against the party to such contract for the breach of any ten.</u>

16. Mr. Ahmed further argued that by Annexure-'A' and 'B' the rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 40 and 42 of the Constitution have been violated and as such the impugned notices have been made without any lawful authority and are of no legal effect On reference to these Articles we do not find any force in this contention in view of the facts and circumstances of the instant case.

17. So far as the contention of the petitioner regarding malafide action in issuing the impugned notices are concerned we do not find any malafide on the part of the authority as because it was not done during the period of lease-hold interest which expired in 1986. Moreover, it is found that the petitioner was asked for taking out forms for the purpose of extension of lease which it did not can we say in consideration of these facts that there is any malafide on the respondents in issuing notices? Our answer is in the negative.

For the above discussion, the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Appellate decree No. 803 of 1968.
lawyer:
D.M. Rahman, Advocate ------ For the Appellant. 
Md. Moslemuddin Sarker and Kh. Saiful Haque Advocate ------ For the Respondent Nos. 1 (1) to 1 (8).
parties:
Gaher Ali Mollah ------ Appellant. 
vs.
Hajera Khatun & ors ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal arises out of the suit being O.C. Suit No. 26 of 1966 for cancellation of the sale deed executed by Plaintiff-appellant Rangbi Bewa in favour of defendant-respondent No. 1 Abed Ali. 

2. Short facts giving rise to this appeal may briefly be stated thus. Plaintiff is a Pardanshin and illiterate village woman aged about 70 years old and often suffers from various ailments like Asthma and cough. Defendant-respondent vendee of the impugned sale deed (Ext. 1) is the plaintiffs husband's sister's son. On 13th Chaitra, 1372 B.S. plaintiff went to defendant No. 1's house and requested him to make arrangement for her medical treatment and accordingly defendant-respondent No. 1 agreed to make arrangement for her medical treatment and persuaded her to accompany him to Pabna Town for medical treatment. He also told her that he would arrange her admission into Pabna Hospital. Accordingly she accompanied respondent No. 1 to Pabna on 25th Chaitra, 1372 B.S. On reaching Pabna respondent No. 1 gave out that her thumb impression would be required to get her admitted into hospital and on such representation plaintiff-appellant put her thumb impression on some blank papers. Thereafter defendant respondent came back with plaintiff-appellant to Village with a bottle of medicine and told her that admission to hospital was not possible. Subsequently towards the end of Chaitra, 1372 B.S plaintiffs brother, with whom plaintiff resides after the death of her husband, came to know that a fraudulent kabala was created by defendant No. 1 with the help of the blank stamp papers on which appellant's thumb impression was taken on fraudulent misrepresentation of fact. Thereafter a certified copy of the said sale deed was taken from the Sub-Registrar's Office, Pabna by plaintiffs brother and he learnt that a sale deed was created in respect of the suit land by taking risotto deceitful means. In fact the sale deed in question was procured by practicing fraud on plaintiff appellant in collusion with deed writer and others. In fact there was no contract for sale and no consideration was paid to the plaintiff-appellant Plaintiff is an old, illiterate, pardanshin village woman and she did not have any independent and disinterested advice prior to the execution and registration of the impugned sale deed. In fact the sale deed in question is tainted with fraud and as such liable to be cancelled. 

3. Defendant-respondent No. 1 alone contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all material allegations made in the plaint. Defence version, in. short, is that suit is not maintainable in present form that the suit was not instituted by the plaintiff-appellant that plaintiff-appellant was in need of money, so she proposed to sell the suit land and the talk of sale was liaised with respondent No.1 and Taka 1,000/- was settled as price of the disputed land. Plaintiff-appellant transferred disputed land by registered sale deed for valuable consideration and the contents of the sale deed was read over to her and she having fully understood the contents of the sale deed executed it on receipt of the consideration money. It is further stated in the written statement that plaintiffs brother Afsaruddin obtained a sale deed from plaintiff in respect of other land by fraudulent means and they tried to resist defendant-respondent from purchasing the suit land but failed and that in order to defeat the right of pre-emption of defendant respondent the suit has been instituted on false allegation in the name of the plaintiff-appellant. In these circumstances the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence led by both the parties came to the finding that sale deed in question was obtained by defendant respondent fraudulently and collusively without giving any chance to plaintiff-appellant to know the true import of the transaction and that she did not get independent and disinterested advice in the matter and on this finding the learned Munsif held the impugned sale deed as void, inoperative and accordingly decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by the decision of the trial court, defendant-respondent preferred appeal before the District Judge, Pabna and the appeal was heard by the Learned Subordinate Judge, Pabna. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record differed with the finding of the trial Court and held that sale deed in question is a valid and bonafide document for valuable consideration and that plaintiff-appellant being fully aware of the contents of sale deed, executed it voluntarily on receipt of consideration money. He further held that prior to execution and registration of the impugned sale deed plaintiff-appellant got independent and disinterested advice in the matter and on this finding he allowed the appeal reversing the decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit. 

5. The learned Advocate for the appellant has urged that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in not adverting to the reason assigned by the trial court in support of his finding that the learned appellate court wrongly held that onus lies on the plaintiff-appellant to prove that she received independent advice before execution and registration of the impugned sale deed and that he also erred in fact in holding that deed was read over and explained to the plaintiff-appellant who being conversant with import of the transaction voluntarily executed the sale deed in question on receipt of consideration. It is further urged by the learned Advocate for plaintiff appellant that impugned sale deed was obtained by practising fraud on old pardanshin woman like plaintiff-appellant and that onus in this regard was wrongly placed on plaintiff-appellant. 

6. In reply to this contention the learned Advocate for the respondent relying very much on the judgment of the appellate court submitted that the learned appellate court made a threadbare discussion of the evidence on record and correctly held that no fraudulent means was resorted to in the matter of obtaining the impugned sale deed from the plaintiff-appellant and that the appellant got independent advice from her close relation D.W. 4 Abdul Karim and she having fully understood contents of the deed executted it by putting her left thumb impression voluntarily.

7. I have been taken through the judgment pronounced by both the courts below as well as evidence on record. Admittedly plaintiff-appellant Rangbi Bibi is illiterate, ignorant, weak and pardanshin village woman aged about 80 years. She acquired title to the suitland on the basis of deed of gift from her husband. It was the definite case of the plaintiff appellant although that she was suffering from asthma and Cough and the respondent Abed Ali Sarder who happened to be the plaintiff-respondent's sister's husband's son took her to Pabna Town on her request to get her medically treateel there and having reached town defendant-respondent obtained her L.T.I. on a Blank Sheet of paper on misrcprcscntation of fact that her left thumb impression would be required to get her admitted into the hospital and this manner the sale deed in question ext. l was procured by practising fraud on her and on rnisrcsprescntation of fact. It is also admitted that after the death of her husband plaintiff-appellant has been living with her brother. The trial court having scrutinised the evidence carefully, held that independent and disinterested advice was not made available to her the execution and registration of the impugned deed exbt. 1 and this protection she is entitled to have and since no evidence was led by the defence side to show that such advice plaintiff-appellant got the matter prior to the execution of the sale deed, it is liable to be cancelled. The learned appellate Court did not consider this aspect of this case from correct stand point. There is no endorsement in the impugned sale deed Exbt. 1 to the effect that its contents were read over to the plaintiff-appellant. D.W. Abed Ali Mridha is the scribe of the disputed sale deed. He stated in his evidence that sometime endorsement in a deed is not appended but invariably contents of a deed is read over to the executant. He fraudulent means was resorted to in the matter of obtaining the impugned sale deed from the plaintiff-appellant and that the appellant got independent advice from her close relation D.WA Abdul Karim and she having fully understood contents of the deed executed it by putting her left thumb impression voluntarily, asserts in his evidence that impugned sale deed Ext. 1 was read over to plaintiff-appellant and that he saw passing of consideration to the tune of Taka 1,000-. Evidence of this witness was not accepted by the trial court with easy mind inasmuch as he was of the pinion that scribe Abed Ali and defendant No. 1 were very thick and thin with each other. D.W. 5 Abed Ali has admitted that he knew defendant No.1 from long before and that he wrote many of his deeds previously. Therefore it is evident that defendant- respondent Abed Ali was in full control of the situation obtained at the time of writing of the deed in question and that he being placed in priviliged position was able to divert the course of event to his advantage. It is admitted by scribe Abed Ali (D.W. 5) that he wrote the impugned sale deed with reference to a deed of gift. But he said that it was returned to the executing plaintiff-appellant. But under normal circumstance title deed of the vendor is retained by the vendee, so that in future vendee's title to land is not questioned. In the instant case no plausible explanation has been offered why the deed of gift with reference to which impugned sale deed (Ext. 1) is purported to have been written, was handed over to plaintiff-appellant. D.W. 6 Nuruzzaman and D.W. 7 Abdul Mannan arc said to be the attesting witness to in the impugned sale deed but their evidence do not in any way help to prove execution of sale deed and passing of consideration. D.W. 6 stated in his examination that he simply attested the deed on the request of scribe Abed Ali. D.W. 7 also stated the same fact. He further stated that consideration was not paid in his presence. But according to defence version writing of the impugned sale deed, its execution by sale plaintiff appellant and passing of consideration, all took place simultaneously in a single sitting. Had it been a fact there is no reason why attesting witness (D.W. 6 and 7) did not have occasion to see passing in of consideration money. They did not assert in their evidence that the contents of the deed was read over to plaintiff-appellant in their presence; and that she received independent and disinterested advice from her well wisher before the execution of the deed in question and that they saw plaintiff-appellant to execute the impugned sale deed. The appellate court did not look into the question as to whether independent and in disinterested advice was received by plaintiff at the time of the execution of the impugned sale deed. 

8. In this respect the learned first appellate court placed much reliance on the testimony of D.WA Abdul Karim. Trial Court declined to place reliance on his testimony on the ground that he also joined hand with defendant No.1 in the nefarious activity in the matter of obtaining the impugned sale deed. D.W. 4 Abdul Karim happens to be brother of respondent defendant No.1 who is a vendee to the impugned sale deed. It has been admitted by the respondent- No. 1 Abed Ali that D.W. 4 Abdul Karim and plaintiff-appellant lived at two different villages. He has further admitted that Jalalpur has been mentioned in the impugned sale deed as address of the plaintiff-appellant. D.W. 4 Abdul Karim resides at village Bonagram. No reason has been assigned by the defence side why old and ailing women like plaintiff appellant would come to different village to have a talk of sale of disputed land finalised with respondent defendant No. 1. Even if it is assumed that she went there, she is supposed to be accompanied with her brother with whom she resides. But no evidence has been led to prove that any body on her behalf was present at the time of talk of the alleged sale of the disputed land. This circumstance obviously can not convince the reasonable mind that any talk of alleged sale was held at the house of D.WA Abdul Karim. In fact Abdul Karim and respondent No.1 formed an unholy alliance with defendant respondent No. 1 who brought into existence the impugned sale deed by laking resort of fraudulent means. Trial Court appreciation of evidence in this regard appears to be correct. 

9. It has already been pointed out that the executant of the impugned sale deed Ext. 1 is illiterate pardanshin, weak, old and ignorant village woman. Requirement of law in this regard is that the party who wants to uphold a document against such woman, onus is on him to prove that independent and disinterested advice in the matter was received by her. Merely reading over and explanation of contents of the deed will not meet requirement of law and unless this basic requirement is fulfilled the document executed by illiterate, pardanshin and village woman cannot be held to be valid one apart from the question of fraud and undue influence. 

10. In the case of Nibaran Chandra Mukherji and an. Vs. Nirupama Debi and another reported in 26 C.W.N. 517 Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court held as follows:- 

"That it is well' settled that the Court when called upon to deal with a deed executed by a pardanshin lady must satisfy itself upon the evidence first, that the deed was actually executed by her or by some person duly authored by her with a full understanding of what she was about to do; secondly that she had full knowledge of the nature and effect of the transaction into which she is said to have entered; and thirdly that she had independent disinterested advice in the matter." 

In that case the learned Judges further held in the following words:- 

"Independent and competent advice docs not mean independent and competent approval but signifies at any rate advice removed entirely from suspected atmosphere and conveyed in the clear language of an independent mind, free from taint of interest, to the party acting regarding the precise nature and consequence of the transaction." 

11. Thus it is evident from the decision referred above that the party relying on a document executed by any illiterate, pardanshin village woman must satisfy the court that not only the impugned deed was read over and explained to her but also to prove that she understood the contents and that she got independent and disinterested advice in the matter. 

12. In the instant case the trial court rightly held that execution and registration of the impugned sale deed were procured with undue haste and in an atmosphere not free from suspicion. The trial court found that plaintiff-appellant did not have independent and disinterested advice in the matter of transfer as per sale deed (Ext. 1) and this finding is founded on cogent reasons. Admittedly plaintiff-appellant's brother with whom she resides was not consulted. But the learned appellate Court did not consider this aspect of the matter. He did not advert to the reason assigned by the trial court in support of his finding. 

13. Thus regard being had to he facts and circumstances of the case I am of the opinion that the trial court correctly applied the legal principle and held that the content of the impugned sale deed was not read over and explained to the plaintiff appellant and that she did not get independent and disinterested advice in the matter and consequently deeding cannot be held to be valid document handing against her. 

14. In the result, the appeal is allowed with cost. The judgment and decree of the appellate Court are set aside and those of the trial Court are restored.

Send down the lower court records at an early date. 	

End.

lawyer:
