parties:
Khitindra Chandra Bhattacharya and anr ----- Appellants
Vs. 
Jalada Devi ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 28.8.79 passed by the High Court Division in F.A. No.101 of 1976)
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury J:- This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and decree of the High Court Division in F.A. No. 101 of 1976 dismissing the appeal and affirming the judgment decree passed by the District Judge, Mymensingh in Probate Suit No. 5 of 1976.

2. Facts are as follows: Late Digindra Chandra Bhattacharya the predecessor of the appellants instituted a suit being Probate Suit No. 5 of 1974 for grant of Probate in respect of the last will dated 30.12.62 executed by Kitish Chandra Bhattacharya. In the said will the testator appointed his step-mother Jalada Debi, the respondent in this appeal as the first executor subject to the condition that in case first executrix failed to take Probate the second executor Digindra Chandra Bhattacharya would be entitled to take Probate and became the sole legatee in respect of the properties bequeathed under the said will.

3. Jalada Debi applied for Probate which being contentious was returned to her. She instead of filing a regular suit for grant of Probate started transferring the property under the will. Digindra, the second executor filed a suit for injunction being O.C. Suit No. 66 of 1973 restraining Jalada from the disposing of suit property. In this suit Jalada Debi took the stand that the will in question was a forged and fabricated document. It will be noticed at once that she took a stand which can be termed as approbation. In this back-ground since Jalada refused to take Probate Digindra the second executor filed the Probate suit, being Probate Suit No. 5 of 1974. Thereafter Digindra died and an application for substitution of the heirs of Digindra was filed. The learned' District Judge, vide his order dated 5.4.76. I held that if the executor dies before obtaining Probate it cannot be granted to his heirs. The view was taken that substitution under the provision of the Code of Civil Procedure could not be done in view of section 222 read with section 258, 295 of the Succession Act. In this view of the matter the learned District Judge disposed of the Probate Suit as not been maintainable and also it had abated since the executrix Jalada did not also, come forward for the Probate.

4. An appeal was preferred being F.A. No.101 of 1976 before the High Court Division. The High Court Division took the view that the right of the petitioner under the Will would arise only after the death of Jalada Devi. As to the substitution of the heirs of Digindra the High Court Division considered section 222 of the Succession Act as a bar to substitution of the legal representative of the deceased executor. In this view of the matter it was observed:

'Hence the legal representative of an executor is not entitled to a probate and they cannot maintain an application for probate."

Then the High Court Division mentioned a fact which is highly controversial namely whether Jalada is alive or not. The learned Judges expressed "we have also found earlier that Jalada Devi, the first executor being alive, petitioner Digendra had no interest in the property and as such no locus standi to file an application for probate."

It will be useful to clear up the position as to the question whether Jalada Devi is alive or not. In O.C. Suit No. 71 of 1975 Jalada Devi versus Kitish Chandra, the moot question whether Jalada Devi was alive was considered. The learned Additional District Judge came to the conclusion:

"It may be safely presumed that the plaintiff Jalada Devi is not alive and she died some time in 1382 B.S. Since the heirs of the plaintiff were not brought on record by way of substitution within time and since Jalada Devi was the sole plaintiff the suit abated as a whole".

This order was passed on 8.11.79.

5. A review application was filed under Order 47 read with section 151 C.P.C. which was numbered as Misc. Case No. 29 of 1980 It may be noted that when the order in O.C. Suit No. 71 of 1975 was passed the F. A. No. 101 of 1976 was still pending. Being aggrieved by the order in O.C. Suit No.7 of 1975 the Misc. Case No 29 of 1981 wall filed which, however, was rejected on 20.2.80. Thereafter C.R. No. 37 of 1981 was filed before the District Judge Mymensingh.

In such back-ground the contention was that the heirs of Digindra could not be substituted. The learned Judges of the High Court Division in F.A No 101 of 1916 rejected the prayer for substitution.

<u>6. Leave was granted to consider whether the courts below were justified in rejecting the petition for substitution. The learned Judges had proceeded on the assumption:</u>

<u>"It appears that in terms of the Will the petitioner as second executor was entitled to the property after the death of the first executor, namely Jalada Devi. Hence Jalada Devi being alive the petitioner had no interest to obtain a probate of the Will.”</u>

<u>Section 232 of the Succession Act reads as follows:</u>

<u>"232. Grant of administration to universal or residuary legatees-when. (a) the deceased has made a will, but has not appointed an executor, or</u>

<u>(b) the deceased has appointed as executor who is legally incapable or refuses to act. or who has died before the testator or before he has proved the will, or (c) the executor died after having proved the will, but before he has administered all the estate of the deceased an universal or a residuary legatee may be admitted to prove the will, and letters of administration with the will annexed thereof as may be unadministered."</u>

<u>From the above narration of facts as mentioned above it is clear that Jalada Devi initially intended to take probate but when it was found contentious her application was returned to her. She instead of filing a regular suit started disposing all the properties which necessitated a suit for injunction by Digindra. In that injunction suit Jalada for the first time took the stand that the Will was forged. That amounts to her refusal to act as an executor. In the Will it is mentioned that if Jalada dies then Digiudra will be the second executor. That led Digindra to file the Probate suit because Jalada refused to act. Now the contention whether Jalada is dead or alive has led to another set of litigation being O.C. suit No. 71 of 1975 and by order dated 8.9.71 it was found by the learned Additional District Judge that Jalada is no more alive. Until this order h set aside then position remains that Digindra being the next executor was competent to file the Probate suit but Digihdra also died. His two sons filed application for substitution. This petition was refused by order dated 5.4.76 which led to the F.A. No. 101 of 1976. With respect, the learned Judges of the High Court Division have not correctly approached the facts of the case. In the O.C. Suit No.71 of 1975 it was found that Jalada is no more alive and until this finding is set aside by the superior court no contrary assumption can be made by another court while dealing with another subject matter namely whether the heirs of Digindra could be substituted. Numerous adjournments were taken from this court to thrash out the controversy whether Jalada is dead or alive and the C.R.No.37 of 1981 (arising out of O.C. Suit No. 71 of 1975) is stil pending. The learned Judge in the F. A. had erroneously travelled into the path which had unfortunately led them to a blind alley. The position is that, Jalada is dead or alive, had refused to act on the ground that the will itself was forged one. It need not detain us whether she approbated or reprobated in this matter. The clear position emerges is that she refused to act as executor. Section 232(b) reads as follows:</u>

<u>"the deceased has appointed an executor who is legally incapable or refuses to act, or who has died before the testator or before he has proved the will".</u>

<u>In such case an universal or residuary legatee may be allowed to prove the will and letter of administer that the will annexed may be granted to him. Since Jalada refused to act as executor the petition for Probate by Digindra was competent. The question is when Digindra died, whether his sons could be substituted. The courts below have found section 222 as a bar which reads as under:</u>

<u>"(1) Probate shall be granted only to an executor appointed by the Will. (30) The appointment may be expressed or by necessary implication.</u>

<u>When the first executor refused to act the second executor could legitimately file the petition for probate. The nature of the proceeding in a probate suit may be considered. An executor when applies for a probate of the Will of the deceased testator merely asks the court for order in his favour to the effect that the will is duly proved and to administer the estate of the deceased according to the provision contained in the will. As. executor he has no personal interest in the Estate of the deceased but if he is a legatee under the will then a new dimension is added. The object of the executor is to propound the will of the deceased for the benefit of those who take the interest of the will. Thus the maxim action personalis moritor cum persona has no manner of application in such case. For it is in substance not a personal action. In substance Probate means copy of the will certified under the seal of a Court of competent jurisdiction that a grant of administration to the Esatate of Testator vide the definition of Probate in section 2 of the Succession Act. In the absence of an executor an universal or residuary legatee can apply for letter of administration and what the Court grants in such a case is also a copy of the Will certified under the seal of the Court stating that the will is only duly approved and an authority to administer the estate of the deceased according to the direction. In substance the fact of the grant is more or less same. It is true that an executor gets his preferential right to the grant from nomination in the will. While in the other case the grant is by reason of the Court. In either of the cases purpose of the grant is to administer of the estate of the deceased according to the provision of the will. In the will in question Digindra has been nominated as second executor and if Jalada refuses to act or dies Digindra will take the Probate and the will says “তদাবস্থায় তিনি আমার ত্যাক্ত স্থাবর সম্পত্তি নিবিড় স্বত্ব প্রাপ্ত হইবেন।” In this context the question is whether the heirs of Digindra should be substituted.</u>

<u>8. Apparently there are divergent authorities on this point. In Sarat Chandra Banerjee Vs. Nani Mohan Banerjee, 36 cal. 799 Harrington J. held that on the death of the sole executor pending the hearing of the probate suit, the right to sue does not survive in favour of his legal representatives. It was pointed out in that case that executor's right to probate was a personal right derived not from an order of the court but from appointment made by the testator himself whereas the right to be appointed by the Court to administer the assets of the deceased stands on different footing. This decision was not however, followed by the Calcutta High Court in the subsequent cases. In the case of Haripada Saha and another Vs Gobinda Chandra Saha and ors 51 C W.N 917 the dictum passed in the aforesaid case has somewhat been watered down. In the case of Haripada Saha, Subasini was appointed a sole executrix under the will. She filed an application for probate of the Will and 6 days later she died. Her heirs made an application before the District Delegate praying for permission to continue the proceeding as substituted heirs in place of Subasini and they prayed that letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed may be granted to them. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court considered the objection as technical and observed:</u>

<u>"When in substance, the application for substitution was treated as one for letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed on the basis of the respondents' own rights to the property left by the testator "as heirs of Subasini would, we think, be sacrificing justice to mere technicality.</u>

<u>There is undoubtedly a technical defect, but it is not a defect which has in any way affected the merits of the case of the jurisdiction of the Court".</u>

<u>The Patna High Court, on the other hand, took a firm view. In the case of Mt. Phekni Vs. Mt. Manki, A.I.R.1930 Patna 618 took the view that where the sole legatee under will whose application for grant of letters of administration is rejected appeals from the order, but dies during the pendency of the appeal, the heirs of the sole legatee can be substituted in his place for the purpose of carrying on the litigation and obtaining a final adjudication as to whether the will is genuine or not. It was held in that case that the heirs of the sole legatee were entitled to letters of Administration under section 233 of the Succession Act without any question being raised as to their competency. These divergence rulings were reviewed by a learned Single Judge in the case of Jadeja Pravin-sinhji Vs. Jadeja Mangnisinhji and others A.I.R. 1953 Guzrat 32. It was held that an executor named in the win and who may happen to be a beneficiary under the will, in applying for probate does not fight a personal action but fights for the interests of all the beneficiaries under the will. Therefore the action of an executor in applying for a probate is not in substance a personal action In case of his demise pending the probate proceedings the maxim action personalis moritur cum persona does not apply. On the death of the executor, the action which he started does not come to an end. Any of those whom he was representing are entitled to intervene and carry on the proceedings with a modification by way of an amendment praying the court to grant letters of administration with the will annexed.</u>

<u>9. A plain reading of sections 102, 233 and 235 leads us to the conclusion that the residuary legatee may also continue the proceeding and section 222 would not be an impediment to the continuation of the probate proceeding. It is debated whether Jalada Devi is dead or alive. If she is alive then it can assumed that she has refused to take the probate proceeding and in terms of the will Digindra was competent to tile for probate. On the other hand, if she is dead then only Digindra was competent to file the Probate. Now Digindra is also dead, his heirs who are legatees are competent to continue the proceeding for the probate. The High Court Division had considered section 222 in its isolation without viewing the contingencies in the setting of sections 102, 232, 233, 235 and 268. Section 268 reads as under:</u>

<u>"The proceedings of the Court of the District Judge in relation to the granting of probate and letters of administration snail, save as hereinafter otherwise provided, be regulated, so far as the circumstances of the case permit, by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.</u>

<u>This section is very wide but is hedged by the limitation "save as hereinafter otherwise provided." This section makes applicable the procedural provision of the Code of Civil Procedure to the proceeding under the Succession Act in relating to the granting of Probate and letter of Administration. Section 222 precedes section 268. It therefore does not come within the mischief of the saving clause as hereinafter otherwise provided."Illustration (i) to section 222 makes the position clear. A will that C be his executor if B wills not B is appointed executor by implication. And that is covered by sub-section (1). Again a persons who though not expressly appointed as executor, is directed to receive and pay the testator's debts and to get in and distribute his personal estate, must be taken to have been appointed under the will as executor by implication. This is covered by sub-section (2). This proposition is supported by the decision in the matter of Monohar Mukherjee: 5 Cal 756. To take section 222 in its absolute term will be erroneous. Such provisions confer a faculty or power but they do not follow by such words as that anything done contrary to these provisions shall be null and void to all intents'. Such is the legislative practice whenever it is considered to confer a power in absolute terms. Section 222 is not such a provision. An enabling provision without a contrary clause cannot be viewed as a bar. The learned Judges of the High Court Division had fallen into error on this point.</u>

10. Therefore, the conclusion is that this appeal must be allowed. The heirs of Digindra should be substituted in the probate proceeding because Digindra was given a legacy in the will and heirs of Digindra are the beneficiary of the will. Proposition that Jalada is still alive can be debated in the probate proceeding but till it is proved there is no reason to arrest the proceeding on a hypothetical assertion.

In the result, therefore this appeal is allowed. The order of the High Court Division is set aside and the heirs of Digindra be substituted in the probate proceeding. There will be no order as to costs.

End.

caseno:
Civil Revision No. 263/1986 (Rangpur)
Civil Revision No. 1476 of 1990 (Dhaka)
lawyer:
Md. Asaduzzaman, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Md. Abdul Momin Talukdar, Advocate ----- For the Opposite-Parties.
parties:
Abdul Mannan Shah & ors ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Kafiran Nessa being dead her heirs: Md. Abdul Gofur Shah and others ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 13.4.86 passed in Title Appeal No. 25 of 1985 by District Judge, Naogaon reversing those dated 27.2.85 passed by Munsif, Naogaon in OC Suit No. 296 of 1984.

2. Facts giving rise to this Rule may briefly be put thus: Kafiran Nessa, an old lady of 80 years and pardanashin, as plaintiff instituted a suit being OC Suit No. 148 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif, Sapahar for declaration that Hiba-bill-Ewaj deed No. 5223/83 dated 7.7.83 of Sapahar Sub-Registry Office is illegal, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiff. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that her husband died on 10th Chaitra, 1389 BS leaving behind 4 sons and 2 daughters namely Abdul Sobhan Shah, Abdul Kader Shah, Abdul Gafur Shah and Abdus Salam Shah and two daughters namely Jainab and Anwara. The sons are separate in mess and daughters are married. Defendant No. 1 Abdul Mannan Shah is the eldest son of Abdus Sobhan Shah and since his childhood he has been staying with the plaintiff and her husband. Plaintiff and her husband used to love defendant No. 1 very much and he used to look after the affairs of the plaintiff and her husband. Plaintiff got the defendant No. 1 married and has been staying with the plaintiff at village Chachaibari, PS Porsha. After the death of plaintiffs husband defendant No. 1 began to misbehave with the plaintiff and asked her to quit the house and stay elsewhere. He also disclosed that he would not deliver crops of her land. He also disclosed to have acquired title to the properties of the plaintiff by way of a deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj executed by the plaintiff. Following this disclosure the plaintiff, who is an old lady of 80 years, became surprised and asked her 3rd son, Gofur Shah to enquire about the said deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj. Abdul Gofur Shah made search and procured a certified copy of the impugned deed dated 24.11.83 and on perusal of the same plaintiff got details of the deed in question showing plaintiff as executant of the deed. In fact plaintiff never executed and registered such deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj. The cause of action arose on 7.7.83 when the disputed deed was registered.

3. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegation set up in the plaint. The case of the defendant is that the deed is not collusive and the plaintiff has no cause of action to file the suit and the same is not maintainable. Plaintiff has got four sons and 2 daughters who have been living in separate mess. The defendant No. 1 used to live with his grand father and grand mother from his childhood. Defendant No. 1 used to respect plaintiff who voluntarily transferred the suit land measuring 13.29 acres of land to defendant No. 1 on the basis of a Hiba-bil-Ewaj deed dated 7.7.83 and since then defendant has been possessing the suit land. Plaintiff who died during the pendency of the suit transferred the suit land to defendant No. lout of her free will. After the transfer of the suit land to defendant No. 1 other sons and daughters of plaintiff took her by force to the house of her daughter Jainab at Porsha against her will and kept her in confinement and thereafter plaintiffs sons and daughters filed this false suit in her name against her will. The LTI appearing in the plaint and in vokalatnama are not products, of the hand of deceased plaintiff. Defendant No. 1 also denied the allegation of fraud and collusion in the matter of execution and registration of the impugned deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj. Defendant No. 1 claims the impugned deed to be genuine and duly acted upon hence the suit is liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. Pro-defendant No. 2 also contested the suit by filing written statement. The case of pro- defendant No. 2 is that the suit is maintainable and there is cause of action of filing the suit. Deceased plaintiff Kafiran Nessa was his mother. Defendant No. 1 had taken all the properties that belonged to the deceased plaintiff by way of Hiba-bil-Ewaj deed. In fact the suit has been filed by deceased plaintiff. Deceased plaintiff did not transfer the suit land to the defendant No. 1 voluntarily and out of her free will.

5. On the basis of an application filed under section 24 CPC the suit was transferred to the Court of Munsif Naogaon for disposal and it was renumbered as OC No. 296 of 1984. Plaintiff herself deposed in this case on commission as PW 1 defence side also examined 6 witnesses in support of their case.

6. The plaintiff Kafiran Nessa Bibi, who was aged 80 years before her death, deposed in this case as PW 1. In her evidence she asserted that she never intended to make deed being deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj in respect of 13.29 acres of land in favour of defendant No. 1 and she did not execute and register the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj in his favour on 27.3.83 on receipt of Holy Quaran. She categorically denied to have put thumb impression on the impugned deed for the purpose of execution. She also denied to have presented the said deed before the Sub-Registrar for the purpose of registration; she also denied to have executed and registered the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj in favour of defendant No. 1. Her definite case is that taking advantage of her old age and illiteracy and fiduciary relations ship defendant No. 1 in collusion with others created the impugned deed behind her knowledge and got it registered surreptitiously using her name as an executant, She further asserts that the Hiba-bil-Ewaj deed was never read over to her and explained and it was not written according to her instruction. Kafiran Nessa was aged 80 years and pardanashin Muslim lady who was examined on commission on 3.8.84 and she died on 11.11.84. Abdus Sobhan Shah, father of defendant No. 1 declined to be grouped and as such he has been brought on record as pro-defendant No. 2. Kafiran Nessa PW 1 was compelled by her other sons and daughters to file the suit but DW 1 who is recipient of the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj admitted in his cross examination that the plaintiff who was examined on commission, was not confronted with her thumb impressions appearing in the plaint and on the vokalatnama so the plea that the plaintiff did not institute the suit does not stand to reason. In her evidence Kafiran Nessa categorically admitted that she did not put her thumb impression on any deed nor she went to Sub-Registry Office for the purpose of registration and execution of any deed. In her cross examination she asserts herself to be pardanashin lady and she never went to any Court

7. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that Kafiran Nessa stated that it is not fact she did not execute any deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj on 22nd Ashar, 1390 BS and also referred to the statement made by Kafiran Nessa that it is not a fact that she did not give any "land to Defendant No. 1. But her evidence as a whole is to be read and not (piecemeal) basis and reading of isolated portion of statement made by Kafiran Nessa will not help to corroborate the contention urged by the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1. If the deposition of Kafiran Nessa recorded on commission be considered as a whole, it will be apparent that Kafiran Nessa instituted the suit herself with the object of cancelling the impugned deed. She denied to have executed the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj on receipt of piece of Holy Quaran. Nowhere from her evidence it transpires that the disputed deed was read over or explained to her. Father-in-law of defendant No. 1 who figures as attesting witness in the deed of Hiba-bil-Ewaj did not depose supporting the impugned deed.

8. Petitioner defendant No. 1, who deposed in the lower Court as DW 1, admitted that impugned deed was executed and registered at Saphar Sub-Registry Office and that plaintiff put her LTI at village Chachaibari at her residence. No evidence has been led to show that plaintiff Kafiran Nessa made a declaration to give land to defendant No. 1. No evidence was also available on record to prove that Holy Quran was given as Ewaj. DW 1 admits that one Sukendra PW 4 was present at the time of talk but PW 4 Sukendra denied to that such talk was held in his presence. PW 2 identified the lady and stated that he was present at the time of writing of the deed.

9. The learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite-party submits that section 31 of Registration Act empowers the Sub-Registrar to attend the residence of executant but in such case the Sub-Registrar himself is supposed to be present physically to admit execution of deed by the executants. But in the instant case the Sub-Registrar himself was not physically present at the time of execution of the impugned deed by Kafiran Nessa. In this connection the evidence of DW 6 Afsar Hossain will be of much importance. He admits in his evidence that one Dhiren who was not Sub-Registrar was present and not Sub-Registrar himself was present Therefore no-evidence on record to prove the execution of the disputed deed by Kafiran Nessa. Further, it appears from the evidence of DW 6 that the LTI of plaintiff was obtained in the impugned deed at village Doash as it appears from the LTI Register. So the provision as laid in section 31 of Registration Act was not complied with and as such the registration of the impugned deed suffers from illegality.

<u>10. It is settled law that when any deed is being executed by pardanashin lady burden lies on the person who claims the benefit under the deed to establish that the deed was executed by pardanashin lady on her own accord and it was read over to her and she fully understood import of transaction and this burden lies only on the recipient of the deed but this burden was not discharged by defendant No. 1. This protection given to pardanashin lady by special rule of onus is also extended to her legal heirs. Defendant No. 1 also admitted that Kafiran Nessa was a pardanashin woman and illiterate and under such circumstances burden lies upon defendant No. 1 as he relied on the impugned deed of disposition and it is to be proved by him that the deed in question was explained to plaintiff since dead and that she understood the import of the transaction. Thus the burden to prove that pardanashin woman had full knowledge and comprehension about the terms of disposition and that it was her mental act and this burden unless is discharged by person who wants to uphold the disposition the impugned deed cannot be made binding against plaintiff. This view is supported by the ruling reported in BLD 1982 (AD) 139 in the case of Most. Rokeya Khatun Vs. Alijan Bepari and others. It has been stated above that defendant No. 1 himself admitted that Kafiran Nessa since dead was an old, illiterate and pardanashin lady and that he was born and brought up by her and as such defendant No. 1 stood in fiduciary relation with the lady. In such circumstances the onus is on defendant No. 1 to prove that plaintiff prior to execution of impugned deed got independent advice.</u>

11. Special rule is desired to give protection to certain categories of women who suffer from social disability because of pardah system. Pardanshin women are excluded from social intercourse except with very near relation and communion outside the narrow family circle is barred to them.

<u>12. Of course, independent advice in case of transfer of property by pardanashin lady is insisted in Case where transferee stands in fiduciary relation with the lady, onus in such circumstances in on transferee i.e. defendant No. 1 This view is supported by decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 1. But in instant case no material has been brought on record to discharge that onus which lies on defendant No. 1.</u>

13. It is to be observed that burden is to be discharged unless there is some special circumstance calling for its application. In that the donee of the transferer stood in position of active defence or had finduciary relation with pardanashin lady. It is only in such circumstances the transferee will carry additional burden to prove that pardanashin lady had independent and disinterested advice from the person other than the recipient of the impugned document. This view received support in the case of Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury and other Vs. Gani Ahmed and ors reported in 33 DLR (AD) 1.

14. Thus having considered the entire materials on record and the fact that defendant No. 1 who stood in fiduciary relation with deceased plaintiff Kafiran Nessa and that registration of the impugned deed was not made in accordance with law nor there is any evidence on record that Kafiran Nesa, who is an old lady of 80 years and pardanashin, got independent advice before making disposition and that she properly and fully understood the nature of such disposition, I am inclined to hold that the learned District Judge, Naogaon did not commit any error of law resulting in erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the impugned order passed by the learned District Judge in the aforesaid Title Appeal does not call for any interference.

15. In the result, the Rule stands discharged without any order as to cost

The connected Civil Rule No. 1477 (R) 1990 is also discharged without any order as to cost.

End.

A.W Bhuiya, Additional Attorney General B. Hossain, Assistant Attorney General with him instructed by A.W. Mallik, Advocate-on-Record -----For the Appellant. 
Faqueer Shahabuddin Ahmed, Sr. Advocate instructed by Abu Backkar, Advocate-on- Record -----For the Respondent.
parties:
Chairman, National Board of Revenue, Bangladesh ----- Appellant
Vs. 
M/s G.M.G Corporation Ltd ----- Respondent
case_source: From the judgment and order dated April 2,1982 passed by the High Court Division in Reference Case No.1 of 1981.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C.J:- I have gone through the judgments written by Ruhul Islam, Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Shahabuddin Ahmed, JJ and I concurred with the decision of Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.

<u>2. Ruhul Islam J. I have gone through a copy of the judgment written by my learned brother Badrul Haider Chowdhury J. and the one written by my learned brother Shahabuddin Ahmed J. I concur with that of the latter. The question for consideration in this appeal is whether the mortgage deed submitted by the respondent for registration falls under Article 40(b) or Article (c) of the Stamp Act for the purpose of payment of stamp duty. The respondent G.M.G. Corporation Limited while enjoying cash credit facility with the Bank or Credit and Commerce International, briefly stated "BCCI" to the extent of Tk. 60,000,00/- (Taka sixty lacs) by executing a Demand Promissory Note and a deed of hypothecation of raw materials and finished goods as security, applied for raising the limit to Tk. 90,00,000/-. The bank allowed the respondent's prayer for raising the limit to Tk. 90,00,000/- and asked the respondent to execute a deed of mortgage in their favour in respect of their other movable and immovable properties by way of collateral/auxiliary security. The respondent executed a deed of mortgage to meet the requirement of the BCCI offering some immovable properties as the additional security after obtaining no objection clearance from the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, with which the properties were mortgaged. The mortgage deed was presented for registration with stamp duty calculated under clause (p) of Article 40. A question was raised that the mortgage deed was not executed by way of collateral or auxiliary security but it was a primary or principal security, and stamp duty is leviable under clause (b) of Article 40. A Special Bench of the High Court Division heard the reference made by the National Board of Revenue under section 51 of the- Stamp Act and rejected the contention of the taxing authorities and held that the mortgage deed in question was a collateral/auxiliary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40 of the Stamp Act; and the National Board of Revenue by special leave preferred this appeal. The correspondence between the bank and the respondent and the recitals in the mortgage deed clearly support the plea of the respondent that under the mortgage deed some movable and immovable properties are being offered by way of collateral/auxiliary security against the cash credit facility of Tk. 90,00,000/-. It is not the case that the security is being offered against the specified amount of loan of Tk. 90,00,000/- but it is by way of security against the cash credit facility having the limit at Tk. 90,00,000/-, The Demand Promissory Note and the Deed of Hypothecation together construe a mortgage as contemplated under the Stamp Act. The bank, as per terms of the mortgage deed, can fall upon the mortgaged property only when the primary security, namely, the Demand Promissory Note and the Deed of Hypothecation fall short to satisfy the outstanding demand of the bank. In the face of clear recital in the deed in question I find it difficult to accept the contention of the appellant that the mortgage in this case falls under the category of primary or principal security. The deed as drawn up clearly falls in the category of collateral/auxiliary, in' as much as some immovable properties are being offered as collateral/auxiliary or additional security for the cash credit facility raised to the extent of Tk.90.00.000/- in favour of the respondent, and stamp duty is chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. In my view the Special Bench of the High Court Division has correctly answered the question, mid the appeal must fail. Therefore the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.</u>

Badrul Haider Chowdhuiy J. —This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment of the Special Bench of the High Court Division passed in Reference Case No. 1 of 1981 under section 57 of the Stamp Act, 1899.

4. The National Board of Revenue is the appellant. The respondent G.M.G. Corporation Ltd. took a loan of Tk.90,00,000/-(Taka ninety lacs) from the Bank of Credit and Commerce Ltd. securing the loan by execution of duly stamped demand promissory note and hypothecation of goods. The Bank asked for collateral/auxiliary security being further assurance by creating mortgage in respect of the properties of the Company. The respondent offered a property which was already mortgaged with Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (as first mortgage). The Registration authority took the view that the proposed documents were to be stamped under Article 40 (b) of the Schedule I of the Stamp Act and not under Article 40 (c) as has been the contention of the respondent. The Collector upheld the decision of the Registration Authority when moved under section 31 of the Stamp Act. Thereafter the respondent filed a petition under section 57 the Stamp Act before the Chairman, National Board of Revenue for his decision or refer the matter to the High Court Division for deciding what would be the Stamp duty payable on such document. 11. The only question is which of the clauses of Art. 40 (b) or (c) will be applicable.

Article 40 deals with mortgage deeds.

The definition of “Mortgage Deed" is given in section 2(17) is as follows:

"Mortgage deed" includes every instrument whereby for the, purpose of seeking money advanced' or to be advanced 'by way of loan' or an existing or future debt or the performance of an engagement; one person’s transfers 'or creates' to 'or in favour of' another' a right over or in respect of specific property"

It is not restricted to immovable property and it includes pawn a pledge of movable. The definition makes no distinction between legal and equitable mortgage but the Act makes special provision under Art. 6 which relates to that class of documents which should be interpreted as an agreement or memorandum of in mortgage by deposit of title-deeds and' not a mortgage in its own right.

In the Transfer of Property Act section 58 gives the definition of Mortgage as under:

“A mortgage is the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property for the purpose of seeking the payment of money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan, an existing or future debt or the performance of an agreement which may give rise to pecuniary liabilities".'

And the instrument (if any) by which the transfer is effected is called a mortgage-deed. Art. 40 gives the description of the instrument namely mortgage-deed but excludes  Agreement relating to deposit of title-deeds' pawn or pledge (No.6), Bottomry Bond (No. 16), Mortgage of a crop (No. 41), Resnondeatia Bond (No. 56) or Security Bond (No. 57)''. Therefore, in construing a document these salient features are to be kept in view.

12. As regards moveable the transaction may be merely a pledge where possession is given but there is only bailment and not transfer of the property or a mortgage. A mortgage of moveable, if not accompanied with possession is called hypothecation. A pledge is chargeable under Article 6. So far as the question of hypothecation is concerned the possession over the property is detained to the owner and here only certain right in the movable property is transferred to the persons in whose favour the property is hypothecated When the goods themselves have been handed over to tile Bank in whose favour the document has been executed by way of security, the goods in respect of which the document was executed becomes pledged under section 172 of the Contract Act. Such document is chargeable under section 6 also.

13. The distinction between Article 6 and Article 40 is that Article 6 islimited to causes where a loan is in question and Article 40 cover the cases where interest in or rights over property is transferred whether possession is delivered or not as security for the mortgage money. For the purpose of as curtaining which of the articles is attracted the document in question is to be seen. When although words 'pledge' was used in the instrument the document taken as a while the transaction really appeared to be a transfer by way of mortgage, it was held in 21 Cal 241 that the document was a deed of mortgage chargeable under Article 40.

<u>14. The instrument in question show clearly that the Mortgage was intended by the respondent in favour of the Bank of Credit and Commerce Ltd. notwithstanding their earlier hypothecation and pledge of goods by execution of promissory notes, etc. in favour of the same Bank. If that is the position, as it appears to be so, Article 40 is attracted. The same Article starts by saying:</u>

<u>"Mortgage deed, not being an agreement relating to deposit of title- deeds, Pawn or Pledge (No.6), Bottomry Bond (No.16), Mortgage of a crop (No.41), Respondentia Bond (No. 56) or Security Bond (No. 57) these documents are excluded.</u>

<u>Then comes three clauses; Clause (a) reads:</u>

<u>"Whether possession of the property is given or agreed to be given".</u>

<u>That is not the position here</u>

<u>Then comes clause (b) which reads:</u>

<u>"When possession is not given or agreed to be given as aforesaid. Explanation appended to it clarifies the position.</u>

<u>Where the Mortgagor gives to the mortgagee a Power of Attorney to collect rent of a lease of the property mortgaged or part thereof is deemed to give possession within the meaning of this Article. That means in such case it will come under clause (a) and not (b).</u>

15. Clause (c) reads: "When a collateral or auxiliary or additional or substituted security, or by way of further assurance for the above mentioned purpose where the principal or primary security is duly stamped.

<u>16. Rate of duty is less in such circumstances. The instrument in question though drafted in the language which says: "This is a collateral or auxiliary security" and mentioned about "second mortgage". This does not really come under clause (c) because it is not the case here the "principal or primary security is duly tamped".</u>

<u>There is no principal or primary security in the present case which was duly stamped. The only document that was executed was the document of hypothecation and pledge. The expression 'for the above mentioned purpose' can only mean mortgage. The respondent has given mortgage for the first time to the Bank of Credit and Commerce though the respondent has taken previously a cash credit facility by executing promissory note by hypothecation of their goods or pledges which are governed by Article 6. The present instrument cannot be a collateral security because the present instrument is a mortgage deed and it does not relate to any previous mortgage which has been given to the Bank of Credit and Commerce Ltd. Had it been the case that the present mortgage was intended to be a second mortgage to the Shilpa Rin Sangstha, then it could be argued that the present document is merely a collateral security or auxiliary or additional or substituted security by way of further assurance because the principal and primary security is already stamped, namely, first mortgage deed but that is not the case. It is perfectly clear that the object of the instrument was to give to the Bank some rights by way of security. This is not a deed of hypothecation. Therefore it comes under Article 40(b). Reliance may be placed on the case of Secretary to the Commission of Salt etc. Madras V. Mrs. Orr 38 Mad 646 for this proposition. Next, in the case of failure to adjust the loan the respondent covenanted that "the bank shall be entitled to take possession of the schedule properties and/or appoint a Manager or Receiver without intervention of the Court" and further the Bank shall be at liberty to sell the scheduled property".</u>

<u>17. It is well settled that the question of what stamp duty is payable on a document must necessarily be decided on the words of the document and the terms it embodies. Reliance may be placed on a Board of Revenue Vs. Sorrarazu AIR 1976 Mad 1038 (FB) where the Court considered whether a document fell under clause (a) or (b) explaining the words "agreed to be given". It was held that the document in' that case came under clause (b) of section 33 of the Madras Stamp Act. This is the first mortgage so far as the Bank of Credit and Commerce is concerned and in this deed possession has not been given. Therefore, the document comes within clause (b) and not (c).</u>

<u>18. Article (c) deals with a case in which a separate instrument offered an additional or substituted security is executed subsequent to the original mortgage transaction which had been reduced into writing in a previously completed instrument. The respondents have executed promissory note for the purpose of hypothecation to the Bank of Credit and Commerce but the present document is the first document which is being given as a mortgage deed and therefore it could not be said that the present document is executed subsequent to the original mortgage transaction. No such mortgage transaction had taken place previously between the Bank and the respondent. In the case of Mutual Property Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Inland Revenue Commissioner, 196 All England Reports 493 the question was when the second mortgage of freehold property was subject to an existing 6rst mortgage by the mortgagor to a third party contained a covenant by the borrower to pay the second mortgagees by installments under certain circumstances and whether the first mortgage had been duly stamped with the appropriate duty on the amount thereby secured, the set mortgage deed was primary security. It was held as between the mortgagor and the second mortgagees that the instrument was the primary security for the obligation which those parties had created between themselves and was not secondary to the mortgagor's obligation towards the first mortgage, nor was the covenant by the mortgagor to pay to the second mortgagees the amount of the first mortgage merely auxiliary to the first mortgage, It was observed that the appellants were not paying duty twice on the same sum because the sums concerned in the first and second mortgages constituted different obligations between different parties, and the instrument was liable to stamp duty either as a mortgage or as a covenant within Schd. I to the Stamp Act, 1891, on the aggregate of the sums secured by the two mortgagees.</u>

<u>19. This case is on all fours with the present case. Here the mortgagor (sic) was the Shilpa Rin Sangstha and the second mortgage was with BCCI Ltd. The two are entirely different obligations between different parties and therefore clause (c) by no stretch of imagination can come into play to show that the mortgage deed which has been offered by the respondent to the BCCI is auxiliary or additional or by way of further assurance to another primary security. There was no primary security; there was only a hypothecation by the Company to the Bank for cash credit limit and the rate of duty is less under Article 6 whereas when the company wanted to raise the cash credit limit to 90 lacs the Bank asked for security by way of mortgage of moveables and immovable. This was clearly done by the present instrument and therefore it has to be stamped as a mortgage deed because that is all it is. It was done so expressly. There is no scope for interpretation of written document which the parties have expressly put into in writing: There is no question of construing the document favourable to the subject. It is the document between two individual parties and they bargained for what they wanted to do. The only question is what is the rate of duty that should be paid To bring such document within the fold of document purported to be a document of hypothecation is to adopt a process of reasoning which is not sanctioned by law nor the document itself allows such scope. It says that it is deed of mortgage, if it is, as it is, it is not conceivable how the document can escape from being stamped under other than clause (b).</u>

<u>20. K. Krishnamurthy in Indian Stamp Act, fourth edition, cites a decision of the Madras Revenue Authorities and observed "in order that Article 40(c) may apply, there must have been a previous mortgage properly stamped. A document whereby the executant mortgaged certain lands to secure the payment of a sum of Rs. 956 due to the mortgagee under a promissory note previously executed, cannot be treated as a collateral security falling under Article 40(c). It is a primary mortgage and duty is leviable under Article 40(b) The authorities quoted is Mad. B. P. 3011 R. Mis. 28th August. 1902 cited at page 124 of Madras Stamp Manual (1958). The view which we have taken gets support from the above quoted exposition of law.</u>

20A. Mr. Shahabuddin Ahmed argued that the present document is a collateral or additional document by way of further assurance for enhancing the cash credit limit but when questioned about the principal or primary security which is duly stamped he had no answer. The execution of hypothecation and the Promissory notes are chargeable under a different article namely article 6 which provides for lesser rate of stamp duty but in the case of mortgage the duty is higher.

21. Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Additional Attorney General placed before us the entire document and the relevant portions of which have already been quoted earlier in this judgment. Reliance was placed on the decision of Inland Revenue Commissioner V. Hanny Ansbacher & co. (1962) 3 All ER 843 where the House of Lords considered a similar point as to the Stamp duty. In that case the respondents by agreement agreed to purchase all the Ordinary stock of a company for a price payable in two installments. The first installment was duly paid. The second remained outstanding. By Cl. II of the sale agreement the respondent agreed to procure that the sum payable as the second installment should be guaranteed to the extent of 750,000 by a bank. The stamp duty payable on this guarantee was passed at dollars' 1,875 (5 shilling for every dollars 100 of dollar 750,000) on the ground that the guarantee came within the heading "mortgage, bond, debenture, covenant being the only or principal or primary security for the payment or repayment of money in Sch. I to the Stamp Act, 1899" It was held that the guarantee was collateral security to a primary security (the Sale agreement), the primary obligation for payment was that of the respondent under the sale agreement and that was exempt from stamp duty. Therefore, the collateral security, viz. the guarantee, attracted maximum duty of 10 Shillings.

22. This decision reinforces the view taken by us that the mortgage-deed in question could not be taken as a collateral security inasmuch as there is no primary or principal security in this case. The position emerges that the document in question is a mortgage deed and that is the first mortgage which has been offered to the Bank of Credit and Commerce and therefore it is changeable under clause (b). It does not come by any stretch of imagination under clause (c)

In the, result, therefore this appeal is allowed and the judgment of the High Court Division is set aside with costs

Shahabuddin Ahmed J:-I have had the opportunity to go through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my learned brother B.H. Chowdhury J With respect, I am unable to agree on the views taken by my learned brother, and as such, I am giving my vie VIS on the question involved: The question is whether the mortgage-deed executed by the respondent as security against a loan advanced to them is chargeable with duty under clause (b) or clause (c) of Article 40 of Schedule 1 of the Stamp Act, 1899. If the mortgage deed is "a collateral or auxiliary or additional security" for repayment of the loan, in relation to the earlier security by way of Demand Promissory Note and the deed of hypothecation, then it will be chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40; if it is not a collateral/auxiliary security, it will be chargeable under clause (b) of the said, Article.

24. Facts of the case having been already set out and discussed in the judgment of my learned brother I shall only touch on them briefly to explain my view. The respondent, a Manufacturing Industry, obtained, and was already enjoying a loan, up to the limit of Tk.60 (sixty) lacs which was later on raised to Tk. 90 (ninety) lacs, from the Bank of Credit and Commerce International, briefly BCCI, by executing a demand promissory note and a deed of hypothecation of raw materials and finished goods in favour of the BCCI as security for the payment of the loan. The BCCI thereafter asked, the respondent to execute a deed of mortgage in their favour in respect of other movable and immovable properties of the respondent by way of collateral auxiliary 'security for repayment of the' loan. Accordingly, the respondent executed the deed of mortgage in question after having taken permission of another mortgagee, the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsiha, to whom the same properties had already been mortgaged as a security for some other advance of money The respondent paid stamp duty of Tk. 27,000/- (Twenty seven thousand on this mortgage-deed, computed under clause (c) of Article 40 and presented it for registration before the Sub-registrar But the Sub registrar" contended that the mortgage deed was not a collateral or auxiliary security but it  was a primary or principal security, and as such, it was chargeable at the higher rate as prescribed under clause (b) of Article 40. In this way the controversy arose which was ultimately referred to the Special Bench of the High Court Division constituted with three Judges under section 57 of the Stamp Act. The Special Bench after hearing the parties rejected the 'contention of the taxing authorities, namely the National Board of Revenue and held that the mortgage deed was a collateral/auxiliary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. Against this decision of the Special 'Bench of the High Court Division the National Board of Revenue preferred this appeal by special leave granted by us.

25. Schedule I of the Stamp Act is a list of various instruments which are chargeable with duties it different rates as prescribed in the said Schedule. A Mortgage-Deed has been listed against Article 40 of this Schedule. The mortgage deed in question in this case, executed by the respondent in favour of the Beer, being an instrument for securing loan is chargeable under Article 40. Mortgage deeds are chargeable at three different rates as prescribed under clauses (a), (b) and (c) of this Article according to their nature or classification. When possession' of the property which is subject' matter of the mortgage deed is given or agreed to be given by the mortgagor, the mortgage deed will be charge at the rate prescribed under clause (a); this rate is "the same duty as a Conveyance for a consideration equal to the amount secured by such deed," Admittedly, under the mortgage deed in question no possession of the property is given and, as such, clause (a) will not apply thereto. Clause (b) will apply to a mortgage deed when possession is not given or agreed to be given; the rate under this clause is "the same duty as a bond under Article 15 for the amount secured by such deed. At the moment, this rate is two percent of the amount of loan secured by the mortgage deed and computed there under the duty of this mortgage-deed will be Taka one lac eighty thousand. Clause (c) will apply to a mortgage deed if constitutes "a collateral or auxiliary or additional or substituted security or by way of further assurance" for repayment of a loan; rate under this clause is much less- i.e. fifty paisa" for every sum secured not exceeding Tk. 1,000.00; computed on this basis the duty of this mortgage deed comes to taka twenty seven thousand which the respondent has already paid as mentioned above.

26. Appellant's contention is that the 'mortgage deed is- not a collateral/auxiliary additional security but it is a primary or principal security against the loan advanced to respondent in that the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation which are claimed by the respondent to be tile primary or principal security are not a mortgage-deed duly stamped under clause (a) or clause (b) of Article 40. The mortgage deed in question is therefore the primary security chargeable under clause (b). Respondent's contention is that when the loan has already been taken against the security by way of the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation of goods which have also been duly stamped, the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation, are 'necessarily the primary security, and the mortgage deed being required as security in addition to the promissory note and the deed of hypothecation the mortgage deed is nothing but collateral/auxiliary security. A collateral or auxiliary security is a security which is furnished in addition to a security already furnished; a collateral or auxiliary security is enforceable only when the primary security after being enforced falls short of meeting the obligation to repay the loan. There is no dispute that unless there is a primary principal security the question of collateral or auxiliary security cannot arise. In this case the loan was already obtained against the security of a demand promissory note and a deed of hypothecation of goods and these two securities were also duly stamped under Article 6 of Schedule I. Secondly, the Mortgage- deed describes itself as a 'collateral/auxiliary security"; it records that the mortgagee, namely the BCCI required "mortgage" of other assets and landed properties of the borrower as "collateral/auxiliary security" in addition to the security already furnished by execution of the promissory note and the deed of hypothecation. Paragraph IV e) of the mortgage deed reads thus:

"IV. the Bank considered the proposal of the mortgagor and agreed to enhance the limit of Tk. 90 lacs, subject, amongst others, the mortgagor agreeing to".

"IV (e) give collateral/auxiliary security by creating second mortgage in respect of the entire movable and immovable assets of the Company, over and above the primary securities, mentioned herein with due permission of the first mortgagee, namely the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, hereinafter referred to as BSRS and other relevant authorities";

<u>27. The learned Additional Attorney- General appearing for the appellant opened his arguments with a misconception of the respondent's case. He thought that the respondents treated their previous mortgage in favour of the Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangsthea’s the 'primary security and their later mortgage in favour of the BCCI as the "secondary security" and" accordingly argued that these two mortgages to different persons for different sums of money are independent of each other and that the later one cannot be secondary to the earlier one, both being the "primary security". In support of this argument the learned Additional Attorney General has referred to the case Mutual Property Insurance Co. Ltd. Vs. Inland Revenue Commissioner 1926 All Eng. Rep. 493. There is no question that mortgages to two different persons or organization’s -for meeting different obligations are independent of each other, and that they constitute "primary security". But this is not at all the case of the respondent here. The respondents never claim that their mortgage to the BCCI is secondary in relation to their earlier mortgage to the BSRS. Their case is that their mortgage to the BCCI is secondary security in relation to their demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation executed in favour of the BCCI. As such this decision as referred to has got no relevance to the instant case. The fact that the respondent had previously mortgaged the same properties to the BSRS or, for that purpose, to any other person, is irrelevant in the instant case For, so long the value of the property mortgaged is sufficiently high to cover the obligation under both the mortgages, and if the prior mortgagee has no objection to the subsequent mortgage, the mortgagor is at liberty to mortgage the same property to different persons. The question involved in this case is whether the Mortgage Deed in question is a collateral security in relation to the security by way of the demand promissory note and the deed of hypothecation, both the securities being in favour of the same 'lender and in respect of the same loan". It must be borne in mind that the primary security and the collateral security as mentioned in clause (c) are necessarily against the same loan.</u>

28. The learned Additional Attorney- General does not dispute that a promissory note or a deed of hypothecation may constitute security for repayment of loan, but he contends that to be a primary or principal security within the meaning of clause (c), the instrument must be a mortgage deed and that the said deed must be duly stamped under either clause (a) or clause (b) of Article 40. Clause (c), along with clauses (8) and (b), has been already quoted in the judgment of my learned brother upon a reading of this Article. I find nothing in the language of clause (c) which can support this interpretation as sought to be given by the learned Additional Attorney General. Clause (e) shows that a mortgage deed will constitute a collateral or auxiliary security by way of further assurance of the repayment of the loan taken against another security which is the main and primary security. provided the main or primary security has been duly stamped Nowhere in this clause it has been stated that the principal or primary security must be a mortgage deed, and unless violent pressure is brought to bear upon the wording of this clause the expression "primary/principal security must be a mortgage" cannot be read into this clause. According to the language of this clause primary/principal security may be any security which is duly stamped. The promissory note and the deed of hypothecation as security have been duly stamped-at the prescribed rate that is under Article 6 of the Schedule. 'Duly stamped" does not mean 'stamped' only under Article 40; it means stamped under any Article of this Schedule. Again if a primary security is exempt from duty by law it shall be presumed to have been duly stamped. It is argued by the learned Additional Attorney General that the primary security is intended to be a mortgage-deed because this expression primary/principal security has appeared in the same Article 40. I hardly find any substance in this argument, for this Article is intended to show in what conditions a mortgage deed can be differently charged-one condition being that if there is a primary security duly stamped the mortgage deed as secondary security will be charged at the lesser rate under clause (c).

<u>29. In clause (c), the purpose for which a secondary/auxiliary security is required has been stated to be "for the above mentioned purpose"; but nothing has been mentioned 'above' that is in clause (a) or clause (b) as to the purpose of a primary or principal security. Nevertheless, the purpose of a security, principal or collateral when it is, constituted by a mortgage-deed can be gathered from the definition of a mortgage deed. In section 2(17), a "mortgage deed" has been defined to include any instrument whereby, for the purpose of securing money advanced or to be advanced by way of loan one person transfers to another his right over a property. Secondly" clause (c) of Article 40 has been borrowed from clause (2) of the corresponding English section of the Stamp Act, 1891, where the purpose of primary security was stated to be "for payment or repayment of money" and thereafter describing a collateral or auxiliary security its purpose was stated to be "for the above mentioned purpose". But while copying from the English Stamp Act, the expression "for the purpose of payment or repayment of loan" was not included in clause (a)and (b) but in clause (c) while describing a collateral security, the expression "for the abovementioned purpose"-was retained- obviously by the oversight; otherwise the expression "for the abovementioned purpose" in clause (c) carries no meaning. Purpose of a collateral security is necessarily the same as that of a primary security i.e. repayment of loan. It a loan can be taken by executing a demand Promissory note or deed of hypothecation of goods as the only security, there is no reason why such documents cannot constitute a primary security when subsequently additional security is called for.</u>

30. Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmed learned Advocate for the respondent has strongly defended the High Court Division's decision citing a number of decisions' including one from the English jurisdiction. In "National Bank of Pakistan Vs. Fasihuzzaman" PLD 1964 KAR-92, a Special Bench of the West Pakistan High Court constituted under section 57 of the Stamp Act" considered a similar question A loan of Rs. six thousand was advanced by the National Bank to the respondent against a promissory note which was stamped under the Stamp Act; thereafter the Bank required of the respondent to execute a mortgage deed covering his landed property in addition to the promissory note as a secondary note security. Same objection was taken in that case as has been taken before us that the promissory note did not constitute primary security but the mortgage deed was in fact the principal or primary security chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. Alternatively it was contended, if the promissory note were the primary security it must be stamped as a mortgage deed under clause (a) or clause (b). The Special Bench overruled this contention and held that the promissory note was the primary or principal security and the mortgage dead was its collateral or principal security chargeable under clause (c) with an observation that the language of clause (c) cannot be so stretched as to indicate that 'primary security' should be also a mortgage deed. The other cases cited by Faqeer Shahabuddin Ahmed need not be discussed here as reference to those cases was made in this Karachi Bench case.

31. In ''Inland Revenue Commissioners Vs. Henry Ansbacher &Co.", All-Eng. Rep. 1962 (3) P. 843, the House of Lords considered a similar question in an appeal from the decision of the Court of Appeal. That was a case under Schedule I of the Stamp Act, 1891 of which our Stamp Act, 1899 may be called an exact replica. The respondent in that case purchased the originally stock of a Company at a price to be paid in two installments. The first installment was paid at once and for the second installment he executed an agreement- "sale agreement." The creditor required a Bank guarantee also which was then furnished. The stamp duty payable on this guarantee was assessed at £ 1,875 on the ground that the guarantee came within the heading "Mortgage, bond debenture, covenant" being the only or principal or primary security for the payment or repayment of money. This contention of the taxing authorities was rejected by the Court which held the bank guarantee to be a collateral security, that is, a security in addition to the sale agreement which was held to be the primary security. House of Lords observed:

"Although the guarantee came within the heading Mortgage bond debenture, covenant in Sch. I to the Stamp Act, 1891 yet it was not caught by the words followed. viz. "Being the only principal or primary security....for the payment or repayment of money', because, if money became payable, the primary obligation for payment was that of the respondents under the sale agreement, which was a "security" for payment within the words last quoted, although it was not a kind of security that attracted advalorem duty under the heading "Mortgage, bond ... " in Sch. I; accordingly, the guarantee attracted maximum duty of 10s under sub-head (2) of the heading" Mortgage, bond " in Sch. I. for the guarantee was a security collateral to a primary security the -sale agreement) which, being exempt from stamp duty, was "duly stamped" within sub-head "(2)."

<u>32. On consideration of the arguments advanced and on interpretation of clause (c) I hold that the Mortgage-deed in question is a collateral/auxiliary security ill relation to the Demand Promissory Note and the Hypothecation deed which' are the primary and principal security for repayment of the same loan and as such this Mortgage-deed is chargeable under clause (c) of Article 40. The Special Bench of the High Court Division is found to have correctly decided the question of law on proper appreciation of facts of the case.</u>

In the result the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.

Chowdhury A.T.M. Masud J.-I have gone through the judgments written by my learned brothers Ruhul Islam. Badrul Haider Chowdhury and Shahabuddin Ahmed JJ and I concur with the judgment of Badrul Haider Chowdhury J.

ORDER OF THE COURT

By the majority opinion the appeal is allowed with costs and judgment and order of the High Court Division are set aside.

End.
