full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan J: On an application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the decision containing in the Memo No. RD/Land/105/86-138 dated 11.5.89 (Annexure-C) issued by the respondent No. 4 should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as to why the respondents should not be directed to return/restore on de-requisitioning the surplus and unutilised land measuring 1298 square feet or thereabout in CS Khatian No. 543 in CS Dag No. 1174 of mouza Shahar Khilgaon, Dhaka acquired in LA Case No. 63 of 1959-60, to the petitioner or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper.

2. Pending hearing of the Rule, the respondents were restrained from dispossessing the petitioner from the land in question measuring 1298 sq. feet by way of allotment, sale, auction or in any way to any other person or persons and from disturbing the petitioner with the peaceful possession of the land.

3. The facts stated in the writ application out of which the present Rule has arisen, briefly, are stated as follows:

The petitioner being the owner of 12 decimals of land of CS Plot No. 1174 of CS Khatian No. 543 at Mouza Shahar Khilgaon, formerly Police Station Tejgaon/Rarnna and Motijheel now Shabujbagh, District Dhaka having purchased the same for a valuable consideration by a registered deed of conveyance dated 14.10.52 constructed a dwelling house there with kitchen, latrine, etc., and developed a small orchard. The said land and other adjoining lands were acquired by the respondents in LA Case No. 63 of 1959-60 for the purpose of railway diversion scheme at Khilgaon, Dhaka under the provisions of Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. The compensation for the said land of the petitioner was provisionally assessed at Taka 6807/21 and the petitioner received a part payment of Taka 5963.00 as provisional compensation money. In the meantime the scheme for which the land was acquired was completed and small portion of the said acquired land measuring 1298 sq. feet of CS Khatian No. 543, CS Dag No. 1174 remained surplus and unutilized and the same was placed under the disposal of the acquiring authority by the requiring body. It is stated that the possession of the surplus and unutilized land measuring more or less 1298 sq. feet remained with the petitioner who is in possession of the same on payment of municipal taxes in his own name upto 4th quarter, 1987-88. After the promulgation of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 (Ordinance No II of 1982) the Government formulated its policy not to use the surplus land for any purpose other than the purpose for which it was acquired and to return the surplus land to its original owner. On several representations made since 1974 the requiring body recommended for the release of the surplus land of the petitioner as it was found not required by them. The requiring body also proposed to the acquiring authority that the surplus land belonging to the petitioner might be de-requisitioned in favour of the petitioner and accordingly a plan was prepared showing the area of the land proposed to be de-requisitioned under Memo No. 331-W/DR/CW(G)P-V(G), dated 11.5.86. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka keeping in view the policy of the Government de-requisitioned the adjacent land to several persons namely, Mr. Md. Momtazuddin Bhuiyan, his wife and Mr. Ayub Ali Master, but the petitioner's surplus land has remained to be de-requisitioned by the acquiring authority pursuant to the government policy. Thereafter, the petitioner received a Memo being No. RB/Land/105/86-138 dated 11.5.89/12-5-89 from the Assistant Secretary (Landed Property) of the Ministry of Communications, Railway Division (Respondent No. 4) informing him that there was no scope for releasing the property in favour of the petitioner. The petitioner, however, did not receive any communication in this regard from the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka or the Ministry of Land who are the authority in the matter of requisition and de-requisition of the property. The petitioner thereafter sent a notice through his advocate demanding justice by way of de-requisition of un utilized land of the petitioner which was duly received by the respondents but the petitioner has not been favoured with any reply. The petitioner thereafter came to know that the respondents in collusion with each other, with malafide intention have been taking steps to allot the surplus land of the petitioner to some other interested persons to defeat the policy of the Government and to frustrate the law in this regard. It is stated that one Din Mohammad who was inducted in the land by the petitioner as a licensee has been trying to take temporary allotment of the land from the requiring body. Having failed to get back the land from the respondents, the petitioner has filed this application claiming that the petitioner is entitled to get his surplus land restored and the respondents are under obligation to act in accordance with law and return the surplus land to the respective owners of the land adjoining to that of the petitioner. It is further submitted that the requiring body by their aforesaid memorandum has recommended vide Annexure-A series to release the land measuring 378 sq. feet but on final assessment taken later on it is found that the land measuring 1298 sq. ft. is lying surplus after the completion of the project. The petitioner has expressed his desire to return the compensation money if found to have been drawn in excess of the value/cost of the land used by the requiring body. The petitioner having filed this application obtained the present Rule.

4. In the supplementary affidavit filed, the petitioner has re-iterated that in the Daily Ittefaq, Dhaka published on 5.7.93 the Government's decision has been expressed for the return of the lands remaining unutilised by the Directorate of Roads and Highways to the respective owners.

5. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed on behalf of the respondent No. 6, Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong the claim made by the petitioner has been challenged. It is stated that after the land was acquired in LA Case No. 63 of 1959-60 for the construction of the staff quarters of Railway and receipt of compensation money by the owners, the respondents became the owner in possession of the land. It is denied that the scheme for which the land was acquired having been completed, a portion of 1298 sq. ft. which has remained surplus has been placed at the disposal of the acquiring authority by the requiring body. It is asserted that the land in question is still in possession of the requiring body. It is asserted that since the possession was delivered by the acquiring authority to Bangladesh Railway in 1960 the petitioner cannot legally claim to get back the land. The respondents have denied to have any knowledge about the alleged payment of municipal taxes by the petitioner. It is also emphatically denied that the respondents have any knowledge about the proposal for de-requisition of the surplus land acquired for the scheme. With regard to the statements made in paragraph 9 of the petition that the Deputy Commissioner has released certain other land to the original owners, it is stated that release of some land, even if made, cannot be a ground for the release of the land of the petitioner. In the application the grounds taken are that no properly acquired or any portion thereof can be used for any purpose other than the purpose for which it was acquired and, as such, the surplus and unused land measuring more or less 1298 sq. ft. in CS Khatian No. 543 CS Dag No. 1174 of Mouza Shahar Khilgaon, formerly under Police Station Ramna now Police Station Sabujbagh Dhaka cannot be retained by the respondents and the same is liable to be restored to the petitioner in view of the Government policy. It is also submitted that having regard to the fact that the requiring body had surrendered the surplus land in question to the acquiring authority and there being no need of the said land for the purpose for which it was acquired the Memo dated 11.5.89/12.5.89 (Annexure-C) sent by the respondent No. 4 is illegal, void and without lawful authority.

<u>6. At the time of hearing Mr. F1 Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has turned his argument from claiming the release of the land on de-requisition as a matter of right accrued by the law relating to requisition and acquisition of property but laid stress for getting the restoration .of the land in question relying on the principle of promissory estoppel. The learned Advocate submits that in view of the promises made by the requiring body as evidenced from Annexure-A, A-1 and A-2, the petitioner is entitled to get back the surplus land which has been kept unused and unutilised after the implementation and completion of the scheme for which the land was acquired. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the respondents are obliged to return the land giving effect to the promise and therefore the decision containing the Memo dated 11.5.89 and 12.5.89 vide Annexure-C issued by the respondent No.4 is required to be declared as having been made without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. Mr. MI Farooqui then submits that having regard to the fact that the requiring body has surrendered the surplus land in question to the acquiring authority and there being no need of the said land for the purpose it was acquired, the impugned Memo dated 11.5.89 and 12.5.89 Annexure-C sent to the respondent No. 4 is illegal, void and without lawful authority. Being quite aware of the legal position that the property once requisitioned and acquisitioned vested in the Govt, for the purpose of the implementation of the scheme of the requiring body and there is no provision for de-requisitioning the property and the question of abandoning the property from acquisition under the provision of section 18A of the Requisition and Acquisition of Property Act 1982. Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner diverted his argument on a different dimension seeking the relief by way of invoking the aid of the principle of promissory estoppel for the restoration of the land to the petitioner. The learned advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to the Annexure-A, A-1 and A-2 and submits that the Bangladesh Railway vide its memo No. G/1/DR dated 18.4.75 Annexure-A recommended for the release of the land to the party with the remark that the same will not hamper the project. A copy of the said memo was sent to the petitioner. Our attention has been drawn to the letter addressed to the Executive Engineer, Railway Division, Dhaka the Executive Engineer Bangladesh Railway, Dhaka dated 2.1.77 by which certain comments was called for before considering the question of releasing the land in question stating that the said land may be released to the party as it will not hamper any work to the project. Executive Engineer Bangladesh Railway, Dhaka gave a report to the effect that some lands for the said plot No. 1174 has already been de-requisitioned and there is no necessity of keeping the triangular land and the amount of compensation received has also been mentioned thereon. A report has been sent to the Deputy Commissioner to take necessary action. A letter was sent to the Secretary/DGR, Ministry of Communication by the Chief Engineer for the General Manager Bangladesh Railway, Chittagong for approval of de-requisition after observing all formalities as the land was found not necessary at present for railway purpose. Mr. MI Farooque argued that these are all promises on the part of the requiring body and on the basis of the promise the petitioner being in possession of the land paid municipal taxes. It is submitted that the respondents requiring body having opined that the land in question is not required as it has remained surplus after the implementation of the scheme for which it was acquired the authority is under obligation to release and return the same in favour of the petitioner as some other lands of the plots not utilised had already been returned to the respective owners. Mr. Farooqui has cited the case of Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Nationalised Industries Division Vs. Saleh Ahmed and another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs. Saleh Ahmed and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 91 = 46 DLR (AD) 148.</u>

7. In the case referred to above it was decided that "the Government took the decision on agreement to release the Mill in question. Lack of power on the part of the Government so to do is not the plea; rather a belated plea was taken that the decision had been revised by the Government although no such case was made out. Hence applying the principle of promissory estoppel the least that can be said is that the appellant cannot be allowed to act inconsistently and the decision to release the Mill remained binding on them".

8. In the said case, the case of Central London Property Trust Ltd. Vs. High Trees House Ltd. (1947) 1 KB 130, was considered and relied on. The observation made in the cited case by Denning, J was found quoted. The quotation runs as follows:

"Where parties enter into an arrangement which is intended to create legal relation between them and in pursuance of such arrangement one party makes a promise to the other which he knows will be acted on and which is, in fact, acted on by the promise, the Court will treat the promise as binding on the promissor to the extent that it will not allow him to act inconsistently with it even though the promise may not be supported by consideration in the strict sense…………"

9. To bring the instant case within the ambit of the principle of promissory estoppel Mr. MI Farooqui has relied on the case of Motiml Padampat Sugar Mills Co. Ltd. Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and others reported in AIR 1979 (SC) 621. Reading out the judgment of the above referred to case which dealt with promissory estoppel, the learned Advocate invited our attention to a passage from the celebrated Judgment delivered by Bhagwati, J : which reads as follows:

"Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel has been variously called 'promissory estoppel', 'requisite estoppel', 'quasi estoppel' and 'new estoppel', It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppel', it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. The true principle of promissory estoppel seems to be that where one party has' by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppel need not be inhibited by the same limitation as estoppel in the strict sense of the term. It is an equitable principle evolved by the courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason in logic or principle why promissory estoppel should also not be available as a cause of action, if necessary to satisfy the equity. It is not necessary, in order to attract the applicability of the doctrine of promissory estoppel, that the promisee, acting in reliance on the promise, should suffer any detriment. What is necessary is only that the promisee should have altered his position in reliance on' the promise. But if by detriment we mean injustice to the promisee which would result it the promissor were to recede from his promise then detriment would certainly come in as necessary ingredient. The detrimentin such a case is not some prejudice suffered by the promisee by acting on the promise, but the prejudice which would be caused to the promisee, if the promissor were allowed to go back on the promise. If this is the kind of detriment contemplated, it would necessarily be present in every case of promissory estoppel, because it is on account of such detriment which the promisee would suffer if the promissor were to act differently from his promise, that the Court would consider it inequitable to allow the promissor to go back upon his promise. In India not only has the doctrine of promissory estoppel been adopted in its fullness but it has been recognised as affording a cause of action to the person to whom the promise is made. The requirement of consideration has not been allowed to stand in the way of enforcement of such promise. The doctrine of promissory estoppel has also been applied against the Government and the defence based on executive necessity has been categorically negatived. Where the Government makes a promise knowing or intending that it would be acted on by the promisee and, in fact, the promisee, acting in reliance on it, alters his position the Government would be held bound by the promise and the promise would be enforceable against the Government at the instance of the promisee, notwithstanding that there is no consideration for the promise and the promise is not recorded in the form of a formal contract."

10. While relying on the above mentioned case by Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that in the present case the principle laid down in the above cited case relating to promissory estoppel is applicable. The learned Advocate submits that the land though vested in the Government in acquisition after the implementation of the scheme for which the land along with other lands were acquired, has remained surplus and unutilised and the requiring body through its letter having admitted the position sent proposal for the release and restoration of the same to the petitioner with a copy to the petitioner and this being a categorical assurance on behalf of the government that the land will be returned and restored to him and the petitioner acting in reliance of the same assurance having paid the municipal taxes and the Govt. is under obligation to honour the assurance and return the land to the petitioner.

11. Affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No. 1, Mr. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General along with Mr. Md. Altafur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, while refuting the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that there is neither legal nor any equitable obligation on the part of the acquiring authority or the requiring body to release and return the land to the petitioner. It is submitted that though the land was said to have remained surplus after the completion of the scheme it has not been surrendered by the requiring body under sub-section 2 of section 17 nor the Government has withdrawn from the acquisition of the acquired property under the provision of section 8(b) of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. It is submitted that the property having been acquired by the acquiring authority for the requiring body and the compensation having been paid to and drawn by the petitioner, the question of withdrawal from the acquisition did not arise. It is also submitted that the comment given by the Executive Engineer" vide Annexure A-2 cannot be construed as promises from the requiring body and there is nothing to show that the acquiring authority has acted on such assurance. The Executive Engineer or the Chief Engineer acting as General Manager were not the proper authority to give assurance and, as a matter of fact, the authority has not given any assurance which can be treated as a promise giving a scope to the petitioner to make payment of municipal taxes. The learned Assistant Attorney-General, therefore, submits that no equitable right has accrued to the petitioner corresponding to equitable liability on the Government to restore the land in question to the petitioner.

12. Now it is to tie seen whether the respondents are under legal or equitable obligation to release and return the land to the petitioner from whom it was said to have been acquired and has remained surplus after the implementation of the scheme. From the laws relating to the requisition and acquisition of the property it appears that there is no provision for de-requisitioning of the property when the acquisition is complete after receipt of the compensation by the owner from whom the land is taken. So it appears that there is no legal obligation on the part of the acquiring authority to release and return the land to its owner. Even if it is found that the land has remained surplus being not utilised for the purpose of the scheme and stated to be as not required at the moment, there is no legal obligation on the part of the requiring body as well as the acquiring authority to release the land. Now it is to be seen whether there is any equitable obligation on the part of the Government to return the land to the previous owner. The question raised is no doubt of public importance as the claim for the return has been made on the basis of the letter written by the Executive Engineer and also Chief Engineer acting as General Manager, Bangladesh Railway. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has sought to use this writing for invoking the aid of the principle of promissory estoppel. The doctrine of promissory estoppel is comparatively a doctrine of recent origin and it is not as yet well settled as to where and how this principle could be appropriately applied and there is considerable debate over such question even in the country where it originated. The doctrine has been variously called 'promissory estoppel', 'equitable estoppel', quasi estoppel' and 'new estoppel'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and now commonly known as 'promissory estoppel'. It is, as we shall presently point out, neither found in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppel. It is interesting to trace the evolution of this doctrine in England and to refer to some of the English decisions in order to appreciate the true scope and ambit of the doctrine, particularly because it has been the subject of considerable recent development and is steadily expanding. The basis of this doctrine is the interposition of equity and equity has always, true to form, stepped in to mitigate the rigours of strict law.

13. The principle formulated by Justice Denning, as quoted in his own words, are; "that a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and, in fact, acted on, is binding so far as its terms properly apply." The true principle of promissory estoppel, therefore, seems to be that where one party by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal or affect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is, in fact, so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it and it would be inequitable to allow him to de so having regard to the dealings which have taken place between the parties, and this will be so irrespective whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not.

14. We may now go to consider whether the assurance spoken of in the letter Annexures A-1 and A-2 is a promissory estoppel and if not to what extent it is applicable in the present case against the Government. Though it is said that consideration is not essential for the application of principle of promissory estoppel against the Government and the public bodies but it must be inducted into as to whether the commitment of any official of the Government could be construed as assurance and also promise and whether the Government is under obligation to give effect to such assurance if the party is found to have acted on such promise. It has been laid down in the decision cited that the party who has acted on reliance on a promise made by the Government altered his position, is entitled to enforce the promise against the Government even though the promise is not in the form of formal contract. Thus any person or the Government or any statutory body making any promise and, in fact, the promisee acting in reliance on it, alters his position the promise would be enforceable against the promissor at the instance of the promisee, notwithstanding that there is no consideration for the promise and the promise is not recorded in the form of a contract.

15. Relying on the principle laid down in the above mentioned cases Mr. MI Farooqui submits that in the present case not only the Executive Engineer from the side of the requiring body and also the Chief Engineer has written in the note that the parcels of land of the petitioner having not been utilised for the purpose of scheme has remained surplus but they went to the extent of stating that the land can be dc-requisitioned and restored to the petitioner and the copy of the same was sent to the petitioner. These letters have been accepted by the petitioner as assurance and promise on the part of the Government to release the land and restore the same to the petitioner and the petitioner having placed reliance on the said promise paid municipal taxes.

16. On reading the decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner, we have nothing to say against the principle laid down therein with regard to the doctrine of promissory estoppel but in the instant case it is to be seen whether the wishes expressed by some officers could be treated as a promise relying 'on which the petitioner has altered his position and acted to his detriment. From the side of the Government, it is, therefore, contended, that there was no promise either by the requiring body or by the acquiring authority. The expressions appearing in the letters Annexures A, A-1 and A-2 do not reveal that these are promises so as to make the Government obliged to fulfill the same. Furthermore, no such decision has been taken by the highest authority of the requisition body and no proposal was sent to the acquiring authority with the recommendation that the land in question being in excess of the requirement should be released and returned and no such commitment was made by the acquiring authority. Therefore the doctrine of promissory estoppel, in our view, has no manner of application in the present case. The payment of taxes, even if found to have been made, was at the risk and responsibility of the petitioner himself and not at the instance, or on the promise of the authority for the release of the land in favour of the petitioner

<u>17. Mr. Saidur Rahman, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, has referred to the case of Badal Rani Misra alias Badal Rani Goswami and others Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 27 DLR (AD) 65 wherein it has been observed:</u>

<u>"The question relating to the release of requisitioned land falls within the administrative function of the requisitioning authority and if the said authority considered it necessary to seek approval of the Government before passing an order or release of the same, it does not appear now that discretion called for interference by the High Court and how the High Court could pass an order of release under the Requisition of Property Act."</u>

18. In the present case the land of the plot No. 1174 was acquired for the scheme of the Railway authority and after the implementation of the scheme the parcel of the land which has remained unutilised is still under acquisition and for the purpose of the release of the property the Deputy Commissioner of the District is only competent to pass necessary order and here the Deputy Commissioner has neither passed any order for the release nor has given assurance or made any promise for the release of the property. The Government do not admit the possession of the petitioner though the petitioner has claimed his possession. It is not known how the possession of the land which was taken over by the acquiring authority and then handed over to the requiring body could be claimed to be in possession of the petitioner. Nothing could be produced to show that the petitioner got back the possession of the land from the authority. On the contrary, it has been admitted in paragraph 13 of the affidavit-in-reply filed by the petitioner that one Shah Jahan of Multi-purpose Co-operative Society has gone into illegal possession of a portion of the surplus land.

<u>19. The learned Assistant Attorney-General has cited the case of Abdul Mannan Vs. Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, Government of Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 597 wherein it is held:</u>

<u>"The words limiting the power of the Government to withdraw any property from acquisition are contained in the words "at any time before the payment of compensation". If the Government had the power to withdraw any property from acquisition after compensation has been made there would be no finality to the acquisition proceedings nor any sanctity would attach to the government order acquiring any property. If any person, who might have acquired any right to any property after the acquisition of such property by the Government and after compensation has been paid for such acquisition, can be deprived of it, there would be no sanctity attached to such right."</u>

<u>20. As regards the submissions made by the learned Assistant Attorney-General it appears that the power to withdraw any property from acquisition is subject to certain limitations imposed by section 8B of the Act. It is to be seen whether compensation has been paid or not. If compensation has not been paid the order of withdrawal may be made but where finality has reached to the proceeding for requisition and acquisition, no such withdrawal can be ordered after compensation has been made by the authority and received by the party.</u>

21. Mr. MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, having admitted the position that the land in question is still under acquisition, has only claimed to get back the land relying on the principle of promissory estoppel and in order to strengthen the claim of the petitioner in the supplementary affidavit PID handout published in Bangladesh Observer and a news item published in the Daily Ittefaq dated 5.7.93 have been referred to. In the circular directing the officials concerned to return the unutilised lands under the Directorate of Roads and Highways to the respective former owners there being no reference of any authority on the basis of which the circular was issued, we are of the view that the circular cannot and has not acquired the force of law and hence is not enforceable.

22. From the facts and on perusal of the Annexure we are not convinced that there was any promise or even any assurance-from the side of the acquiring authority or the requiring body to return the land which is said to have remained unutilised after the implementation of the scheme and hence the petitioner has acquired no right to get back the land invoking the aid of the principle of promissory estoppel and corresponding liability to the respondents to withdraw from the requisition and return the land to the petitioner.

23. In view of the above, we hold that the decision Contained in the Memo No. RBI Land/105/86-138 dated 11.5.89/12.5.89 Annexure-C issued by the Respondent No. 4 is not liable to be declared asbeing made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and the petitioner is not entitled to get a direction to the respondents to return, restore or de-requisition the surplus and unutilised land measuring 1298 sq. ft or thereabout in CS Khatian No. 543 in CS Dag No. 1174 Mouza Shahar Khilgaon, Dhaka acquired in LA Case No. 63 of 1959-60.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The stay order granted earlier is hereby vacated.

End.

parties:
Golam Morshed ----------- Petitioner. 
Vs.
Farhad Jahan (Mrs.) and ors ------------ Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.: These two Rules obtained under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure have been heard consecutively, but they will be disposed of by common judgment as common questions of facts and law are involved in both.

2. In Civil Revision No. 156 of 1986 the petitioner is a third party. The opposite party No.1 as plaintiff filed on 15.4.85 Title Suit No. 306 of 1985 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract 'against the opposite party No.2 Ruhul Amin Ahmed, opposite party No.3 Dhaka Improvement Trust and opposite party No.4 Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development. The opposite party No.1 averred that the opposite party No.2 was allotted Plot No. NEIL)-4, Road No. 83 Gulshan on 15.8.61 and that he obtained a lease of the same for 99 years by a registered deed dated 30.9.64. He started the construction of a building thereon but could not complete it. He entered into an agreement to sell the said property to the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 for Tk.70,000/- and received an earnest money of Tk. 50,000/- from the opposite party No.1 on 31.1.71 promising to execute and register the sale deed after obtaining necessary permission and clearance certificate from the authority concerned. In part performance of the contract the opposite party No.2 delivered actual and physical possession of the suit property to the opposite party No.1 on 31.1.71. The opposite party No. 1 has constructed 1000 sft. boundary walls on all sides of the suit property, fixed collapsible iron gate in the suit property, planted valuable trees and also erected two rooms with tin shed. She took water line and sewer-age line in the suit property and has been possessing the same to the knowledge of the defendant-opposite parties. The opposite party No.2 received a further sum of Tk. 5,000/- from the opposite party No.1 on 2.2.82 but ultimately the opposite party No.2 failed to execute and register a sale deed in her favour. As such the opposite party No.1 was constrained to file the suit for specific performance of contract.

3. The opposite party No.2, the alleged vendor, did not appear in the said suit but the opposite party Nos. 3 and 4 appeared in the suit and filed a written statement on 11.1.86. The present third party-petitioner filed an application on 19.1.86 under Order 1, rule 10, C.P.C. for being added as a party to the suit. His case is that for arrears of income tax against Mr. Ruhul Amin Ahmed, opposite party No.2, the Income Tax authority put on auction sale the suit land and sold the same by the said auction on 29.12.72 to the third party-petitioner who was the highest bidder. The said auction sale was con-firmed on 30.1.73 and on the same day the possession of the suit land was delivered by the Income Tax authority to the third party-petitioner through a writ of delivery of possession. The sale certificate in respect of the auction sale of the suit land in favour of the third party-petitioner was duly executed by the Income Tax authority and registered in the office the Sub-Registrar, Dhaka. The third party-petitioner is the 16 annas owner of the suit land since his auction purchase and is in possession thereof since 30.1.73. The right, title and interest of the opposite party No.2 extinguished on the very day of auction sale. The plaintiff-opposite party No.1 has fraudulently instituted the suit by creating a false and fraudulent bainapatra for malafide purpose of grabbing the suit land behind the back of the third party-petitioner by misrepresentation of facts. He is a necessary party to the suit.

4. The plaintiff-opposite party No.1 filed a written objection contesting the application of the third party-petitioner. It was contended that the third party-petitioner is a stranger to the contract and his alleged right to the suit property is barred. The third party-petitioner filed Writ Petition No.404 of 1979 in the High Court Division. By judgment and order dated 17.2.82 a Division Bench of the High Court Division found that the third party-petitioner's alleged auction purchase was not fair and a certain letter of his was a piece of forgery. The third party-petitioner has not preferred any appeal against the said decision of the High Court Division. Hence he has no legal right and status in the suit property and is neither a necessary nor a proper party in the suit.

5. Upon perusing the application and the written objection and hearing the parties the learned Subordinate Judge rejected the third party-petitioner's application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. mainly on perusal of the Judgment of Writ Petition No.404/79, holding that the right of the third party-petitioner has been put to an end in the said writ petition.

6. It is against this order of learned Subordinate Judge dated 19.1.86 that the third party-petitioner has obtained the present Rule in Civil Revision No. 156 of 1986.

7. In Civil Revision No.90 of 1987 it is the plaintiff-opposite party No.1 of Civil Revision No.156 of 1986 who is the petitioner. The petitioner has filed a further suit, namely, Title Suit No. 78 of 1986 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka against the defendant-opposite parties for declaration, confirmation of possession and permanent injunction in respect of the self-same land in Gulshan.

8. The averments of the plaintiff-petitioner in this title suit are the same as in the other title suit. In this suit also opposite party No.1, who is the third party-petitioner in Civil Revision No.156 of 1986, preferred an application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. for being added as a party to the suit. He claimed the ownership of the same property by dint of an auction sale by the Income Tax authority, as in the previous civil Revision. Additionally, he stated that after Martial Law was proclaimed on 24.3.82 all writ cases abated and he could not prefer an appeal to the Appellate Division against the decision of the High Court Division in Writ petition No. 404 of 1979, decided on 17.2.82. The opposite party No.1 made an application to the President and Chief Martial Law Administrator for allotment of the suit plot to him on 19.12.85. By order dated 13.1.86 and sub- sequent order dated 8.3.86 the D.I.T. was directed by the Hon'ble President to lease out the suit plot to the opposite party No.1 and report compliance by 15.3.86. Thereafter the D.I.T. allotted the suit plot to the opposite party No.1 by Memo dated 13.3.86 fixing the rate at Tk. 60,00,000/- per bigha. The opposite party No.1 submitted a petition on 20.3.86 to the Chairman, D.I.T. praying for re-fixation of the rate at Tk. 12,00,000/- per bigha for ends of justice. The matter is still under consideration of the Government.

9. The opposite party No. 1 therefore has vital interest over the suit plot by virtue of the allotment made by the D.I.T. The opposite party No.1 claims delivery of possession of the suit plot on 30.1.73, given by the Income Tax. authority. The opposite party No.1 submitted that he was a necessary party and claimed to be impleaded as such.

10. The plaintiff-petitioner filed a written objection and contested the application by stating that the D.I.T. was contesting the suit and the D.I.T. has been restrained by an order of status quo by the High Court Division and so the opposite party No. 1 can neither claim any allotment nor be made a party to the suit in violation of the order of status quo.

11. Upon perusal of the application and writ- ten objection and hearing both sides the learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dated 29.12.86 allowed the application of the opposite party No.1 to be added as a party to the suit on the ground that he got allotment of the suit plot from the D.I:T. and as such his interest in the suit plot can hardly be overlooked, His presence in the suif1 necessary to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit.

12. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioner 'obtained the present Rule.

With regard to Civil Revision No, 156 of 1986 . Mr. M.H. Khandaker, learned Advocate for the third party-petitioner, submitted that it was wrong for the learned Subordinate Judge to reject the application for addition of party on the ground that the right of the third party-petitioner has been put to an end in Writ petition No.404 of 1979, because no question of title can be decided in a writ petition and if any such question has at all been decided then it is not binding on the Civil Courts. He has submitted that the proper course for the learned Subordinate Judge was to admit the petitioner as a party to the suit and' then decide for itself whether the third party- petitioner's auction purchase was good or bad.

13. We have called for the records of Writ petition No. 404 of 1979 and have perused the judgment and order delivered by the Division Bench thereon on 17.2.82. The third party-petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi in the said writ petition calling into question the decision of the Government contained in a letter dated August 8, 1979 signed by a Deputy Secretary and sent in reply to the third party-petitioner's notice served upon the Government. The letter in question, inter alia, conveyed that the original lessee of Plot KI. NE.(L)-4, Road No. 83, Gulshan, Dhaka Mr. Ruhul Amin Ahmed (opposite party No.2) left Bangladesh after liberation and his whereabouts were not known and as such his properties including the plot in question vested in the Government as abandoned property, that the alleged auction sale of the property in execution of Certificate Case Nos. 12 and 13 of 1972-73 at the instance of the Income Tax Officer, . Salary Circle 1, Dhaka was clearly void, ab initio in view of the provisions of P.O. No. 16/72, that consequently the auction purchaser, the third party- petitioner, did not acquire any right, title and interest in the property which vested in the Government from before as abandoned property and that the question of mutating his name and passing a plan in his favour for construction a house on the land does not arise at all. The Division Bench discharged the rule and held that the property in question was an abandoned property, that the auction sale was not held in due observance of all the procedures, that the third party-petitioner did not acquire any right, title and interest in the property which vested in the Government from before as abandoned property.

<u>14. If the third party-petitioner had preferred an appeal or could prefer an appeal before the Appellate Division and the Appellate Division had set aside the aforesaid findings of the High Court Division on any ground whatsoever then that judgment could not have had any efficacy at all. But as long as the said judgment is not appealed against and set aside, its findings and decisions remain binding on both the parties. The third party-petitioner is estopped from resisting the Government's claim that the suit property is an abandoned property. He cannot file and maintain any application for being added as a party to a suit concerning the abandoned property in question and claim an independent title therein. That road is permanently blocked for him.</u>

15. As such the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in rejecting the third party-petitioner's application for being added as a party, because he pleaded an independent title to the property although he is bound by the decision in the writ petition that it is an abandoned property.

16. In the other Civil Revision No. 90 of 1987 the opposite party No.1 (third party-in Civil Revision No. 156 of 1986) has filed his application for addition of party on a different ground. He says that upon the proclamation of Martial Law on 24.3.82 all writ petitions abated and therefore he could not prefer an appeal to the Appellate Division against the judgment and order of the High Court Division dated 17.2.82 in Writ Petition No. 404 of 1979. He, however, made an application to the President and C.M.L.A. for allotment of the suit plot on 19.12.85. Here the opposite party No.1 is giving a goodbye to his claim of independent title to the suit property. He is accepting the status of the property as an abandoned property and praying for allotment of the same. He was in fact allotted the suit plot by Memo dated 13.3.86 by the D.I.T., but the rate of premium per bigha is still in dispute. He has claimed to be added as a party to the suit not on the basis of an independent title to the property but by virtue of a letter of allotment made by the D.I.T. He says that by being an allottee of the suit plot he has acquired an interest and therefore he is a necessary Party.

17. The learned Subordinate Judge has also al-lowed the petition of the opposite party No.1 only on the ground that he has got an allotment of the suit plot.

18. Since in Writ petition No. 404 of 1979 it has been held by this Division that the property in question is an abandoned property and since the opposite party No.1 has at long last reconciled himself to this state of affairs and has come to accept his status as an allottee of a Government property, he can very well be added to this suit for the purpose of upholding the findings in Writ petition No.404 of 1979. The judgment and order in the aforesaid writ petition is a public document. The petitioner in Civil Revision No. 90 of 1987 is not a party to it, but the judgment can be placed before the Court as a relevant fact The opposite party No. 1 has every locus standi to place this judgment before the trial Court as a relevant fact.

19. In that view of the matter we do not find any ground for interference as far as Civil Revision No. 90 of 1987 is concerned.

20. In respect of Civil Revision No.156 of 1986 however, we may add. that if the third party-petitioner changes his stand and again approaches the trial Court for being added as a party to the suit not on the basis of acquiring an independent title therein but on the basis of being an allottee of a Government property, then, like Civil Revision No. 90 of 1987, he may have every locus standi to be added as a party to the suit, but as at presently constituted, his present application cannot be acceded to, because he is estopped from questioning the abandoned character of the suit property.

In the result both the Rules are discharged but without any order as to costs. The connected Civil Rule in Civil Revision No. 90 of 1987 is also discharged.

End.
