parties:
Mustafizur Rahman ------ Appellant 
vs 
Md Amjad Hossain ------ Respondent.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated June 12, 2002 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2214 of 1994)
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is defendant's appeal by leave against the judgment of June 12, 2002 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2214 of 1994 making the Rule absolute upon setting aside the judgment and decree dated January 30, 1994 of the Court of Joint District judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Jessore in Title Appeal No. 301 of 1990 affirming those of dated October 21, 1990 (in the leave granting order inadvertently written June 29, 1983) of the Court of Assistant Judge, Jikargacha, Jessore (in the leave granting order inadvertently written 2nd Court of Munsif, Jessore) in Title Suit No.36 of 1989 (in the leave granting order inadvertently typed Title Suit No.417 of 1978) dismissing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration that the Heba-bil-ewaz deed bearing No.394 of 1989 executed on 5-2-1989 and presented for registration on 7-2-1989 in respect of the property described in the schedule attached to the plaint is fraudulent; forged, fabricated, void, collusive and not binding on the plaintiff.

2. The plaintiff (since deceased) was the maternal grandmother of the defendant and she executed and registered 2 (two) Heba-bil-ewaz deeds on the date as mentioned hereinbefore in favour of the defendant, herein the appellant, grandchild through her predeceased daughter Rokeya and another in favour of a daughter of the plaintiff.

3. Facts averring which the suit was filed, in short, are that, the defendant i.e. the appellant herein, is her grandson through her deceased daughter Rokeya, that she is an old, blind and illiterate woman and she was taken to Jikargacha for treatment and on that date i.e. 22nd Magh, 1395 BS, defendant fraudulently obtained her thumb impressions on some papers and later on by using those papers brought into existence Heba-bil-ewaz deed in his favour in respect of the land measuring 1.67 acres. It is also the case of the plaintiff that she never intended to execute any Heba-bil-ewaz deed in favour of the defendant and that the said Heba-bil-ewaz deed was not acted upon since she is in possession of the property and enjoying the same, that she became certain about the Heba-bil-ewaz deed so created by the defendant No.1 upon obtaining certified copy thereof on February 14, 1989.

4. The suit was contested by the defendant by filing written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stating, inter alia, that the plaintiff used to live with her son Amjad Hossain and he sold some of his property as well as the property of the plaintiff and he appropriated the money got upon selling plaintiff's land. The said conduct of her son Amjad annoyed the plaintiff, that Amjad Hossain used to misbehave with her and also used to torture her to grab her property, that Amjad Hossain made demand of the share of the land which he would get after death of the plaintiff, that the plaintiff gave land to Amjad Hossain which he would have inherited from his mother but still then he demanded share from the land that was with the plaintiff after transferring to Amjad Hossain, that in the background of the said fact the plaintiff decided to make gift of her property in favour of her two daughters, Rahela and Khatun Bibi as well as in favour of the defendant who is the son of her deceased daughter Rokeya Khatun, that Khatun Bibi being well off declined the proposal of her mother and asked her mother to make a gift of the property in favour of Rahela and the defendant and thereupon the plaintiff on her free will made the gift in favour of Rahela and the defendant and that the defendant went into possession of the property so gifted to him and enjoying the same. It is the contention of the defendant that the plaintiff being forced by her son Amjad Hossain filed the suit making untrue statements.

5. It may be mentioned during the pendency of the suit Rativan Bibi, the plaintiff, died leaving her heirs i.e. her sons Amjad Hossain and Abul Hossain, daughters Rahela and Khatun Bibi.

6. The trial Court dismissed the suit on the finding that the suit is not barred by limitation, that the Heba-bil-ewaz deed is a genuine one, that Rativan Bibi executed and registered the deed in question on her free will, that allegation of fraud in the execution and registration of the document has not been established, that Rativan Bibi executed two deeds on the same day, one in favour of her daughter Rahela and another in favour of the defendant but she is questioning only the genuineness of the document executed and registered in favour of the defendant and as regard the other document no complaint has been made and no relief has been sought against the other document i.e. Heba-bil-ewaz deed made in favour of Rahela, daughter of Rativan Bibi. The trial Court also held that the suit was not maintainable since plaintiff being a party to the document did not pray for cancellation of the same but filed the suit seeking merely declaration that the deed is fraudulent and not binding on her.

7. As against the judgment and decree of the trial Court, the plaintiff went on appeal but without any success. Thereupon the plaintiff moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule.

8. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding ".... the original plaintiff Rativan was definitely an old lady. The very fact that plaintiff allegedly executed the heba-bil-ewaz deed by putting her left thumb impression clearly proved that she was an illiterate lady and, as such, burden was upon the defendant, namely, the recipient of the deed, to prove that she executed and registered the same having independent advice and was fully aware about the contents of the deed following the principle of special onus of proof not a single natural independent witness deposed that Rativan executed and registered the heba-bil-ewaz in question voluntarily having been fully aware about its contents. Thus, the defendant failed to discharge his special onus.....”

9. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division failed to consider the material fact that on the self-same date another Heba-bil-ewaz deed was executed and registered by Rativan Bibi, the plaintiff, in favour of her daughter, Rahela and no exception was taken by the plaintiff as regard the said Heba-bil-ewaz deed resorting to the plea of Rativan's being old, illiterate and 'pardanashin', nor any plea was taken in respect of the Heba-bil-ewaz deed in favour of Rahela that the said deed was not acted upon, that DW 6, as independent witness, deposed that he knew Rativan Bibi and he identified the thumb impression of Rativan Bibi in the deed in question and that he was present at the time of execution of the deed in question, that DW 2 stated that he knew Rativan Bibi and he read over the contents of the deed in question to Rativan and thereupon she, upon being fully aware about the contents of the document, voluntarily executed the deed by putting thumb impression but the High Court Division did not consider the evidence of these witnesses.

10. The question of special onus with regard to a transaction entered into with a pardanashin lady and the question of proof of an independent advice is indispensable in case of a transaction where the protection to a pardanashin woman is available came up for consideration before this Division in the case of Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury and others vs Gani Ahmed and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 1. (also reported in 1979 BSCR, 375) and after reviewing good number of cases, it has been observed, "On a review of the authorities cited above, it is manifest that this special rule of onus has been devised to give protection to certain categories of women in the Indian subcontinent who suffer from some social disabilities because of purdah system. Pardanashin women are excluded from social intercourse, except with very near relations and communion outside the narrow family circle is barred to them. It applies to all pardanashin women, literate or illiterate. The criteria is, whether she is a pardanashin or not. It is, of course, a question of fact. Next, we get, that the protection granted to the pardanashin ladies has been extended to ignorant and illiterate women though not strictly speaking pardanashin.

11. "If, in a case of transfer by a pardanashin lady, a dispute arises as to its validity, the onus is always on the party who seeks to hold the transferor to the terms of the deed to satisfy the Court on evidence that she substantially understood the disposition and she executed the deed with full understanding of what she was doing and effect of the transaction. It is to be observed that independent advice by itself is not an essential burden to be discharged, unless there are some special circumstances calling for its application, in that the donee or the transferee stood in a position of active confidence or had fiduciary relationship with the pardanashin lady. It is only in such cases, the donee or transferee will carry the additional burden to prove that the lady had independent and disinterested advice from persons other than the recipient of the document"

12. In the aforesaid case the question whether the rule of special onus laid down for the protection of pardanashin women can be extended to a person other than the pardanashin lady but claiming interest through her and in that connection it has been observed. "It is true that there is some observation in the authorities cited above, which is apt to lead one to think that whenever there is a challenge to the validity of a document executed by a pardanashin woman, though she might not herself be a party to the suit or challenging it, any person claiming through her impeaching validity of the disposition may also get the benefit of the special rule of onus granted to her. Could this rule be extended to this extent? We think, though it is difficult to spell out the said onus from the cited authorities, nonetheless, the ambiguity of the language is there and it requires clarification in the social context of the day, when there has been active steps for emancipation of women and the social condition has greatly changed and is changing. To allow the special rule of onus granted to the pardanashin lady to extend to any one other than the pardanashin lady herself, will not only be a retrograde step, but may, in many cases, work to the disability of the lady. The rule is for the protection and should not be so applied as to make it either a disability in the exercise of her full right to the property or to convert a bonafide transaction into one of suspicion and make it subject matter of frivolous litigation. This will be more so, when there will be distance of time and the disputing parties will be persons other than original parties to the deed. It may be that the party relying on the special rule of onus might be claiming adversely to her".

13. The question of special onus also came up for consideration before this Division in the case of Rokeya Khatun vs Alijan @ Alijan Bepari and others reported in 34 DLR (AD) 266. Therein it has been observed "Once it is shown that the impugned disposition was by a pardanashin woman the burden lies upon the party or parties who set up and rely on the impugned deed of disposition to show that the deed had been explained to and understood by the party under the disability. Thus, so far as the burden to prove that the pardanashin woman had full knowledge and comprehension about the terms of the disposition, and that it was her mental act, is upon those who want to uphold the disposition". In the case the question of extension of the rule of special onus laid down for protection of pardanashin woman whether can be extended to a person other than the pardanashin lady but claiming interest through her also considered in the background of the observation made in the case of Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury and others vs Gani Ahmed and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 1.

<u>14. The proposition of law relating to special burden of proof in respect of the Heba-bil-ewaz deed in question if considered in the background of the admitted facts that on the self same date Rativan Bibi executed 2 Heba-bil-ewaz deeds, one in favour of the defendant who is the son of Rativan Bibi's deceased daughter Rokeya and another in favour of Rativan Bibi's daughter Rahela and that as no exception was taken in respect of the Heba-bil-ewaz deed in the name of Rativan Bibi's daughter Rahela, conclusion can safely be arrived at that Rativan Bibi executed the Heba deed in favour of her grandson through her daughter at the relevant time deceased and in favour of her another daughter totally of her own free will and she (Rativan Bibi) executed the deed being fully aware of the contents thereof and the nature of the transaction as deposed by the DWs 2 and 6 in respect of whom hardly any exception legally sustainable can be taken. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that while the said Division considering the transaction in question in favour of the defendant referring to the concept of special onus with regard to a transaction entered into by a pardanashin lady failed to consider the material fact that Rativan Bibi on the same date executed 2 (two) documents, one in favour of the defendant and other in favour of her daughter Rahela and registered the same subsequently on the same date, but taking exception only in respect of the transaction in respect of the defendant. It has already been mentioned that the defendant has established by the evidence of PWs 2 and 6, that Rativan Bibi, the grandmother of the defendant, executed the document in favour of the defendant after being aware of the nature of the transaction.</u>

15. In the instant case another important question of law escaped the notice of the High Court Division as to maintainability of the suit. The trial Court dismissed the suit, amongst others, on the finding that the suit was not maintainable since Rativan Bibi being party to the document, in respect whereof declaration was sought was required to ask for cancellation thereof.

16. The High Court Division while setting aside the concurrent judgment of the courts below, was of the view that defendant on whom there was special burden was required to establish that Rativan Bibi (an illiterate lady), executed and registered the same "having independent advice and was fully aware about the contents of the deed".

<u>17. It has already been mentioned that on the self-same date Rativan Bibi executed 2 Heba-bil-ewaz deeds, one in favour of the defendant and another in favour of her daughter Rokeya and later on registered the same. The date of presentation of the deeds for registration is the same. DW 2 has deposed that he read over the document to Rativan Bibi and thereafter she executed the deed. DW 6 has deposed about the execution of the deed by Rativan Bibi. The very fact that Rativan Bibi is taking only exception in respect of the transaction made in favour of the defendant but not taking any exception in respect of transaction made in favour of her daughter Rokeya, demonstrates that she was quite aware of the nature of the transaction made in favour of the recipient of the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds executed by her. The undenied fact is that defendant is the grandson of Rativan Bibi through her predeceased daughter Rokeya i.e. the mother of the defendant was dead at the time of making the transaction, Heba-bil-ewaz deed, in favour of the defendant and in the background of the said fact, the transaction in question in favour of the defendant by Rativan Bibi was quite probable since she has already allotted the property to her sons which they would have inherited on her death.</u>

<u>18. The plaintiff has filed the suit alleging fraud in bringing into existence the deed in question. The law is now settled that one who alleges fraud for setting particular transaction, the burden lies on him. In this connection reference may be made to the case of Harmes and another vs Hinkson reported in AIR 1946 PC 156 and the case of Paresh Chandra Bhowmick vs Hiralal Nath and others reported in 36 DLR (AD) 156.</u>

<u>19. That the transaction in question was not the product of fraud or undue influence is evident from the fact as stated hereinbefore, that Rativan Bibi on the same date executed 2 Heba-bil-ewaz deeds, one in favour of the defendant and another in favour of her daughter and lateron registered the said deeds on the same date, but taking exception only in respect of the transaction made in favour of the defendant. Had the transactions been the product of fraud, coercion or undue influence or had the transactions been not the product of Rativan's free will and that had the Heba-bil-ewaz deeds been not executed and registered by her without understanding the nature of the transaction and of being unaware of the contents of the documents, Rativan Bibi would, in the normal course of conduct and behaviour, have taken exception to both the transactions instead of that she is taking exception only in respect of one transaction i.e. the transaction which was made in favour of the defendant, and this shows lack of bonafide on her part and that she being influenced by some other interested persons, as contended by the defendant by the sons of Amzad, one of the sons of Rativan Bibi, instituted the suit.</u>

20. In the background of the discussions made hereinbefore we find merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Abdur Razzaque Miah, Advocate with Nurul Mustafa, Advocate—For the Appellants. 
Sarder Abul Hossain, Advocate—For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Mokbul Ahmed Mia alias Moqbul Ahmed and others ----- Appellants
Vs. 
Md Golam Mostafa and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
SM Ziaul Karim J: This appeal, at the instance of defendant Nos. 2-5 appellants is directed against the judgment and decree dated 25-9-1988 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Feni in Title Suit No. 48 of 1985 partly decreeing the suit.

2. Short facts leading to this appeal are, that on 11-8-1985 the respondent No. 1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 48 of 1985 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, Feni for declaration that registered kabala deed Nos. 5849-5852 dated 18-8-1982 as described in the Schedule 'Ka' of the plaint in respect of 1.50 acres of land out of 1.62 acres in Plot No. 464 as described in Schedule 'Kha' of the plaint are fraudulent, inoperative, without consideration, and antedated with that of the plaintiff's registered kabala deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982.

3. The plaintiff's case, in brief, is that 1.62 acres of land described in Schedule 'Kha' of the plaint had originally belonged to Mojibul Haq (defendant No. 1) and his brother Nurul Haq; subsequently, on 23-4-1982 defendant No.1 transferred his share equivalent to 81 decimals of land to the plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 26,000 that, thereby the right, title and interest of defendant No.1 was extinguished in the Schedule property. Subsequently, the plaintiff came to learn that defendant No.1 earlier created antedated 4(four) registered kabala deeds dated 18-8-1982 in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 showing the date of execution on 21-4-1982 in respect of 1.50 acres of land by which the defendant Nos. 2-5 were claiming title over the suit land. The defendant No.1 had no authority to transfer such land. The plaintiff further came to know that one Shamsul Haq purchased 3(three) stamps bearing Nos. 32373, 32374 and 32375, each of price of Taka 1,500 from Comilla Treasury by which defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 5 created kabalas in their names; that on query, on 6-10-1982 plaintiff came to learn that originally those stamps were purchased by one Lakhi Ahmed. One Joynal Abedin was shown as purchaser of stamp bearing No. 12327 dated 15-4-1982 used by defendant No. 4 but 15-4-1982 was public holiday and no stamp was sold on that day. The defendants collusively created those antedated deeds. Hence the suit.

4. The defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that he transferred 11 decimals of land to plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but the plaintiff fraudulently replaced 11 decimals by 81 decimals and Taka 10,000 by Taka 26,000, when the matter was brought to light, he refused to register sale deed in favour of plaintiff. But subsequently, the matter in issue was settled at the intervention of VP Joynal Abedin, MP to the effect that the plaintiff would return back 70 decimals of land, thereafter both parties kept their respective deeds with him but subsequently, he lost those deeds.

5. Defendant Nos. 25 appeared in the suit by filing joint written statement, contending, inter alia, that the suit land originally belonged to Nirmal Kumar Shil and others who transferred the same to defendant Nos. 2-5 by 5(five) registered kabala deeds dated 28-4-1981 at a consideration of Taka 60,000. Subsequently, it was found that the Khatian in respect of suit land was prepared in the names of defendant No. 1 and his brother Nurul Haq, but to avoid complexity they again purchased the suit land from defendant No. 1, who got 1.62 acres of land by amicable settlement with his brother. No fraud was practiced for execution and registration of deeds. On 15-4-1982 Joynal Abedin collected the stamps. It was also stated that defendant No. 1 transferred 11 decimals of land to plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but it was shown as 81 decimals at a consideration of Taka 26,000; that the matter was settled between the parties and to that effect plaintiff promised to return back 70 decimals of land. VP Joynal Abedin MP was the mediator, to whom both parties kept their respective deeds but subsequently, he lost the same. They prayed to dismiss the suit.

On the pleading following issues were settled:

(a) Whether the suit was maintainable in the present form?

(b) Whether the plaintiff was entitled to get a decree as prayed for?

(c) Whether the suit was barred for defect of party?

(d) Whether the relief claimed was properly valued and the suit filed with sufficient court fees?

6. In course of trial plaintiff examined 5 (five) witnesses and defendant Nos. 2-5 also examined 5(five) witnesses in support of their respective cases. On the contrary defendant No. 1 was also examined as witness.

7. By the impugned judgment and decree the learned Subordinate Judge, partly decreed the suit. Hence the appeal.

8. Mr Abdur Razzaque Miah, the learned Advocate appearing with Mr Nurul Mustafa, Advocate, supports the appeal and submits that the suit land belonged to defendant No. 1 and his brother Nurul Haq in equal share. Subsequently, by amicable settlement defendant No.1 got 1.62 acres of land, who thereafter transferred 1.50 acres of land to the appellants by 4(four) registered kabala deeds dated 18-8-1982 which was executed on 21-4-1982. He adds that defendant No.1 transferred only 11 decimals of land out of 1.62 acres of land to plaintiff by registered kabala deed dated 23-4-1982 at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but the plaintiff fraudulently managed to get 81 decimals of land registered showing the consideration for Taka 26,000. He submits that as per provisions under section 47 of the Registration Act, the sale deed which was executed earlier but registered later in point of time will prevail over the sale deed executed later but registered earlier in the point of time. The learned Counsel further submits that the plaintiff failed to prove his own case. In support of his contention, he referred the case of Md Naimuddin Sarder vs Md Abul Kalam Biswas and another reported in 39 DLR (AD) 237 wherein it is held:

"Plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendant's case is no ground for passing a decree in favour of the plaintiff."

He adds that the suit is barred for defect of parties, inasmuch as Nurul Haq, brother of defendant No. 1, was not made party. Moreover, without partition, suit itself is not maintainable. The learned Counsel has contended that the plaintiff filed the suit for declaration that four deeds described in the Schedule 'Ka' of the plaint are fraudulent, inoperative and antedated, but such declaration having effect of cancellation of deed, so in view of the provision laid down in section 7(iv)(c) of the Court Fees Act advalorem fees to be paid for institution of suit. In support of his contention, he referred the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs Faizun Nesa Chowdhury reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46 wherein it is held:

Section 7(iv)(c) of the Court Fees Act—

"Advalorem fees to be paid for cancellation of a document."

The cancellation of document is much more than a declaratory relief; that it is a substantive relief, and that advalorem court fee will be necessary for such a relief under section 7(iv)(c) of the Court Fees Act.

9. The learned Counsel lastly, submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court failed to weigh and sift the evidence on record as required by law and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

10. Mr Sarder Abul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for respondent No. 1, opposes the appeal and submits that the defendant No. 1 transferred 81 decimals of land described in the Schedule of the plaint to the plaintiff vide registered kabala deed dated 23-4-1982. He adds that with a view to frustrate registered sale deed of plaintiff, the defendant Nos. 25 fraudulently managed to show the date of execution of their sale deeds on 21-4-1982. He submits that record of right stands in the name of the plaintiff and he has been paying the rent. He adds that evidence regarding collecting of stamps suffers from glaring inconsistencies and contradictions. The defendant Nos. 2-5 also failed to prove his case. In support of his contention, he referred the case of Haque Brothers Limited and others vs Shamsul Haque and others reported in 39 DLR 290 wherein it is held—

Section 101 of the Evidence Act

—"Burden of proof lies on the person who asserts that a fact exists."

He also referred the case of Government of Bangladesh and another vs Mashiur Rahman and others reported in 2 MLR (AD) 316 wherein it is held:

"Fact of fraud is a matter of inference from proved facts and circumstances of each case and the evidence received by the court. Each circumstance by itself may not tell much, but when a bundle of circumstances are taken together they may bring to light a fraudulent or dishonest plan to commit fraud."

He also relied upon the case of Haji Karamat Ali Master vs Lehajuddin Talukder & others reported in 41 DLR 447 wherein it is held:

"Onus of proof—

It is for the defendant to prove that the disputed document was executed on the purported date—mere assertion in the written statement cannot be treated as evidence—Document being between two brothers registered at a different Sub-Registrar's office and attesting witnesses being close relations of the recipient, there are strong circumstances in favour of collusion."

Mr Hossain lastly submits, that the learned Judge of the trial Court after considering the evidence on record rightly decreed the suit which calls for no interference by this Court. Thus, the appeal is liable to be dismissed.

11. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides, let us now weigh and sift the evidence on record adduced by the parties.

12. PW 1 Md Golam Mustafa is the plaintiff. He deposed that 1.62 acres of land appertaining to Plot No. 464 belonged to Majibul Haq (defendant No. 1) and his brother Nurul Haq. On 23-4-1982 Majibul Haq transferred 81 decimals of land to him by registered kabala deed at a consideration of Taka 26,000. He proved his kabala deed as Exhibit 1. Nurul Haq did not give up his share of 81 decimals of land in favour of Majibul Haq. On 18-8-1982 defendant No.1 transferred 1.50 acres of land by four kabala deeds in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 showing execution prior two days of the registration. He proved the kabalas under challenge as Exhibits 2-2(ga). He added that one Shamsul Haq and Lakhi Ahmed were shown as purchasers of stamps from Comilla Treasury Office on 29-3-1982 and 15-4-1982 respectively which were used for the aforesaid four deeds. So, he sought for declaration that the said deeds were antedated, illegal and inoperative, etc.

13. PW 2 Bazlur Rahman deposed that he was present at the time of registration of 81 decimals of land in favour of plaintiff.

14. PW 3 ASM Zahangir Kabir, son of Nurul Haq. deposed that his father did not give up his share in favour of defendant No. 1.

15. PW 4 Abul Kasem and PW 5 Sadrul Amin Munshi merely produced the register book of sale of stamps.

16. DW 1 Kubbat Ahamed is the defendant No. 3. He deposed that earlier on 21-4-1981, recorded tenant Nirmal and others transferred the suit land to them vide six registered kabalas. Subsequently, it was found that in SA Khatian the names of defendant No.1 and his brother were recorded. To avoid complexity they again purchased 1.50 acres of land from defendant No.1 by registered kabala deeds which were executed on 21-4-1982. On 23-4-1982 defendant No.1 transferred 11 decimals of land in favour of the plaintiff.

17. DW 2 Abdul Mannan, DW 3 Maku Mia deposed that the plaintiff was not in possession in the suit land. DW 4 Nurul Islam was the witness of the deeds under challenge.

18. Defendant No.1 ATM Mujibul Haq deposed that he became owner of 1.62 acres of land by amicable settlement. On 23-4-1982 he transferred 11 decimals of land to plaintiff at a consideration of Taka 10,000 but the plaintiff fraudulently managed to get registered 81 decimals of land showing consideration price of Taka 26,000. Subsequently, the matter in dispute was settled at the intervention of VP Joynal Abedin MP and the plaintiff promised to return back rest 70 decimals of land.

19. These are all of the material evidence adduced by both parties.

20. We have gone through the plaint, written statements, depositions of the witnesses, all exhibits, impugned judgment and decree and given our anxious considerations to the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides.

21. Admittedly, the defendant No. 1 transferred 1.50 acres of land to defendant Nos. 2-5 by four registered kabala deeds bearing Nos. 5849-5852 dated 18-8-1982 showing the execution date on 21-4-1982 in respect of 1.50 acres of land. It is the case of the plaintiff that defendant No. 1 transferred 81 decimals of land from the same schedule in favour of him vide registered Kabala deed No. 4668 dated 23-4-1982 but defendants disowned it.

22. Now the question which calls for our consideration is, whether the deeds which were executed earlier and registered later will prevail upon the deeds which were registered earlier, and those deeds were antedated and the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law, resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned judgment and decree.

23. On critical analysis of the evidence on record, we find that one Shamsul Haq purchased 3(three) stamps bearing Nos. 32373 to 32375 each at price of Taka 1,500 from Comilla Treasury on 29-3-1982, and the same were used by defendant Nos. 2, 3 and 5. We further, find that one Lakhi Ahmed purchased stamp bearing No. 12327 on 15-4-1982 from the Comilla Treasury which were used by defendant No. 4. It appears that the stamps used for four kabalas were purchased prior to its execution dated i.e. on 21-4-1982. So, the same cannot be regarded as antedated comparing with that of the kabala deed dated 23-4-1982 of the plaintiff.

24. It is well settled that in the case of successive transfers of the selfsame property in favour of the different persons by a common vendor by registered documents, the dispute as to the precedence of one document over the other is to be determined in accordance with the principle laid down in section 47 of the Registration Act, which provides:

"A registered document shall operate from the time from which it would have commenced to operate if no registration thereof had been required or made, and not from the time of its registration."

25. It is clear that a document that has been registered relates back to the date of its execution and when the question of title as between the two contestants claiming on the basis of successive documents executed by the selfsame vendor must be determined with reference to the title to the later on the date of execution and not of registration.

26. In the case of Fazar Ali and others vs Afzal Mia and another reported in 9 DLR 258 wherein it is held-

"Suppose a man purchases a property 'A' on the 7th of a month and another man purchases the self-same property on the 9th of the month and the first man got the kabala registered on the 13th and the second man got that kabala registered on the 12th of the month. Now the question arises as to which document will prevail. There is no doubt the answer would be that the kabala which was executed earlier would prevail over the kabala executed later, though registered earlier. So, the date of registration is not a criterion for the purpose of determining when the sale takes effect, though without registration certain transactions may be perfected."

<u>27. In the instant case we find that the defendant No. 1 executed four kabalas on 21-4-1982 but the same were registered on 18-8-1982 but defendants No. 1 executed and registered kabala in favour of plaintiff on 23-4-1982, so, in our view, the kabalas which were executed on 21-4-1982 by the defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant Nos. 2-5 shall prevail.</u>

28. In the case of Rafiqul Islam (Md) vs Mir Abdul Ali reported in 44 DLR (AD) 176 wherein it is held-

"Registration Act

Section 47

Sale deed executed earlier but registered later in point of time will prevail over sale-deed executed later but registered earlier. The criterion in such cases for the purpose of determining when the sale takes effect is not the date of registration but the date of execution of the deed itself."

It further appears to us that the plaintiff instituted the suit by fixed court fees making the following statement:

“নালিশী ৪ টি কবলার লিপিকৃত মূল্য নং ৭৪,০০০ টাকা আদালতের এলাকা নির্নয়ের জন্য বর্তমান মোকদ্দমা তায়দাদ ধরা হইল। কিন্তু বর্তমান মোকদ্দমা ঘোষনামূলক প্রতিকারের মোকদ্দমা বিধায় ৪ টি কবলার জন্য ২৫ ঙ ৪= ১০০ টাকা পৃথক ৪ টি ঠিকানায় কোর্ট ফি যুক্তে বর্তমান মোকদ্দমা দায়ের করা গেল।”

<u>29. The plaintiff sought for declaration that four kabalas described in schedule "Ka" of the plaint are fraudulent, inoperative and antedated. Such declaration having the effect of written instrument void or voidable and the same will come within the purview of section 39 of the Specific Relief Act. Now we shall consider whether the suit is maintainable without advalorem court fees.</u>

30. For the convenience of understanding the provisions of sections 39 and 42 of the Specific Relief Act read as hereunder:

"Section 39-When cancellation may be ordered—Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court may, in its discretion, so adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

If the instrument has been registered under the Registration Act, 1908, the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation."

Section 42-Discretion of Court as to Declaration of Status or Right:

"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the Court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.

Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do."

31. In view of the aforesaid provisions we hold that the declaration as sought by the plaintiff having effect of written instrument void or voidable. In the case of Sufia Khanam Chowdhury vs Faizun Nesa Chowdhury reported in 39 DLR (AD) 46 wherein it is held:

Specific Relief Act (I of 1877)

Section 42

Suit for mere declaration that an instrument was void without a prayer for the relief of cancellation.

A suit for mere declaration that an instrument was void without a prayer for the relief of cancellation. It appears that the wordings of these two sections, 39 and 42, are such as to create some confusion in a casual mind about the nature of reliefs contemplated therein when a suit is brought for declaration of nullity and, or for cancellation of any written instrument.

Relief by declaration of nullity of any instrument and also relief by cancellation of the instrument provided in section 39.

Section 42 does not specifically provide for declaration of nullity of any written instrument; nevertheless a decree for nullity of an instrument in view of the general provision therein comes under section 42.

If a person's right and title is clouded by an instrument he may seek a declaration under section 42 to nullify the effect of such an instrument.

Relief by declaration of nullity of any instrument and also relief by cancellation of the instrument have been specifically provided for in section 39, Specific Relief Act. Section 42 does not specifically provide for declaration of nullity of any written instrument; nevertheless a decree for nullity of any instrument comes in under this section in view of the general provision therein as to declaration of any legal character as expressed in the words "any person entitled to any legal character". If, by an instrument, a person's right and title is clouded or threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title is clouded or threatened, he may seek a declaration under this section to the effect that by the instrument his right and title has not been affected or that any other person who denies his title or claims title in himself has not acquired any right or title thereby.

<u>32. The instant suit is a suit for declaration and in view of the aforesaid principle the same is maintainable without advalorem court fees. In this regard we are unable to accept the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant.</u>

33. Having regard to the facts we are in respectful agreement with the principles enunciated in the decisions as referred by the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 but the facts leading to those cases are distinguishable with that of the instant case, we are, therefore unable to accept the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the respondent No. 1 but, on the contrary, other legal plea taken by the learned Counsel for the appellant prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

34. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative we are led to the conclusion that the impugned judgment and decree suffers from illegality and impropriety which calls for interference by this Court. Thus, the appeal having merit succeeds.

35. In the result the appeal is allowed with cost. The impugned judgment and decree dated 25-9-1988 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Feni in Title Suit No. 48 of 1985 is hereby set aside. The suit stands dismissed.

Send down the lower Court's records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule, arising out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, is directed against the Judgment and decree dated 23-10-1996, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola allowing. Title Appeal No. 141 of 1986 and thereby setting aside those of the learned Assistant Judge, Charfasson, Bhola, passed on 28-8-1986 dismissed Title Suit No. 385 of 1985.

2. The relevant facts are that the opposite party No. 1 instituted the above noted suit as plaintiff against the petitioner and brothers (principal-defendant Nos. 1-7) for Specific performance of Contract by way of execution and registration of a heba deed on the basis of unregistered 'Ekrarnama'. Plaint case was that the land measuring 4'80 acres previously belonged to Habibur Rahman Khondaker, who executed an unregistered deed of agreement and transferred possession of the land to his son plaintiff Abdul Kader on 30-4-1976 but he promised to get the said heba deed registered within a few days. However, the original owner handed over delivery of possession of the suit land to the plaintiff on the very day of execution of the deed. Since then the plaintiff has been in possession of the said 4.80 acres of land. Soon after the execution of the deed, the father of the plaintiff died on 5-7-1976 and could not register the executed heba deed during his lifetime. So the plaintiff requested his brother and other heirs of the deceased to execute and register a heba deed in favour of the plaintiff, and accordingly, the defendant Nos. 8-11 transferred their shares to the plaintiff by a registered heba deed dated 20-8-1976. But the principal-defendant Nos. 1-7 i.e. one daughter and another daughter's heirs, having their share to the extent of 0.88 acres (suit land) at last refused to execute and register heba deed conveying the suit land in terms of the 'Ekrarnama' in the month of Chaitra 1383 BS and, as such, the plaintiff filed the suit to enforce performance of the contract specifically against the defendant Nos. 1-7 treating the executed unregistered deed of gift dated 30-4-1976 as an agreement of transfer.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-7 contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that their predecessor Habibur Rahman Khondaker being owner of the suit property, never executed and registered the alleged 'Ekrarnama' or deed of gift dated 30-4-1976. Rather he died leaving 4 sons in plaintiff and defendant Nos. 8-10 and 2 daughters in defendant Nos. 1 and 11 and also other heirs in defendant Nos. 2-7 who are successors-in-interest of deceased daughter Lutfan Nahar. Accordingly, the defendant Nos. 1-7 have inherited the suit land amicably and they have possession in the said land. In order to deprive the defendant Nos. 1-7 the plaintiff created the alleged 'Ekrarnama' for execution and registration of a heba deed in connivance with the defendant Nos. 8-11. So, the defendant Nos. 1-7 have no obligation to execute and register any deed of gift transferring the suit land to the plaintiff.

4. At the trial, the learned Assistant Judge, examined 4 PWs and 3 DWs and admitted several documentary evidence for consideration. After due consideration be found that the plaintiff could not prove genuineness of the Ekrarnama and also possession of the plaintiff clearly and, as such, he dismissed the suit by the Judgment and decree dated 28-8-1986.

5. On appeal, preferred by the plaintiff, the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola allowed the same on setting aside the Judgment of the trial Court with the findings that the owner of the suit land executed the Ekrarnama and handed over possession of the suit land to the plaintiff and, as such, the defendant Nos. 1-7, being heirs of the original owner, are liable to execute and register a heba deed in favour of the plaintiff and accordingly the suit was decreed by the appellate Court.

6. Mr NH Khandker assisted by Mr Md Anwarul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners, submits that the alleged 'Ekrarnama' is neither a deed of gift nor it is enforceable against the defendant Nos. 1-7 in a suit of specific performance of contract. Because there was no existence of any Contract to be performed. He submits that it was a mere promise to transfer the suit land by way of gift and, as such, after the death of the donor promissor his heirs are not bound by such promise. It is submitted that the plaintiff did not get delivery of possession on the basis of the said 'Ekrarnama', According to his submission, the defendant Nos. 1-7 challenged the executing signatures of the 'Ekrarnama' and the plaintiff should have asked for expert's opinion to prove genuineness of the deed and having failed to do so, the plaintiff cannot also succeed in the suit. But the learned Judge of the appellate Court without considering the facts, circumstances and material evidence on record most illegally decreed the suit resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and, as such, it cannot be legally sustained.

7. Mr Shamsul Alam assisted by Mr Abul Basher, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits that there are material evidence on record to prove that the owner of the suit land executed the 'Ekrarnama' and handed over delivery of possession of the suit land to his youngest son (plaintiff). The learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola compared the executing signatures available in Exhibit 2 with those of another old registered deed (Exhibit 6) in a lawful manner under section 73 of the Evidence Act and found the signatures of Habibur Rahman Khondaker on the 'Ekrarnama' genuine. He submits that the plaintiff got physical possession on the basis of the 'Ekrarnama' (Exhibit 2).But since the owner Habibur Rahman promised to get heba deed registered, but failed to do so, and he expressed of his pious wish of making gift as contained in the 'Ekrarnama' and that on his death his heirs should execute and register the intended deed of gift the defendant Nos. 1-7 are liable to perform their part of the contract like the defendant No. 8-11. He submits that some of his heirs i.e. defendant Nos. 8-11 had already performed their part of the contract by executing and registered a heba deed transferring their portion of share to the plaintiff. Therefore, the remaining heirs i.e. the defendant Nos. 1-7, are also bound to convey their share to the plaintiff through execution and registration of a heba deed as contemplated in the 'Ekrarnama'. He further submits that the learned Subordinate Judge, Bhola passed his Judgment in its true perspective of the whole affairs after true consideration of the evidence on record and, as such, there is nothing to be interfered with.

8. The main question involved in the case is whether the alleged 'Ekrarnama' is a deed containing legal contract specifically en-forcible by any court of law in the present nature of the suit.

<u>9. Admittedly, the father of the plaintiff-defendant No. 1, 8-11 and predecessor-in interest of the defendant Nos. 2-7 namely Habibur Rahman Khondaker was owner of 4.88 acres including the suit land. It appears from the Exhibit 2, that the said owner, in fact, executed a deed of gift conveying the entire 4.88 acres including the suit land to his youngest son plaintiff on 30-4-76. It is clearly stated in the deed “আমার অগত্য স্নেহের নিদর্শন স্বরুপ ও তোমার লেখা পড়া ও ভবিষ্যতের জন্য আমার খাস দখলীয় জমি হইতে ৪.৮০ শতাংশ জমি যাহার মূল্য অনুমান ৫,০০০ পাঁচ  হাজার টাকা হইবে তাহা তোমাকে হেবা-প্রদান করিলাম। উক্ত হেবার সম্পত্তি অদ্যই তোমাকে দখল বুঝাইয়া দিলাম।”</u>

<u>10. Subsequently, it is stated in the deed that he would get the heba deed registered very soon, but if he dies in the meantime, his heirs would get the same registered or it would be registered through court.</u>

<u>11. According to section 149 of the Mohammadan Law, there are 3 essentials to the validity of a gift or heba. These are (a) declaration of gift by the donor, (b) acceptance of the gift either express of implied by the donee, and (c) delivery of possession of the subject matter of the gift by the donor to the donee as contemplated under section 150 of the Muslim Law. So, it is evident from the recital of Exhibit 2 that the essential ingredients of the gift or heba, according to the Muslim Law, are in existence and transaction of gift appears to be a complete one. So, Exhibit 2 is neither a deed of agreement of 'Ekrarnama', nor it is a promise to make any gift on any future date as has been wrongly pleaded by the plaintiff in the suit. The document, as it is before the court, is a written heba deed executed by the admitted owner of the property to one of his sons out of love and affection. It appears further that the said admitted land owner stated in the deed that he also purchased other properties in names of his remaining 3 sons and, as such, intended to make gift of the land measuring 4.88 acres for distribution of his property equally amongst the sons. It further appears from the record that other 3 sons and one daughter who are defendant Nos. 8-11 had already executed and registered deed on 20-8-1976 (Exhibit 3) transferring their shares in recognition to their father's intention expressed in Exhibit 2 and they also admitted ownership of the plaintiff in the said land.</u>

<u>12. For obtaining a decree in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, the plaintiff must have to prove first, that there was an existence of lawful contract in between the parties. The contracts are those agreements which are made by free consent of the parties with lawful consideration. There must be an offer, acceptance and consideration of the contract. Exhibit 2 does not disclose any such ingredients of lawful contract which can be placed to enforce through the court of law. Neither the defendant Nos. 1-7 are parties to the deed nor they have any liability to perform any part of the alleged contract to make conveyance of the suit land to the plaintiff. Gift is a personal right to give away any property by the owner himself, which is neither heritable nor it can be delegated to any other person. So, after death of the owner, his heirs are not bound by any such promise, even if any. Moreover, when it is apparent from the Exhibit 2 that it is a complete deed of gift having no necessity to get it registered the plaintiff had already become the owner of the gifted property by operation of law and, as such, the defendant Nos. 1-7 cannot be also asked to convey the suit land as they cannot claim ownership in the property which had already been gifted by their predecessor. Registration is not necessary for a valid gift under the Mohammadan Law.</u>

<u>13. ‘Ekrarnama’ is a deed of agreement for reconveyonce of the land sold by a kabala. Here in the present case, the term 'Ekrarnarna’ has been misused merely by quoting the word in the deed as no question of reconveyonce of any land was involved. On the plain reading of the document (Exhibit 2) it is clear that the deceased had executed purely a deed of gift having no scope to call it a deed of agreement or 'Ekrarnama'. In such a view of the matter the suit as has been brought by the plaintiff is a misconceived one and it is unfortunate that both the courts below considered the said deed as 'Ekrarnama' and ultimately, the appellate Court decreed the suit erroneously without having any agreement to be specifically enforced in the court of law.</u>

<u>14. So far as possession is concerned, finding of the learned Subordinate Judge appears to be based on documentary and oral evidence. Exhibit 2 stands to show the plaintiff already got possession at the time of execution of the deed on 30-4-1976 from the admitted owner. The defendant Nos. 8-11 who are sons and daughter of the original owner also admitted plaintiffs possession and ownership in recognition to the unregistered deed of gift. It appears that khatian No. 68 has also been prepared in the name of the plaintiff and he has been paying rents for the suit land including other lands vide Exhibit 4 series. In a violation Miscellaneous Case the defendant Nos. 1-7 did not contest in assertion of their physical possession in the suit land. The plaintiff was previously granted temporary injunction in the original suit to protect his possessory right against the defendants. Moreover, there is oral evidence in support of the plaintiffs possession too.</u>

<u>15. So far the genuineness of the Exhibit 2 is concerned, the learned Subordinate Judge, has made comparative study of the executing signatures of this deed with those of an old unassailed registered kabala dated 25-6-1968 which is admitted in evidence; as Exhibit 6. The court is quite competent to ascertain genuineness of execution of document by making such comparison under section 73 of the Evidence Act. The plaintiff has also oral evidence in this respect. I have also closely examined those two sets of signature of Habibur Rahman Khondker appearing on the two deeds and found those to be of the same hand.</u>

<u>Thus, I am unable to accept the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner to the effect that the plaintiff has failed to discharge their onus to prove genuineness of the deed, as the signatures were not sent to the Handwriting Expert for examination and opinion. So, the views as has been taken by the trial Court, about the execution of Exhibit 2 and possession are erroneous due to misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence on record as mentioned earlier. The learned Subordinate Judge, appears to have arrived at a proper findings on those issues.</u>

<u>16. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties at the fag end of hearing, frankly conceded that due to wrong advice of the local lawyers, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract which was not tenable in law. So, the suit may be sent back on remand in order to provide opportunity to the plaintiff to bring suitable amendment to the plaint seeking declaration of title to the suit land on the basis of the deed of gift. It appears that the suit was filed in the year 1980 only for having a decree for Special Performance of Contract with specific cause of action for such nature of the suit. There is no further cause of action to get the plaint amended by declaration of title which is quite different in nature altogether. So, such amendment after a long period of time is neither necessary nor can be allowed at the revisional stage. When the deed of gift is found to be genuine and the plaintiffs possession in the suit land is well established there may not be any necessity for further declaration of title. If the plaintiff feels it necessary in future to get his title declared there will be bar to bring such a suit from the fresh cause of action. Therefore, the prayer for sending the suit on remand is refused.</u>

17. With the aforesaid observations, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned Judgment and decree are hereby set aside and the suit stands dismissed only on the ground of maintainability of the suit in the nature it has been filed. The stay order connected with the Rules is vacated.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: This appeal, by leave, has arisen out the following facts: 

Government could not run Deshbandhu Sugar Mills (the Mills) properly because of multifarious difficulties. In 1983, the Government of Denmark sanctioned a grant to the Government of Bangladesh to the tune of 200 million Danish Crooner out of which, 65 million was allocated to the Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corporation for the above Mills, which is equivalent of Taka 15,34,45,000, has been described as long term loan against the said allocated grant but no re-lending agreement was executed between the Ministry of Finance and the Corporation for adjustment of the aforesaid loan. The writ respondents on several occasions floated international tenders and invited bid from the interested persons to sell the Mills, but in vain. The writ petitioner offered Taka 1,60,00,000 when the writ respondents made a counter offer to the writ petitioner to sell the Mills at Taka 2,35,00,000. The writ petitioner by his letter dated 19th October, 1999 accepted the offer and agreed to buy the Mills. Thereafter, writ respondent No.2 by Letter of Intent dated 5th March, 2000 requested him to pay 25% down payment within 1(one) month of issuance and the writ petitioner paid Taka 52,87,500. An Inventory Committee at the request of the writ petitioner was formed. The Government informed the writ petitioner that the Ministry of Finance imposed certain conditions which included (i) 10% down payment of the long term loan of Taka 15,34,44,990, (ii) the balance amount would be payable with 1 (one) year's rebate within 9 (nine) year's in half yearly installments bearing an interest at the rate of 8%. The writ petitioner opposed the above decision and proposed to pay with 1(one) year's rebate in 40 equal half-yearly installments with interest at the rate of 8% per annum. The fund allocated out of the Danish Grant was not a loan. The writ petitioner is ready to enter into a contract with regard to long term loan but the writ respondents willfully and deliberately delayed the process of handing over the possession of the Mills to him by imposing an additional condition demanding payment of 10% down payment of the long term loan beyond the terms of the tender. 

2. The writ respondent No. 2 claimed that at the time of purchase of the tender schedule, the writ petitioner was supplied with a valuation report and a profile which clearly mentioned that long term loan liabilities should be borne by the bidder; that the Government of Denmark granted the amount to the Government of Bangladesh for BMR (Balancing, Modernization and Reconstruction) of the Mills and re-allocated the same to the BSFIC as long term loan; that in the Privatization Policy, 1996 it has been clearly mentioned that the buyer has to accept all long term loans and from a plain reading of the letters of the writ petitioner, it becomes crystal clear that the buyer was ready to re-pay the long term loan and once the writ petitioner has agreed the repayment of loan, he is now debarred from saying that he is not bound to assume the long term liabilities. 

3. The point involved in this appeal was whether the writ petitioner was liable to pay the long term loan of the Mills. On consideration of annexure-B to the writ Petition, the High Court Division came to the conclusion that the money sanctioned by the Government of Denmark was a tied grant and thus the question of repayment of the grant did not arise, inasmuch as, the grant given by the Government of Denmark being not a loan, the writ petitioner was not liable to pay back the long term loan. On the other breath, the High Court Division on construction of clause 5.1 of the tender document observed that the writ petitioner was not supposed to pay back the long term loan as directed by the writ respondents. These observations apparently are inconsistent and made without application of Judicial mind. 

4. It has been mentioned in annexure 'B' that subject to clause 5.1, the bidder shall take the entire liability of the Mills on the date of execution of the agreement as per book value of the Inventory Committee's Report. Clause 5.1 relates to the liability of the Mills, wherein it was clearly provided the purchaser shall take the responsibility of the outstanding liability of the financial organizations like Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha, Bangladesh Shilpa Bank, Commercial Bank including foreign loan or any other loan given to the Mills as per terms to be settled by the parties and that the purchaser was required to arrange with those financial organizations for repayment the long term loan before the execution of the agreement. The High Court Division based its decision relying upon the Letter of Intent but it failed to notice that it was clearly mentioned therein that sides the price quoted by the writ petitioner, he was required to settle the outstanding liabilities of the Mills as per terms of the tender. The writ petitioner did not dispute the said amount as not the liability of the Mills but he avoided the liability on an imaginary ground that it being 'tied grant' and as no re-lending agreement was executed, he was not liable to pay the same. 

5. Mr Fida M Kamal realizing these facts tries to make out a third case that since there is no re-lending agreement was executed between the Government and that Mills' authority, the said amount could not be taken as loan. We find fallacy in the contention of learned counsel. Learned counsel endeavored so such to convince us by referring Annexures-N and P to the writ Petition and the audit report of the Mills for the year ending 30th June, 1986 submitted on 26th November, 1986 that the said amount was not shown as long term loan. According to Mr Kamal in the audit report, the auditors observed "we were given to understand that no re-lending agreement was executed for the loan". Mr Kamal submitted that in Annexure-K, the Director, Planning and Development, Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corporation wrote to the Secretary, Ministry of Industry on 21st April, 1999 to the effect that the money used from the Danish grant in the Mills were not shown in the BMR project as its liability from BSFIC. 

6. In Annexure-N, which is a letter written by the Director, the Bangladesh Sugar and Food Industries Corporation to the Secretary Ministry of Industries, it was pointed out that the fund provided by Danish Government would be treated as loan and the said amount was reflected in the audited account of the Mills and also in the profile of the Mills as well, and therefore the said amount was required to be realized from the purchaser. Similar statements were made in annexure-O to the writ petition, which was also written by the Deputy Director to the Secretary Ministry of Finance. Besides these documents, in the audit report of the Mills for the year ended on 30th June, 1999, the auditor commented in Paragraph 11 as under: 

11.0 Foreign Loan Tk.11,18,45,094.91 This Consists of the following:

DANIDA Loan for new                                                              82,741,094.91

DANIDA Loan for

re- imbursement                                        2.91.04.000.00

                                                                                                  11,18,45,094.91

11.1 DANIDA Loan for new mills (70%) Tk. 82,741,094.91

This represents 70% of total import cost of machinery and spares for installing new null in place of old one (Letter reference No.PIE/L/PO(VI) Sugar 58/81 (Part) dated 4.9.1983 of Ministry of Commerce).

11.2 DANIDA Loan for reimbursement Tk. 2, 91, 04,000.00

The amount had been received as per memo

No. Shilpa/Dev-1/R/119                       1,06,04,000.00

Ref/DSM/RPA/35-86/21                       1,85,00,000.00

            dated 02.05.87                        2,91,04,000.00

7. This audit report was prepared just before the Mills was sold to the writ petitioner on 19th October, 1999, wherein the Danish grant was shown as loan against cost of machinery and for renovation of the Mills. Therefore, the writ petitioner could not deny the said amount which he himself assumed as the Mills long term loan.

8. The tender document, annexure-B, clearly provided that the long term loan be borne by the purchaser, and the writ petitioner Knowing the terms, participated in the bid. He also assumed the said liability as long term loan as will be evident from his admissions and the documents submitted by him. Annexure-F is the Inventory Sub-committee's report submitted on his prayer for ascertaining the Mills liability, and in paragraph 3, the said amount was shown as long term liability of the Mills. In the minutes of the said committee annexure-G, in which the writ petitioner was present, it was unanimously resolved that the Mills liability was Taka 15,34,44;990. In his representation, annexure-H, the writ petitioner while assuming the liability of the said amount requested the Privatization Commission to reconsider its decision sympathetically for making down payment of 10% of the said amount. As the said commission refused his prayer, the writ petitioner by his representation dated 3rd May, 2001, Annexure H(1), agreed to pay 5% down payment of the said amount. 

9. Besides, the writ petitioner in the paragraph 11 of the writ petition assumed the liability of the long term loan stating 'The petitioner opposed the above decision and proposed, inter alias, payment of long term loan with one year's rebate in 40 equal half early installments with interest at the rate of 8% per annum." The writ petitioner made the above statement in reply to the Ministry of Finance's imposition of condition for repayment of long term loan of taka 15,34,44,9990. 

10. After filing the writ petition the writ petitioner prayed for interim order or handing over the Mills subject to furnishing a bank guarantee for an amount equivalent to 10% of the long term loan. His prayer was allowed and pursuant thereto he gave a Bank Guarantee. Thereafter, in the agreement, Annexure X(2), he acknowledged the said liability, subject of course, to the decision of the writ petition. These documents proved that the writ petitioner had assumed the long term loan and after getting delivery of possession, he adopted devices to delay the payment by raising various pleas. Mr Kamal frankly conceded that the writ petitioner was compelled to give the bank guarantee by assuming the long term loan as there was delay in the delivery of possession. This submission is devoid of substance in view of the writ petitioner's representations made in annexures H and H(1), the terms in annexure 'B' and the statements in annexure E, F, G as discussed above. The writ petitioner cannot deny the repayment of the long term loan in view of his admissions made in the writ petition, and the agreement, the terms in clause 5.1 of the tender document, annexure-B, his representations in annexures H and H-1. He is now stopped from denying the liability. 

11. An estoppels arises when a representation is acted upon as true by the party to whom it is made. Generally the elements of estoppels are the representations made under circumstances which amounted to an intentional causing belief in another. The principle which is incorporated in section 115 of the Evidence Act is a simple and equitable doctrine which lays down that if a person has acted to his detriment or altered his position on the basis of any declaration, act or omission of another person that other person will not be allowed in any proceedings between himself and the other person to go back upon it to the detriment other party. The rule is that the party will not be allowed to go behind the facts admitted in writing. If a person has by his conduct permitted the other party to believe that the agreement was other than it is embodied in the document, and has caused him to act upon that belief, he cannot fall back upon section 92 of the Evidence Act and thereby escape the consequence of his own action.

12. In this case the representation of the writ petitioner is so proximate and not the remote cause of leading the writ respondents to act to their prejudice. The principle is that a party cannot both approbate and reprobate; he cannot say at one time that a transaction is valid and thereby obtain some advantage to which he could only be entitled on the footing that it is valid, and at another say that it is void for the purpose of securing some further advantage. When the writ petitioner by executing an agreement assumed the liability, he is precluded from denying the same. 

13. Now the question is whether the writ petitioner was liable to pay 10% down payment of long term loan of Taka 15,34,44,990 as communicated to him in accordance with the privatization Nitimala, 2001. True, the writ petitioner cannot be saddled with terms for payment of the long term loan as per Nitimala, 2001, but at the same time we would like to make it clear that he is under obligation to pay as per terms of the tender document and he cannot avoid the said long term loan for indefinite period. If he does not agree to pay the loan as per decision of the Privatization Board, the authority would realize as per law it deems fit since the writ petitioner was not agreeable to the terms despite assuming the amount as liability of the Mills. The writ petitioner has averted the payment for 10 years without just cause. 

14. The High Court Division has totally over looked the above admitted facts and the admission of the writ petitioner and on a misconception of law, made the rule absolute. The judgment of the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with. 

The appeal is allowed with costs of Taka 50,000. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside. 

End.
