full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the defendant No. 1 calls in question the legality and propriety of the order No. 15 dated 3-6-1992 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Durgapur, in Other Class Suit No. 11 of 1992 allowing an application for temporary mandatory injunction directing the defendant to reinstate the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 to his former post which he held before suspension.

2. The opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed other class suit No. 11 of 1992 in the court of Senior Assistant Judge, Durgapur, claiming the following reliefs:

(ক) ১ নং মূল বিবাদী কর্তৃক বিগত ইং ১৯-৩-৯২ এবং ৪-৪-৯২ ইং তারিখে বাদীর প্রতি ইস্যুকৃত চিঠিসমূহ চক্রান্তমূলক, বেআইনী, পন্ড, বাতিল, অকার্যকরী, ক্ষমতা বর্হির্ভূত এবং বাদীর প্রতি বাধ্যকর না থাকা মর্মে এক ঘোষণামূলক ডিক্রী প্রচার করিতে ও

(খ) মোকদ্দমা চলাকালীন সময়ে ১নং বিবাদী ও সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্তৃপক্ষ যাহাতে বাদীকে অপসারণ করিতে না পারে তৎ মর্মে অস্থায়ী নিষেধাজ্ঞার আদেশ দিতে ও

(গ) যাবতীয় আদালত ব্যয় বাদীর পক্ষে বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে ডিক্রি দিতে

(ঘ) প্রমান ও অবস্থামূলে আেইন ও ইকুইটি মতে বাদী অন্য যে কোন প্রতিকর পাইতে পারেন তাহা্ও পাওয়ার ডিক্রী দিতে মর্জি হয়।”

3. On the allegation that he has not defalcated any money whatsoever of the provident fund and the defendant-petitioner most illegally and arbitrarily put him under suspension from the service with effect from 10-4-1992 and there are cases pending between the parties regarding illegal defalcated amount.

4. The aforesaid suit was filed on 9-4-92 and on the very date an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 was filed by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 for restraining the defendant petitioner from giving effect to the latter dated 4-4-92 and after hearing the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 the trial Court was pleased to issue a show cause notice and did not pass any order of interim injunction. The defendant petitioner entered appearance and filed written statement contending that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 was entrusted with the provident fund and the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 without depositing any amount to the provident fund defalcated an amount of Taka 1,05,321.00 and, as such, he was asked to show cause as to why he should not be dismissed from service. The plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 on an earlier occasion also challenged a similar show case notice and he had filed other class suit No. 13 of 1991 and the aforesaid suit was dismissed on 5-9-91 on the ground of maintainability as there was no cause of action for the said suit. Thereafter the defendant petitioner served another show cause notice upon the plaintiff opposite party on 19-3-1992 and the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 replied to the said show cause notice. The reply is neither convincing nor satisfactory and the defendant petitioner vide letter dated 7-2-91 asked the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 to deposit Taka 1,49,909.00 within 21-4-91 but he did not comply with the aforesaid order and thereafter the defendant petitioner vide letter dated 4-4-92 suspended the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 with effect from 10-4-1992.

<u>5. Defendant petitioner also filed written objection denying all the material allegations made in the application under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and stating, inter alia, that while the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 was given charge of provident fund he defalcated huge amount of money and he was directed to deposit the said amount. On his failure to comply with the direction, the defendant-petitioner issued a show cause notice why he should not be dismissed from service. The reply was not found satisfactory and, as such, he was placed under suspension vide letter dated 4-4-1992 with effect from 10-4-1992 and the defendant-petitioner has every right to initiate a departmental proceeding against an employee for any sort of misconduct committed by him and pursuant to departmental enquiry the plaintiff opposite party No. 1. was put under suspension till finalisation of the disciplinary proceeding and the suit as well as the prayer for temporary injunction is not maintainable.</u>

6. The plaintiff opposite party No. 1 ultimately, did not press his application under Order 39 rule 1. Instead of that on 14-11-1992 he filed an application under section 151 of the Code praying for temporary mandatory injunction against the defendant petitioner for restraining him from giving effect to the letter dated 4-4-92 and to restore the status quo ante by rescinding the letter dated 4-4-92. This application filed under section 151 of the Code was resisted by the defendant- petitioner by filing a written objection stating more or less the same thing as stated in the written objection earlier against the application under Order 39 rule 1.

7. The trial Court after hearing both the sides and on perusing the papers filed by the parties passed an order of temporary mandatory injunction on 3-6-1992 and directed that the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 will remain in his post from which he was suspended earlier and the order will be effective immediately. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order the defendant petitioner preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge. Netrokona, which was registered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 1992 and the aforesaid Miscellaneous appeal was disposed of vide order dated 13-8-1992 whereby the learned District Judge rejected the Memo of appeal holding that the order passed by the trial Court was an order under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and not under Order 39 rules 1 and 2, as such, the order was not an appealable order and he further observed that the appeal is incompetent and with those observations the learned District Judge returned the Memo of appeal to the defendant-petitioner for taking appropriate steps, if so desired by the defendant-petitioner. Thereafter the defendant petitioner preferred this revisional application impugning the order of the trial Court dated 3-6-1992 and obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr Subrata Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant petitioner, submits that the suit filed by the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 has no cause of action inasmuch as the employer has inherent right to initiate disciplinary action against an employee and can also put an employee under suspension pending domestic enquiry. The learned Advocate further submits that the defendant-petitioner being the highest executive of the organisation has every right to investigate any allegation and to look after the affairs of an employee and is competent to take departmental action and the order of temporary mandatory injunction in the instant case suffers from wanting of any illegality and also created great inconvenience to the internal administration of the defendant-petitioner organization. The learned Advocate further submits that the trial Court absolutely misconceived the legal aspect of the case and wrongly held that suspension is a punishment although he clearly observed that an organization has every right to initiate a departmental proceeding against an employee and failed to appreciate the fact that an employer has inherent right to suspend an employee. The learned Advocate further submits that the instant suit as well as the application under section 151 for temporary mandatory injunction is not maintainable inasmuch as over the self-same cause of action the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 earlier filed another suit namely, Other Class Suit No. 13 of 1991 which, on contest, was dismissed by the court on the ground of maintainability and, as such, over the self-same cause of action a second suit is not maintainable and is barred by the principle of estoppel by judgment as well as by the principle of res judicata. He further submits that in the instant case in granting the prayer for temporary mandatory injunction the trial Court also lost sight of the fact that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 did not approach the court with clean hands inasmuch as by the suit as well as the application under section 151 the plaintiff-opposite party has willingly and deliberately suppressed the fact of filing the earlier suit over the self-same cause of action and this ground alone is sufficient for rejecting the application for temporary mandatory injunction. The learned Advocate further submits, with much emphasis, that the learned Assistant Judge committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice as he has travelled beyond his jurisdiction in granting temporary mandatory injunction in favour of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 after discussing threadbare on the merits of the case and thereby committed an illegality in determining an interlocutory matter like temporary mandatory injunction. The learned Advocate further submits that by the order of suspension dated 4-4-92 which was given effect from 10-4-92 the plaintiff-opposite party was temporarily suspended from service pursuant to departmental action and it was not punishment and, as such, the trial Court on misconception of law and fact, held that the instant suspension is punishment and thereby granting of temporary mandatory injunction is illegal and without jurisdiction. The learned Advocate further submits that in the instant case the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 failed to make out a case for obtaining an order of temporary mandatory injunction inasmuch as there is no imminent grave danger to the life or the property of the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 nor there is any extreme emergency. Mr Chowdhury further submits that the impugned order is also illegal in view of the fact that the financial loss which is being suffered by the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 due to suspension order is compensatable by money and, as such, an injunction cannot be granted. The learned Advocate also submits that since it is a service matter there is no scope for any civil Court to interfere with the departmental proceeding by issuing an order of temporary mandatory injunction or any temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code whatsoever.

9. Dr Ahmed Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party, firstly, submits that this revisional application is incompetent inasmuch as the impugned order is appealable under Order 43 rule 1(r) of the Code of Civil Procedure because now it is well settled that a temporary mandatory injunction can be passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 in that view of the matter they could have challenged the order dated 13-8-1992, whereby the learned District Judge returned the Memo of Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 1992 but instead of that they have impugned the order dated 3-6-1992 of the trial Court whereby the temporary mandatory injunction was granted and for this proposition of law he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1941 (Mad) 210, wherein it has been held that a temporary injunction in mandatory form can be issued under Order 39 rules 1 and 2. Dr Ahmed Hossain further submits that the plaintiff-opposite party was never entrusted with the job of collecting money of the provident fund rather, as Assistant Secretary of the organisation he has requested to deposit the contribution to the fund and if there be any defalcation the accountant is responsible for the same and the plaintiff-opposite party cannot be held responsible for any such defalcation. Dr. Ahmed Hossain further submits that the trial Court have rightly held that without just cause an employee cannot be placed under suspension by the employer. Dr Hossain next submits that in the instant case admittedly there are pending litigations between the parties. The defendant-petitioner has already filed money suit No. 2 of 1991 against the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 which is pending in the court and it is not fair and proper on the part of the employer to suspend an employee and initiate departmental proceeding without waiting for the result of the said money suit and thereby the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 has been doubly jeopardised. Dr Ahmed Hossain further submits that the fact that the earlier suit was dismissed on the ground of maintainability will have no bearing in the instant case in view of the fact that over the self-same defalcated amount a money suit is pending in a civil Court and until that suit is finalised the defendant- petitioner is not entitled to take any action against the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 with regard to the same amount either in law or in equity and, as such, the trial Court has rightly passed the impugned order granting temporary mandatory injunction. Dr Ahmed Hossain further submits that the property as contemplated in Order 39 rules 1 and 2 includes the job of a person and, as such, by placing the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 under suspension his right of job has been interfered with and this is sufficient for the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 to maintain the suit.

<u>10. Before we consider the submissions made by Mr Subrata Chowdhury on the merit of the impugned order it would be better if we first advert to the point raised by Dr. Ahmed Hossain regarding competency of the instant revisional application. It is contended by him that an order of temporary mandatory injunction can be passed under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 and consequently the impugned order is appealable under Order 43 rule 1(r) and, as such, the revisional application is incompetent. As against that it is submitted by Mr Subrata Chowdhury that in the instant case the trial Court did not grant temporary mandatory injunction in exercise of its authority under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 but by invoking its inherent jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. On a perusal of the impugned order it also appears that the application praying for temporary mandatory injunction was filed under section 151 of the Code and it also appears that the learned Assistant Judge exercised his jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code. Be that as it may, the defendant-petitioner preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Netrokona, against the impugned order dated 3-6-1992 and it is stated by the defendant petitioner in paragraph 10 of this revisional application that at the time of hearing of that appeal before the learned District Judge the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 resisted that appeal on the ground that the impugned order was passed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, as such, the impugned order was not appealable and the learned District Judge accepting the contention raised by the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 before him returned the Memo of appeal. From the counter affidavit filed by the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 before this court it appears that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 did not deny the statements made by the defendant petitioner in paragraph 10 of this revisional application. It, thus, appears that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 before the learned District Judge took the stand that the appeal is not maintainable because the impugned order was passed under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and giving a go-bye to the said stand the plaintiff-opposite party before this court contends that the impugned order was passed under Order 39 rule 1 and, as such, the appeal was maintainable and this contention of the plaintiff-opposite party cannot be accepted for the sake of administration of justice and to meet the ends of justice, as one cannot be allowed to approbate and reprobate at the same time. Be that as it may, let us consider this aspect of the case on merit also. It is now well settled that a temporary injunction on the mandatory form can be granted under Order 39 rule 1. It is also well settled that Order 39 rule 1 is not exhaustive and it is also well settled by now that if a case is not covered by the provision of Order 39 rule 1 the civil Court can grant injunction under its inherent jurisdiction Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as under:</u>

<u>"1. Cases in which temporary injunction may be granted. Where in any suit it is proved by affidavit or otherwise</u>

<u>(a) that any property in dispute in a suit is in danger of being wasted, damaged or alienated by any party to the suit, or wrongfully sold in execution of a decree, or,</u>

<u>(b) that the defendant threatens or intends to remove or dispose of his property with a view to defraud his creditors".</u>

<u>From that it is crystal clear that the instant case does not come within the purview of Order 39 rule 1. Order 39 rule 2 reads as under:</u>

<u>"Injunction to restrain repetition or continuance of breach-(1) In any suit for restraining the defendant from committing a breach of contract or other injury of any kind, whether compensation is claimed in the suit or not, the plaintiff may, at any time after the commencement of the suit, and either before of after judgment, apply to the court for a temporary injunction to restrain the defendant from committing the breach of contract or injury of a like kind arising out of the same contract or relating to the same property or right."</u>

<u>11. It is now well settled that in the absence of any statutory provision protecting a servant it is not possible in law to grant a decree against an unwilling master that the servant is still in service and therefore no mandatory or temporary injunction can be granted in the case of an employee who is governed by the rule of master and servant. In that view of law it is crystal clear that the instant case does not come within the purview of Order 39 rule 2. In the case reported in 7 DLR 666, it has been held that a civil Court can grant temporary injunction if the situation is not covered by Order 39 rules 1 and 2 by invoking its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the case reported in 20 DLR 501, it has been held by a Division Bench of the Dhaka High Court that what the applicant mentioned in an application for temporary injunction does not matter. It is circumstances of the application which determines the matter of relief granted by the court. In that case the application was filed praying for temporary mandatory injunction under Order 39 rule 1 but the court found that though the application was filed under Order 39 rule 1 but, in fact, the court exercised its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter their Lordships held that the revisional application was maintainable before the High Court Division as that order was passed not under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 but under section 151 of the Code. From a perusal of Order 39 rules 1 and 2 it appears that the instant case is not covered by the provisions of Order 39 rules 1 and 2. It also appears from the materials and evidence on record that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 was conscious about that and keeping that point in mind the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 did not press his application under Order 39 rule 1 which was filed on 9-4-92. Instead on 4-9-92 he filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction and from a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the learned Assistant Judge entertained this application as an application under section 151 of the Code and treating the application as an application under section 151 of the Code it has exercised its inherent jurisdiction in granting relief sought for. In that view of the matter I am of the opinion that in the instant case the trial Court exercised its jurisdiction under section 151 of the Code and in that view of the matter in the instant case this revisional application before this court is well maintainable.</u>

<u>12. Before we embark upon merits of the impugned order it would be profitable for us if we see what is meant by ''suspension''. According to the Oxford Dictionary the word ''suspension'' means action of debarring or state of being debarred especially for some time, from a function or privilege; temporary deprivation of one''s office or position, the state of being temporarily kept from being or deprived of something. It has been held in the case of Abil Mohammad Khan, vs. State of MP reported in AIR 1958 (MP) 44, that the meaning of the word "suspend" has been given in the dictionary as to debar usually for a time from the exercise of a function or employment or a privilege specially to deprive temporarily of one''s office. It is now well settled that suspension of an employee does not amount to dismissal or termination of contract or service. Suspension, in general terminology, therefore, means an order issued by the employer whereby the employee is prevented from discharging his duties of employment, when the act of employer does not amount to termination of service or dismissal of employee from service. Such a servant continues to be in service.</u>

13. Here it may be mentioned that there is a difference between suspension by way of punishment and suspension on administrative grounds. Suspension on administrative grounds may be ordered under two circumstances :

(1) During the pendency of departmental enquiry.

(2) During the pendency of criminal investigation or trial.

When a suspension is ordered on administrative ground there is no element of punishment involved in it. It is something transitional or temporary. It is only a temporary deprivation of his functions. Suspension in these cases is not a quasi-judicial act. It is purely administrative and the person suspended remains a servant.

<u>14. It is now well settled that an employer has got an implied right to suspend an employee. Suspension is not a punishment but is a disciplinary matter in aid of disciplinary proceedings. It has been held in the case of Agnihotram Ananthascharyula vs. Executive Officer reported in AIR 1958 (AP) 325, that the power to suspend pending enquiry is necessarily incidental to the power to conduct an enquiry and inflict punishment and therefore, the punishing authority will have implied power to suspend. In the case of Nurugadas vs. State of Madras, reported in AIR 1964 (Mad) 518, it has been held that the power to suspend pending enquiry is an administrative power and it is not necessary to give an opportunity to the delinquent employee to explain the charges on the basis of which he is sought to be suspended. In the instant case the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 was asked vide letter dated 19-3-92 to show cause why he shall not be suspended and he showed cause but the same was not found satisfactory and, as such, vide letter dated 4-4-92 he was suspended with effect from 10-4-1992. The plaintiff opposite party challenged the notice dated 19-3-91 in the court by filing TS No. 13 of 1991 which was ultimately dismissed for default. Here it should be remembered that it is purely discretionary for departmental authority to place a person under suspension during departmental enquiry and, therefore, the decision cannot be interfered with by civil Courts or by High Courts in their writ jurisdiction. It has been held in the case of DN Janju vs. State of J&K, reported in AIR 1964 (J&K) 14, that the High Court, while exercising powers in a writ cannot consider whether an order of suspending a government servant was or was not based on proper material provided the order was passed by the competent authority.</u>

15. The civil Court has power to grant injunction both under the Code of Civil Procedure and Specific Relief Act. It is an established principle that no contract will be specifically enforced if it can be adequately compensated by grant of damages. The contract of employment falls into this category and in case work is denied to an employee contrary to the contract then it can be effectively compensated. No temporary injunction can, therefore, be granted to restrain the employer from enforcing the order of suspension in view of the provisions of the Specific Relief Act.

16. In the instant case the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 admittedly is an employee of an organisation namely, Garo Baptist Convention (GBC), an organisation incorporated as voluntary organisation under the provision of Society Registration Act and, as such, this is a body corporate under the said Act. The employee of such organisation is governed by the rule of Master and Servant and when an employee is governed by the rule of master and servant he cannot bring any action against his employer calling in question any order of suspension, dismissal, discharge or termination whatsoever because it is hit by section 21(a) and (b) of the Specific Relief Act. It has been held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in a case reported in 13 DLR (SC) 228, that the declaration of nullity against a dismissal order is not maintainable when the relationship is governed by the rule of Master and Servant. That decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court was quoted approvingly by our Appellate Division in the case of Bata Shoe Company which is an unreported decision wherein their Lordships of the Appellate Division applying the above principle observed, "an employee cannot be forced upon an unwilling master." Such declaration cannot be given in law and only relief, if at all, could be a claim for damages but in this case the plaintiff did not frame his suit for damages, therefore, under the law he cannot claim any relief''. Similarly, in the instant case the relationship between the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 and the defendant-petitioner is a relationship of master and servant. In a case where there is a contract between a master and a servant, the master agreeing to pay the salary and the servant agreeing to render personal service it is obvious that money compensation is full relief, for all that the servant was entitled to under the contract was his salary. When a master, in breach of his contact, refused to employ the servant the only right survives to the servant is the right to damage and a decree for damages is the only decree that can be granted to him. If the master illegally suspends, terminates, dismisses or discharges an employee a suit for declaration of nullity of the same cannot be brought either in the writ jurisdiction or under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act before the civil Court. It has been held in 31 DLR (AD) 234, that when the relationship between the parties is governed by the rule of master and servant a declaration of illegality of an order of dismissal from service in civil Court or in the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division is not maintainable. The only remedy is one for damages for wrongful dismissal.

17. On a perusal of the records it appears that the defendant-petitioner before the learned Assistant Judge raised an objection to the effect that this application filed by the plaintiff-opposite party under section 151 of the Code for temporary mandatory injunction was not maintainable and the Assistant Judge observed that the application was maintainable but in arriving at such finding the learned Assistant Judge absolutely ignored this legal aspect of the case and, as such, erroneously held that the application was maintainable. Admittedly, the GBC is an organisation incorporated and registered under the Society Registration Act, and, as such, the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 is governed by the rule of Master and Servant and in that view of the matter not only the application under section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code but the suit itself is not maintainable as framed. This legal aspect of the case was not considered at all by the trial Court in holding that the application under section 151 is maintainable.

18. Dr. Ahmed Hossain tried to impress upon me that since over the self-same matter money suit No. 2 of 1991 is pending it is not proper for the defendant-petitioner to continue with the departmental proceeding until the said money suit is disposed of by the concerned court because thereby the plaintiff-opposite party has been clearly put to double jeopardy. This contention of Dr. Ahmed Hossain is not tenable. It has been held by our Appellate Division in a case reported in 34 DLR (AD) 304, that pendency of a criminal case is no bar for the employer to initiate a departmental proceeding against the employee over the self-same matter. In that case a criminal case was started against two government servants and they were exonerated from the charges of criminal offence by a competent court. Even then they were punished for the same offences invoking the provisions of President''s Order No. 9 of 1972. On a writ petition challenging the legality of the dismissal order the High Court Division allowed the writ petition on the grounds, amongst others, that since the respondents were discharged from the criminal case, their removal from service amounts to double jeopardy. In the appeal, the Appellate Division observed that "The view taken by the learned Judge on the question of application of the rule of double jeopardy appears to be totally misconceived. Discharge from the criminal case for the charge levelled against them, by itself cannot be ground for disentitling the competent authority to initiate departmental proceeding on the allegations and award punishment in accordance with the service rules. Similarly, if the delinquent employee escapes punishment in a departmental proceeding, that by itself cannot be a ground for discharging him from the charges in the criminal case started against him. The question of application of the rule of double jeopardy may be examined from another aspect. If the delinquent employee is found guilty of the charge in a departmental proceeding, for which the maximum punishment may be dismissal; whereas if he is found guilty of the same offence in a criminal case he is liable to suffer ''punishment'' as provided in the law. So, in any view of the matter, the rule of double jeopardy has no application in the instant case. It is thus, clear that the rule of double jeopardy is not applicable in the instant case.

19. It appears from the impugned order that the learned Assistant Judge granted the prayer for temporary mandatory injunction on the ground that since litigations are pending between the parties the defendant-petitioner ought to have waited for the outcome of those proceedings but this is not a valid ground in the eye of law. An employer need not wait for an indefinite period for the outcome of a case and even if that case is decided in favour of the employee he would not be able to dismiss the employee on the basis of that decision of the civil Court. In any event an employer has got to initiate a departmental proceeding to punish an employee. The learned Assistant Judge absolutely misconceived this legal aspect of the case and erroneously held that the defendant petitioner ought to have waited for the result of the pending case.

20. It is an admitted fact that the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 is an employee of the defendant petitioner. Section 16 of the General Clauses Act provides that power to appoint includes power to suspend and dismiss. Thus the employer has inherent power to suspend or dismiss an employee and we have already noticed that when the service is governed by the contract even if the dismissal or suspension is illegal there is no remedy against that and all that the employee is entitled to claim is his compensation as damages. In the course of argument Mr. Chowdhury has referred to and relied on the decision reported in 29 DLR (SC) 168, wherein their Lordships of the Supreme Court held that temporary injunction should not ordinarily be granted in cases where permanent injunction cannot be granted. In service matter an employee cannot ask for permanent injunction. It is further held in that case that if threatened injury can be compensated by monetary payment, temporary injunction cannot be granted. In another decision the Supreme Court held that when a threatened injury could be compensated by monetary compensation the Court will be slow to grant interlocutory injunction. In the instant case due to the suspension all that the plaintiff opposite party will suffer during the period of suspension is that he will not get the full pay and allowances during the period of suspension but this is for temporary period and ultimately if the charges are not proved in the domestic enquiry he will be reinstated and will get full arrears salary. On the other hand, if he is found guilty the defendant petitioner may be dismissed. In the event of dismissal, of course, he will not get full salary but retain the subsistence allowance already received. It is to be noted that in the present case the plaintiff''s grievance of injury, in substance, is one of a pecuniary loss. A party, in order to get interlocutory injunction, must claim, inter alia, a legal right, and allege an injury which is not repairable by monetary compensation. In the instant case plaintiff-opposite party has failed to prove that he has a legal right not to be placed on suspension. Moreover, the alleged injury is compensatable by monetary payment. In that view of the matter also the impugned order is not sustainable in law.

<u>21. It is now well settled that suspension is not punishment and no pre-hearing is necessary for placing an employee under suspension pending departmental action. In the instant case it appears that before placing the plaintiff-opposite party under suspension a show cause notice was issued and he also submitted an explanation thereto and after considering the same the plaintiff-opposite party was placed under suspension. The trial Court also failed to notice this aspect of the case.</u>

22. During the course of argument Mr. Subrata Chowdhury also relied on the decision reported in 26 DLR 10, wherein it has been held that a civil Court cannot interfere, by granting an injunction, with the internal administration of an organisation. In that case the trial Court by granting temporary mandatory injunction restrained the college authority from appointing a professor in a college and that order of temporary injunction was set aside by the High Court holding that in a service matter the court cannot grant temporary injunction particularly when it amounts to interference with the internal management of the institution. In the instant case admittedly, the relationship between the defendant-petitioner and plaintiff-opposite party is governed by the rule of Master and servant and, as such, the plaintiff-opposite party No. 1 cannot claim as of right to be retained in the service. This legal aspect of the case was lost sight of by the trial Court in allowing the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It further appears from perusal of the impugned order that in granting temporary mandatory injunction the learned Assistant Judge failed to consider the legal requirement of granting an order of temporary mandatory injunction that is, whether the plaintiff has prima facie case, whether the injury or threatened injury is compensable by money and whether the balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff. On a perusal of the impugned order it appears that the learned Assistant Judge also failed to direct himself in that regard. It thus, appears to me that the impugned order suffers from a lot of illegalities and infirmities and in any view of the matter it cannot be sustained in law. I, therefore, find considerable force in the submissions of Mr. Subrata Chowdhury.

23. In the result the Rule is made absolute and the order No. 15 dated 3-6-1992 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Durgapur in Other Class Suit No. 11 of 1992 allowing an application for temporary mandatory injunction is set aside.

In view of the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to cost. On 25-7-1995 the learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner filed an application for impugning the order dated 13-8-1992 passed by the learned District Judge in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 10 of 1992 and that application was kept with the record to be considered at the time of delivery of the instant Judgment. Since this Court has already found that the impugned order has been passed by the learned Assistant Judge not under Order 39 rule 1 but under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure the instant civil revisional application is maintainable and application filed by the defendant-petitioner on 25-7-95 need not be considered and the same is disposed of accordingly.

End.

Rafique-ul Huq with Ahsanul Karim with Faheemul Huq and M Shakhawat Hossain, Advocates — For the Appellant. 

AJ Mohammad Ali, Additional Attorney-General — For Respondent No. 1. 

MA Gaffar, Advocate — For Respondent No. 2.

full_judgment:
AK Badrul Huq J : In challenge of appropriateness of a decision recorded by learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 187 of 1999 setting aside an arbitration award on turning down a request offered by awardee for making Arbitration Award Rule of Court, the awardee as appellant knocked the door of this Court on presentation of this appeal under section 39 of The Arbitration Act, 1940 (for short The Act) for a verdict to install the Award Rule of Court on overturning the decision of learned Subordinate Judge.

 

2. Lifeblood of episode escalating to crescendo of the present appeal springing out of Arbitration Proceeding may succinctly be taken heed of which are as follows:

A. A Latif Company Limited represented by its Managing Director is the First party-appellant. Project Director and Executive Engineer, Local Government Engineering Department (for brief LGED) are Second party-respondents.

B. Second party-respondents floated tender for construction of 112 metre long pre-stressed Bridge on Mouchak-Tea Garden-Fulbaria road over Turag river under District-Gazipur.

C. Appellant obtained Bid documents which consisted of Instrument of Tender, BD Form No. 2911.

D. Appellant participated in the tender and quoted price for total Taka 99, 49,729.80. Rate quoted was the lowest. Work order, though, issued on 4-11-1995 fixing six (6) months’ time for completion of work but was delivered on 28-11-1995 after twenty-four (24) days of issuance of work order. Contract was signed on 7-2-1996.

 E. Appellant made start of work and completed all preliminary works needed for construction of the Bridge.

F. Dispute arose in respect of the work.

G. Appellant was blacklisted on 3-4-1997 and contract stood terminated and security money was forfeited.

H. Appellant made an entreaty to respondents to resolve the dispute under clause 25 of The Instruction of Tender BD Form No. 2911 on 10-4-1997.

I. First party-appellant, thereafter, on 4-5-1997 laid a petition under section 20 of The Act for appointment of an arbitrator before learned Subordinate Judge, Third Court, Dhaka. Petition has been renumbered as Title Suit No. 187 of 1997 on transfer to the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka.

J. Second party-respondent presented written objection to the said petition.

K. Both First party-appellant and Second party-respondent on presentation of a joint petition submitted name of an arbitrator. Order No. 6 dated 16-10-1997 is an evidence to the said factual matrix. Learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka appointed Mr Md Asaduzzaman, Bar-at-Law and former Judge, as sole arbitrator.

L. First party-appellant put forward statement of claim on 15-10-1999 which are catalogued hereunder:

"Schedule of Total Claim

1. Damage for loss of goodwill value                                             

Taka                                       10,00,00,000

2. Arrear contract money excluding 1st running bill for Taka 6,94,589.00

Taka                                            92,55,140

 

3. 20% business loss for withholding payment of arrear contract money for

Taka                                            18,51,028

 

4. Wages and salary for 7 months paid to the workers, engineers and staffs due to delay in amending drawing and giving layout beginning from 4-11-1995 to 14-5-1996

Taka                                            92,55,140

 

(a) 2 (Two) Engineers @ 15,000 per month (15000 x 7)

Taka                                              1,05,000

 

(b) Staff 6 (six) Nos. @ 20,000 per month (20,000 x 7)

Taka                                              1,40,000

 

(c) Labour for Piling work 20 Nos. @ 120 per day (4-11-1995 to 14-5-1996) = 20 x 119 day x 120

Taka                                              4,58,400

 

5. Hire charges of Piling machine @ 30,000 per month (30,000 x 7)

Taka                                              2,10,000

 

6. Unrecovered advances to sand and stone suppliers.

Taka                                              2,00,000

 

7. Unrecovered advances paid to cement suppliers.

Taka                                              1,00,000

 

8. Unrecovered advances paid to MS Deformed Rod suppliers.

Taka                                              2,00,000

 

 

Total Taka =                        11,25,19,568

 

9. Business loss for illegal detention of claimed amount for Taka 11,25,19,568.00 @ 20% per year From the cancellation of contracts and black list of the company in April/97 to filing of statement of claim in 1999 i.e. 3 years.

Taka                                    6,75,11,740.80

 

Gross Total Taka =        18,00,31,308.80

M. Second party-respondent offered a rejoinder to the statement of claim surged forward by appellant raising contentions that (a) statement of claim was baseless and without substance, (b) materials brought by the appellant were unspecified and below quality and, (c) respondent had already paid running bills covering works performed by appellant.

N. Sole arbitrator passed an award on 5-2-2000 and award was filed in Court on 25-4-2000. Arbitrator allowed claim for Taka 6, 00, 00,000 (six crore) out of claim of Taka 10, 00, 00,000 (Ten crore). Arbitrator allowed claim for Taka six crore out of Taka ten crore as listed in item No. 1 of claim which was damage for loss of goodwill value. Arbitrator, also, allowed Taka 92, 55,140 shown in item No. 2 of claim. Arbitrator allowed Taka 18, 15,028 noted in item No. 3 of schedule of claim which was for business loss for withdrawing arrear contract money for Taka 92,55,140. Arbitrator rejected the claim listed in item Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9.

O. First party-appellant, thereafter, on 25-4-2000 presented a petition before Court under section 14(2) read with section 17 of The Act for making the Award Rule of Court.

P. Second party-respondent for setting aside the award filed a petition under section 30 read with section 33 of The Act. In the petition dispensation in the matter of payment of award money was sought.

Q. Learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Dhaka by Judgment dated 8-1-2001 set aside the award on refusing to make the Award Rule of Court. In setting aside award learned Judge held:

 i. Court got the right to see whether arbitrator committed any illegality and performed misconduct in giving award even if the defendant (respondent) did not deposit security money.

 ii. Plaintiff (appellant) admittedly, did not perform any preliminary work of Bridge construction within stipulated period.

 iii. Direction by arbitrator in the matter of payment of running bill and arrear rent was nothing but misconduct and

iv. Award dated 5-2-2000 was not lawful and illegality and personal misconduct of arbitrator stood manifested and award was not to be made Rule of Court.

3. Having felt resentful of the above adjudication, appellant approached this Court in this appeal.

 4. Mr Rafique-ul Huq, learned Counsel along with Mr Ahsanul Karim, Mr Faheemul Huq and Mr M Shakhawat Hossain, learned Counsels appeared in support of appeal.

5. First-respondent Project Director was represented by Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Additional Attorney-General Mr MA Gaffar, learned Counsel stood to champion cause of Executive Engineer, Local Government Engineering Department, Gazipur.

6. Decisions rendered by learned Subordinate Judge have been stormed pressing into service a good number of contentions from the side of First party-appellant. Contentions advanced had been given rejoinder in bringing home arguments. Plethora of authorities have been placed from the Bar in support of respective contentions.

7. On authorities it is conveniently observed that a decision is an authority for what it actually decides. It cannot be quoted for a proposition that may seem to follow from it. Every judgment must be read applicable to the particular facts proved or assumed to be proved. Generality of expression that may be found cannot be intended to be exposition of whole law but must be regarded as governed or qualified by particular fact of the case in which such expression occurs. It is neither desirable nor permissible to pick out a word or a sentence from the judgment divorced from the context of the question under consideration to support the reasoning. Decisions which are not relevant and carry no bearing in resolving controversies shall not be dealt with by us and we shall not make an idle parade of discussing those decisions to encumber Judgment.

8. First branch of contention moved forward is that under section 33 of The Act deposit of award money or furnishment of security for payment of award money is a must and no objection under section 30 is maintainable unless statutory deposit is furnished and deposit not given as security along with objection that objection is no objection in the eye of law and Court is bound to make the Award Rule of Court and whether arbitrator misconducted or not could not be looked into in absence of deposit as provided under section 33 of The Act and Court acted without jurisdiction in setting aside the award and Court was bound to make the Award Rule of Court. Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim and Brothers and another, 1988 BLD 369, Bangladesh Water Development Board and others vs Progati Prakaushali and another, 49 DLR 335, Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh, 4 BLC 407 and Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha (RAJUK) vs MN Alam and Associates Ltd and another, 54 DLR 161 have been relied upon in support of contention.

9. Contention advanced was countered from the side of Second party-respondents in bringing home contentions that since arbitrator acted without jurisdiction and the award was ex facie illegal and invalid it was liable to be set aside, no matter whether the objection as mandated under section 33 of The Act had been laid or not and Court can suo motu see legality and validity of the award. Messrs R Sim and Co, Narayonganj vs Messrs Pak Industries (Jute Mills) Ltd Tanbazar, Narayanganj, 8 DLR 305 and Chief Engineer, Roads and Highways Department, Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Messrs Concord Engineers and Construction Limited, an unreported case have been referred to in aid of the contention.

10. Section 33 of The Act enshrines.

Any party to an arbitration agreement or any person claiming under him desiring to challenge the existence or validity of an arbitration agreement or an award or to have the effect of either determined shall apply to the Court and the Court shall decide the question on affidavits;

Provided that where the Court deems it just and expedient, it may set down the application for hearing on other evidence also, and it may pass such orders for discovery and particulars as it may do in a suit; Provided that no application challenging the existence or validity of an award or for having its effect determined shall be entertained by the Court unless the applicant has deposited in the Court the amount which he is required to pay under the award or has furnished security to the satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such sum or for the fulfilment of any other obligation by him under the award.

 11. The second proviso had been added by Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978 which came into force on June 1, 1979. The proviso providing deposit of award amount or furnishment of security for same to satisfaction of Court became a pre-requisite condition if an application is presented to challenge existence or validity of the award or for having its effect determined and in the absence of deposit of award money or furnishment of security for same to satisfaction of Court, application or written objection contemplated under section 33 of The Act is no application or written objection in the eye of law and not at all entertainable.

12. In Bangladesh Water Development Board vs Nasim and Brothers and another (supra) the debate that arose was whether letter of guarantee which was submitted long after the filing of application under section 33 of The Arbitration Act was a valid deposit as contemplated under law. It had been held that deposit under section 33 of The Arbitration Act is a condition precedent for entertainment of application challenging award and without deposit it is to be construed as if there was no application in the eye of law. It has been further held that guarantee that was filed long after is no deposit under law.

13. In Bangladesh Water Development Board and others vs Progati Prokaushali and another (supra) similar question was dealt with. It has been held that failure to make deposit as required by proviso to section 33 of The Arbitration Act rendered the written objection/ application under section non-existent in the eye of law.

 14. In Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh (supra) the legal consequence of an application directed to challenge existence or validity of award or for having its effect determined in absence of deposit of amount required to be paid under award or furnishing of security for same came up for a decision. It has been laid down that proviso providing deposit of amount required to be paid under award or furnishing security for same became a pre-requisite condition where an application is presented to challenge existence or validity of award or for having its effect determined.

15. In Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkha (RAJUK) vs MN Alam and Associates Ltd., and another (supra) the defendant-petitioners did not make any deposit as required under section 33 of The Arbitration Act. In the line of the enunciation of law in the above noted three (3) authorities it had been observed that the application under section 33 of The Arbitration Act is a nullity in the eye of law for non-compliance of the proviso to section 33 of The Arbitration Act.

16. Ratio decidendi of the above authorities is that deposit of award money or furnishment of security envisaged in section 33 of The Act is a condition precedent for entertainment of an application challenging the validity of award and without deposit of award money or furnishment of security application in the form of written objection will be no application nor objection in the eye of law. In respectful adherence to the proposition of law propounded in the above authorities we are of this meditated view that the application in the form of written objection laid under section 33 of The Act was no application nor written objection and the same was not at all entertainable.

17. In Messrs R Sim and Co Narayanganj vs Messrs Pak Industries (Jute Mills) Ltd, Tanbazar, Narayanganj (supra) it has been held that where an award is illegal and void for want of jurisdiction apparent on the face of it, it is not necessary that the parties should file objection to the award within the time prescribed under Article 158 of The Limitation Act. The Judgment is dated February 17, 1956. On that date the mandatory requirement of deposit of award amount or furnishment of security for the same along with the objection was not in the Arbitration Act and the said requirement of deposit of award amount or furnishment of security was added in the second proviso by The Law Reforms Ordinance of 1978. In the referred case no objection against the award was laid but in the case before us objection was filed and mandatory deposit of award money or furnishment of security for the same was not made. Moreover, the award, also, cannot be typified as illegal and void. The referred case got no manner of application in the fact and circumstances of the case before us.

18. In Chief Engineer, Roads and Highways Department, Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Messrs Concord Engineers and Construction Limited (supra) the award delivered by arbitrator was declared to be without jurisdiction and authority with the view that appointment of arbitrator was premature and arbitrator did not assume jurisdiction as per law. The cited case is quite distinguishable and not applicable in the fact and circumstances of the instant case.

In respect of the said case it is profitably noted that propriety of the Judgment of the above case is under challenge before Appellate Division and the Judgment did not reach to finality.

19. Court adopted the view that it got the right to see whether arbitrator in giving award committed any illegality or misconduct even in the event of non-deposit of award money or non-furnishment of security for the same and Court virtually rested its view taking into account the contentions incorporated in the written objection presented under section 33 of The Act and, thus, committed a substantial error in the decision. The first branch of contention having carried substance is accepted.

20. The thrust of second branch of contention is that Court committed a patent illegality in setting aside the award on declining to make it Rule of Court on ground of illegality committed by arbitrator and, also, misconduct on the part of arbitrator and misconduct was not misconduct contemplated under section 30 of The Act. Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh (supra). Begum Khadija Akhtar Banu and another vs AKM Amanullah and another, BCR 1985 (AD) 8, Dandasi Shahu vs State of Orissa, AIR 1987 Orissa 274, Messrs Moosa Usman and Company Ltd, Karachi vs Hajee E Dosso and Sons and another, PLD 1971, Karachi 899 and Trading Corporation of Pakistan Limited vs Messrs Aslam Syed and Company and three others, PLD 1973, Karachi 65 have been pressed into service in support of the contention.

21. Contention pressed has been spurned from the side of respondent raising contentions that arbitrator misconducted (a) by basing his finding on no evidence, (b) by basing his finding upon misconception of fact and (c) by assessing the arrear bill on baseless calculation and by mode of payment.

22. Section 30(a) of The Act postulates that an award shall not be set aside except on the ground that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself in the proceeding under section 30(a). "Misconduct" is, thus, the ground for setting aside an award.

23. The word "Misconduct" should be interpreted in the sense in which it is used in English Law with reference to arbitration proceeding. It does not necessarily imply moral turpitude but it includes neglect of duties and responsibilities of arbitrators. "Misconduct" does not necessarily at all imply anything in the matter of fraud. It does not mean personal turpitude such as corruption and bribery. "Legal Misconduct" means misconduct in the judicial sense of the word not from a moral point of view and means honest erroneous breach of duty.

 24. In Corpus Juris Secundum Vol 58 page 818 "Misconduct" is stated hereunder:

"Both in law and in ordinary speech the term "misconduct" usually implies an act done wilfully with a wrong intention, and conveys the idea of intentional wrongdoing. The term implies fault beyond the error of judgment; a wrongful intention, and not a mere error of judgment; but it does not necessarily imply corruption or criminal intention, and, in the legal idea of misconduct, an evil intention is not a necessary ingredient."

25. In Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Volume II page 57 it is stated:

 "the expression 'misconduct' is 'of wide import' and includes: "on the one hand, bribery and corruption and on the other hand, a mere mistake as to the scope of authority conferred by the agreement of reference or an error of law appearing on the face of the award. Thus misconduct occurs if the arbitrator or umpire, as the case may be, fails to decide all the matters which are referred to him; if by his award he purports to decide matters which have not, in fact, been included in the agreement of reference; if the award is inconsistent."

26. "Misconduct", thus, means conduct amounting to moral turpitude, breach and neglect of duty, failure to perform essential duties, mishandling of arbitration proceeding causing displacement of Rules of justice and lack of integrity and impartiality.

 27. Respondent did not surge forward any case of personal "Misconduct" of arbitrator. Case of "Misconduct" had been projected.

 28. The foremost charge of "Misconduct" highlighted from the side of respondent was exceeding of jurisdiction in taking into consideration the blacklisting order and arbitrator had no jurisdiction to look into the order blacklisting the contractor. Taking into account the order of blacklisting on the part of arbitrator might be assailed to be erroneous but definitely could not be and cannot be characterised as "Misconduct".

29. The other "Misconduct" canvassed was misconstruction of contract and misconception of fact. This, also, cannot be brought within the mischief of "Misconduct" as used in reference to arbitration.

30. Another limb of "Misconduct" has been attributed to findings based on no evidence or on misreading of evidence.

31. Arbitration is a settlement of dispute on rendering a decision not of a Court of law, Civil, Criminal or Revision but of the arbitration and arbitrator has been excluded from the definition of the word "Court" as per section 3 of The Evidence Act, 1872 and arbitrator is not bound by the technicalities of The Evidence Act and he does not adjudicate nor does he sit as a Court or Tribunal and he is neither a Court nor a Tribunal. It is not the requirement of law that the arbitrator must give reasons in support of his findings and award is not liable to be set aside on the ground that arbitrator has not given reasons in support of his findings. Proceeding before arbitrator need not be conducted with such meticulous care as is required in ordinary Court of law. So long as there is substantial compliance with the principles of natural justice an arbitration award cannot be quashed. But it is, also, to be borne in mind that arbitration procedure should not be opposed to natural justice. Arbitrator considered claims of appellant and rejoinder to the claims by respondent, letters and correspondences carried by parties, legal notices, supplementary affidavit filed by appellant and, thus, it cannot be at all suggested that the findings of arbitrator rested on no evidence or on misreading of evidence. The case cannot be termed as a case of no evidence as there was documentary evidence on record of arbitration proceeding. It is settled principle of law that insufficiency of evidence or that Court would have taken a different view on the basis of evidence on record of arbitration proceeding would not warrant any interference with the arbitration award.

32. The last branch of "Misconduct" projected is that arbitrator misconducted by assessing arrear bill upon baseless and wrong calculation and there had been misconception of the mode of payment.

33. In reply to statement of claims set forth by appellant it had been categorically stated that First Party appellant had already been paid running bills covering the works he (appellant) had done. It is, thus, admitted by respondent that appellant performed works; volume of work is, of course, disputed. Arbitrator on a analysis and consideration of works performed and papers and documents passed award of Taka 92, 55,140 on exclusion of first running bill for Taka 6, 94,589. From materials on record and supplementary-affidavit it came to light that the appellant mobilised and stored stone, claps, sand and other construction materials and awarding of Taka 92, 55,140 cannot be marked as "Misconduct".

34. In Begum Khadija Akhtar Banu and another vs AKM Amanullah and another BCR 1985 (AD) 8 (supra), it had been held that arbitration is a settlement of a dispute by the decision not of a regular Court of law and an arbitrator does not adjudicate and he does not sit as a Tribunal and he is not bound by the technicalities of the Evidence Act and his award is not a Judgment, decree or order of any Court and an award of arbitrator can only be set aside by Court on limited grounds set forth in section 30 of The Arbitration Act.

35. In Mol Enterprise Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh (supra) the appellant was requested to export 5000 monkeys and in violation of the clause 33 of the agreement sold 6(six) Rhesus monkeys to the Armed Forces Radiobiology Research Institute For Neutron Bomb Radiation experiment. Misconduct on the part of the appellant had been raised before arbitrator. Arbitrator was of the positive view that selling of 6 monkeys out of 5000 monkeys, if it caused a breach of clause 33 of the agreement, would not be a material breach leading to terminate agreement and such decision cannot be characterised as misconduct. Arbitrator delivered award. Award was under challenge before the Court. It has been held that there had not been any misconduct on the part of the arbitrator and it cannot be said that arbitrator misconducted himself in making the award.

36. In Dandasi Shahu vs State of Orissa, AIR 1987 Orissa 274 arbitrator was alleged to have made an unreasoned lump sum award in appellant's favour with interest. Learned Subordinate Judge set aside the award taking view that award was in quite access having no nexus with work value and, as such, unreasonable. Learned Subordinate Judge found that lack of nexus could be construed as an error apparent on the face of award. High Court of Orissa taking into account a good number of authorities of different High Courts of India as well as Supreme Court of India observed: Mere fact that award amount is an access of contractual amount is no ground to vitiate award. It is difficult to uphold the finding of learned Court below that because excessive payment had been made to appellant having no nexus to work value and error apparent on the face of award had been committed and, as such, it is unreasonable. There is no rule of law nor any precedent that if award is in respect of a heavy amount it should on the face of it be deemed as unreasonable, wrong and illegal so as to be set aside.

37. In Messers Moosa Umar and Company Ltd, Karachi vs Hajee E Dosso and Sons and another, PLD 1971 Karachi 899 the legal controversy which cropped up was whether Court while examining award under section 30 of The Act is competent to set aside award on ground that arbitrator had adopted a wrong basis for assessing amount of damages. While dealing with point it has been held that even if arbitrator had not awarded damages upon settled principles still then award could not be challenged on ground of legal misconduct.

38. In Trading Corporation of Pakistan Limited vs Messers Aslam Syed and Company and three others, PLD 1973, Karachi 65 it had been held that wrong basis of assessment of damages could not furnish a ground to attack an award.

39. Through judicial pronouncements it has been well settled that a high amount or excessive amount awarded by arbitrator does not make an award illegal.

40. Court set aside award on question of illegality of award and "Misconduct" of arbitrator taking into account the case set up by respondent in the application under section 33 of The Act. It has already been stated that application under section 33 of The Act was no application in the eye of law and that was nonexistent and the decision reached by Court on "Misconduct" suffers from patent illegality and decision cannot be sustained in law.

41. Moreover, Court found personal "Misconduct" of arbitrator but case of personal "Misconduct" had not been set up by respondent and only "Misconduct" had been broached Court, travelled beyond its jurisdiction in finding personal "Misconduct" with arbitrator. In view of above discussion and authoritative judicial pronouncements we are of this considered view that contention pressed into service from the side of appellant got merit and contention advanced from respondent is bereft of substance and same stands ruled out.

42. Third branch of contention advanced from side of appellant is that Court like a Court of appeal looked into merit of the case and on giving various findings on merit set aside award which is not permissible in law. Province of East Pakistan vs Messrs Architect Engineering Company, represented by heirs, 20 DLR 469, Messrs Rising Sun Traders Ltd vs Chittagong Port Authority and another, 43 DLR 1, Bangladesh Telegraph and Telephone Board vs Lithi Enterprises Ltd 46 DLR 123, Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh 4 BLC 407, Puri Construction Pvt Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1989 SC 777 and Food Corporation of India vs Joginder Pal, Mohinder Pal and another and Food Corporation of India vs Messrs Veshno Rice Millers, AIR 1989 SC 1263 have been put forth in support of contention.

43. Jurisdiction of Court to interfere with an award of an arbitrator is undoubtedly a limited one. The adjudication of arbitrator is generally binding upon parties to arbitration proceeding and it is not open to Court to attempt to probe into mental process by which arbitrator reached his conclusion and, also, to Court to re-assess and re-appreciate evidences to find whether an arbitrator had committed any illegality and error. Court cannot sit on appeal upon conclusion of arbitrator by re-examining and re-appreciating evidences considered and assessed by arbitrator. It is not the function of Court to disturb finding of arbitrator, if it has been reached bona fide.

44. In Province of East Pakistan vs Messers Architect Engineering and Company, represented by heirs (supra) the controversy was whether it was open to appellant to ask High Court to go into details of claim and counter-claim or to reassess question as it was a court of appeal. A Division Bench of High Court held:

when dispute has been referred to arbitration, Court's jurisdiction to interfere with findings of arbitrator is very limited and confined to grounds specified in section 30 of The Arbitration Act.

It is not open to appellant to ask to go into details of claim and counter-claim or to reassess question as if this Court was a Court of appeal from a decision of a Civil Court in its original jurisdiction and Court does not act like a Court of appeal against arbitrator's decision.

45. In Messers Rising Sun Traders Ltd vs Chittagong Port Authority and another (supra) question arose in a proceeding arising out of arbitration whether Court can be regarded as a Court of appeal from decision of an arbitrator. The question had been answered in the following language:

In a proceeding arising out of arbitration a Court cannot be regarded as a Court of appeal from a decision of arbitrator. It can set aside an award only on limited ground set forth in section 30 of The Act. If an award is otherwise valid a Court cannot interfere with it or review it. Our superior Courts have always expressed opinions in favour of non-interference unless findings are perverse causing injustice or arbitrator has misconducted himself or proceeding or award improperly procured or it was otherwise invalid.

46. In Mol Enterprises Inc vs Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh, (supra) observation of a Division Bench of a High Court Division is couched in the following terms:

In a proceeding under section 14 of The Act the court is not to be regarded as a court of appeal and the court cannot sit in appeal over the decision of the arbitrator. The court can only interfere if the award is bad on the face of it or there is an error of law apparent on a mere perusal of the award. In the absence of any such indication if the award substantially decides the actual dispute between the parties, it would not render the award as invalid or without jurisdiction. Further observation is in the following language:

Arbitrators are supposed to be laymen not conversant with niceties of law and rules and if the award is badly stated it cannot for that reason, be considered as a ground for setting aside the same. Arbitrators are not bound by the technical rules of procedure which the courts are required to follow. It is sufficient if the arbitrator gives a decision which determines the rights of the parties in consideration of the subject matter of reference. The award need not be a reasoned judicial decision and nor need it for the reasons conclusion.

47. In Puri Construction Pvt Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1989 SC 777 it has been held:

When a court is called upon to decide the objections raised by a party against an arbitration award the jurisdiction of the court is limited, as expressly indicated in the Arbitration Act, and it has no jurisdiction to sit in appeal and examine the correctness of the award on merit.

48. In Food Corporation of India vs Joginder Pal, Mohinder Pal and another and Food Corporation of India vs Mis Veshno Rice Millers, AIR 1989 SC 1263 observation recorded in Puri Construction Pvt Ltd vs Union of India had been considered and in the line of the observation it has been laid down:

It is not necessary for a court to examine the merits of the awards with the reference to the materials produced before the arbitrator. The court cannot sit in appeal over the views of the arbitrator by re-examining and reassessing the materials.

49. Proposition of law emerged from the above judicial authorities is that court cannot sit on appeal upon the conclusion of the arbitrator by re-examining and re-appreciating the evidences examined and appreciated by arbitrator.

50. Examination of the judgment under challenge in the appeal indicates that Court exceeded its limited jurisdiction in disposing of the application laid under section 14 read with section 17 of The Act and virtually sat on appeal. The third branch of contention holds water and is accepted.

and
