59. Doctrine of "Waiver" and 'Acquiescence" is now looked into. "Waiver" has been stated in Black's Law Dictionary, 6th Edition in the following terms:

 "The intention or voluntary relinquishment of a known right, or such conduct as warrants an inference of the relinquishment of such right, or when one dispenses with the performance of something he is entitled to exact or when one in possession of any right, whether conferred by law or by contract, with full knowledge of the material facts, does or forbears to do something the doing of which or the failure of forbearance to do which is inconsistent with the right, or his intention to rely upon it. The renunciation, repudiation, abandonment, opportunity to take advantage of some defect, irregularity, or wrong. An express or implied relinquishment of a legal right. A doctrine resting upon an equitable principle, which courts of law will recognise."

In Corpus Juris Secundum (CJS) 92 Page 1041 "Waiver" is stated as such:

 "Waiver" is defined as the voluntary and intentional relinquishment of a known right, the voluntary and intentional relinquishment or abandonment of a known existing legal right, advantage, benefit, claim or privilege, which except for such waiver the party would have enjoyed. "Waiver" is also defined as the voluntary relinquishment, or intentional abandonment or relinquishment, of a known right, benefit, privilege or advantage, which, but for such waiver, the party would have enjoyed; and the word "waiver" also means the intentional or voluntary relinquishment of a known legal right which is at the time available; the intentional relinquishment of a known right with or after knowledge of the facts; the voluntary relinquishment or renunciation of some right; a forgoing, giving up, or renouncement of some benefit or advantage, which, but for such waiver, the party would have enjoyed; the intentional relinquishment of, or refusal to accept, a right; the relinquishment of a known or existing right; the voluntary relinquishment of a right or advantage; the voluntary yielding up of some existing right; the voluntary or intentional giving up of a known or existing right. "Waiver" is frequently defined in terms of a surrender, as, the voluntary surrender of a right; the voluntary surrender or relinquishment of a known legal right or the intentional doing of an act inconsistent with the claiming of it; the voluntary abandonment or surrender, by a capable person, of a right known by him to exist, with the intent that such right shall be surrendered and such person forever deprived of its benefit; or such conduct as warrants an inference of the relinquishment of such right." "Waiver" is, thus, an act of waiving, the act of intentionally relinquishing something as a right, the act of not insisting upon such right, claim or privilege belonging to a person who executes the same, the voluntary surrender of a right, the voluntary abandonment or surrender of a right known by him to exist.

 "Waiver" is one of the most familiar of the Doctrines of law, a technical Doctrine of very broad and general application.

"Acquiescence" stated in Corpus Juris Secundum (CJS) IA page 279 is hereunder: "Acquiescence.

The word, it has been said, implies acceptance or approval, active assent, active consent, assent, assent or consent, consent, also knowledge, and power to contract. The word has been employed as meaning conduct recognising the existence of a transaction and intended to carry the transaction, or permit it to be carried, into effect; some act not deliberately intended to ratify a former transaction as existing, and intended, to some extent at least, to carry it into effect, and to obtain or claim the benefits resulting from it.

It is also defined as meaning consent by silence; consent to conditions; giving up or abandonment of claim; inaction while an act is being performed; intentional failure to resist the assertion of an adverse right; mere silence, a refusal to speak when one ought to speak for the protection of others, or to act in time to prevent others from doing acts of which the dilatory one afterwards complains; passive compliance; quiescence under such circumstances that assent may be inferred. The word is further defined as meaning release or abandonment of ones rights, if, having rights, he stands by and sees another dealing with his property in a manner inconsistent with such rights, and makes no objection while the act is in progress; resting apparently satisfied, without objection; resting satisfied with or submission to an existing state of things; silence and inaction; silent but conscious consent; silent passive assent; submission; tacit encouragement.

In addition, it has generally been said that "acquiescence" is where a person who knows that he is entitled to impeach a transaction or to enforce a right neglects to do so for such a length of time that under the circumstances of the case the other party may fairly infer that he has waived or abandoned his right."

 "Acquiescence" as stated in Wharton's Law Lexicon 14th Edition is consent, either express or implied.

 "Acquiescence" is, therefore, acceptance, active assent and active consent, consent by silence, giving up, abandonment of claim which a person can perform and enforce.

60. In Government of Bangladesh and others vs Messrs Samir and Company (supra) along with other questions, question of jurisdiction of Court to appoint arbitrator acting under clauses (a), (b) and (c) of sub-section I on expiry of 15 clear days service of notice by party making application before Court and effect of putting no objection to appointment of arbitrator came up for consideration. It has been held that if a Court exercises power of appointment before expiry of the prescribed period and party concerned after being served with notice of proceeding does not choose to raise an objection to exercise of Court's power in this regard, this lapse on part of Court will no doubt be deemed to be waived and validity of order of appointment by Court cannot be subsequently impugned.

 61. In Salamat Khan vs QG Ahad (supra) there was an arbitration agreement and that was modified by deleting second arbitration and umpire clause stipulated between parties and that was accepted by respondent. Appellant not only submitted to jurisdiction of sole arbitrator but participated in arbitration proceeding, though, not wholeheartedly. Appellant appeared before arbitrator from time to time but did not appear in final stage of arbitration proceeding. It has been held that appellant by his participation in arbitration proceeding has by his conduct accepted modified arbitration agreement and his subsequent conduct, also, revealed that he did accept modified agreement.

62. In Government of Bangladesh, represented by Director of Movement and Storage Department of Food vs Jalaluddin Ahmed (supra) it has been observed that when arbitration proceeding continued beyond four months with parties raising no objection and conclusion is that party concerned has waived his right to raise any objection to award passed by arbitrator.

63. In Adamjee Sons Limited vs Jiban Bima Corporation (supra) it has been held that where parties submit to arbitration without intervention of Court and making prayer for passing award such parties cannot be allowed to take objection to validity of award on ground of want of jurisdiction of arbitrator on plea that reference was not in Court.

 64. In Prasum Roy vs The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority and another (supra) observation of the Supreme Court of India is couched in following language:

where though a party is aware from beginning that by reason of some disability, matter is legally incapable of being submitted to arbitration, participates in arbitration proceeding without protest and fully avails of entire arbitration proceeding and then when he sees that award has gone against him comes forward to challenge the whole of arbitration proceeding as without jurisdiction on ground of a non-disability, same cannot be allowed. Principle applies both before and after making of award. Principle is that a party shall not be allowed to blow hot and cold simultaneously. Long participation and acquiescence in proceedings precludes such a party from contending that proceedings were without jurisdiction.

 65. In State of Orissa vs Dandasi Sahu (supra) it had been laid down:

It is well settled that when parties choose their own arbitrator to be Judge in dispute between them they cannot when the award is good on the face of it object to decision either upon law or on fact.

66. In Messrs Haji Moosa Ismail & Ca vs Amin Agencies Ltd (supra) it has been held that a party who wishes to raise any objection against a proceeding before an arbitrator must do so at earliest without waiting for result of award to go against him. It has been, also, held that both parties after filing statements of claims when parties have consented to wait for decisions of arbitrator after having given the statements of their claim and having filed certain documents upon which they relied, it was too late for a party to urge objection about misconduct of arbitrator and objection stands rejected.

 67. In Messrs Habib & Sons vs Messrs Virak Co (supra) it has been observed that after participating in arbitration proceeding and by not raising any objection to jurisdiction of arbitrator, the party waived their objection to jurisdiction of arbitrator to deal with matter and any irregularity in appointment of arbitrator was cured by conduct of party.

68. In Messrs Pakistan Builders Co, Karachi vs Pakistan (supra) it has been stated that party submitted to jurisdiction of arbitrator and filing their claim before arbitrator cannot raise objection after filing of award that arbitration was premature.

69. Proposition emerging from above authorities is that a party after participating in arbitration proceeding and by not raising any objection to jurisdiction of arbitrator to deal with arbitration matter party waived his right in putting forward any objection to jurisdiction of arbitrator to arbitrate the dispute and pass award after the award.

70. We now propose to address ourselves to the authorities referred to from the side of Second party-respondent. In Hasmat Ali Jamaddar and others vs Asmat Ali Jomaddar (supra) award given was an award of arbitration of five of seven arbitrators and award was not award of majority but an arbitration of majority of arbitrators.

It has been held: It is one thing to say to abide by the award of the majority of the arbitrators and quite a different thing to say to abide by the arbitration of majority of the arbitrators. Since the objecting party never agreed and submitted to such arbitration, the award is without jurisdiction and void and need not be avoided. In the case in hand both the parties agreed and submitted to the jurisdiction of the arbitrator Mr Md Asaduzzaman and participated in the arbitration proceeding. The cited case is of no assistance to Second party-respondent.

71. In Government of Bangladesh and another vs Messrs Mashriqui Textiles and others, 35 DLR (AD) 123 both the parties to the agreement agreed that the dispute be settled by arbitration as provided in clause 7 of the contract and arbitration agreement provided that Secretary, Ministry of Commerce would nominate the arbitrator but the plaintiff apprehended that the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce might not take an impartial view of the matter and for that matter was trying to make out a case for appointment of a new man in place of the Secretary. It has been held: If the court is satisfied that the arbitration agreement should be filed then the court would refer the dispute to arbitrator to be nominated by the Secretary of the Ministry and question of charge of arbitrator is not relevant when the parties agreed upon his appointment in the agreement. In this case, both appellant and respondent had agreed on the appointment of Mr Md Asaduzzaman as arbitrator to arbitrate the arbitration proceeding on laying a joint petition and participated in the proceeding. The cited authority got no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the case.

72. In Chief  Engineer, Roads and Highways Department, Government of The People's Republic of Bangladesh vs Concord Engineers and Construction Limited (supra) it has been held that the appointment of the arbitrator was premature as no occasion arose for referring the dispute to the arbitrator and the award given by the arbitrator was void ab initio and nullity in the eye of law. The cited case is quite distinguishable and not at all applicable in the fact and circumstances of the present case.

73. Respondent having submitted to jurisdiction of arbitrator by filing joint petition and accepting the order of the Court appointing Mr Asaduzzaman as the sole arbitrator and in participating in arbitration proceeding and in not challenging the authority of arbitrator to pass the award now cannot question the validity of the award. There had been waiver and acquiescence on part of Second party-respondent and the same is completely debarred from raising question of jurisdiction for first time in this appeal. The observation of Pickford J in (1909) 2 KB 948 may aptly be taken notice of: All the cases of waiver proceeded from the principle that if a person knows of a disqualification in the arbitrator or defect in the proceedings and shall continue to go on with the reference before him, he cannot afterwards object, because he must be taken to have waived the disqualification or defect.

74. The vehement argument surged forward from the side of Second party-respondent could not impress us and it stands rejected.

 75. The only surviving points now fall for consideration is (i) whether the award can be set aside or it can be made Rule of Court, and (ii) whether decision recorded by Court warrants interference by this Court in its appellate authority.

76. In approaching the points it can conveniently be observed that interminable time consuming complex and expensive Court procedure impelled Jurists and Legislators to search for an alternative forum less formal, more effective and speedy resolution of disputes avoiding procedural claptrap and this led to the passing of Arbitration Act of 1940 but experience shows that the procedure by way of arbitration proceeding chosen by parties for expeditious disposal has become more complex and ordeal for a party graced with an award and hardship starts after award.

 77. Filing of an award in Court is sine qua non to an order either under section 17 making judgment in terms of award or to an order setting aside it on the ground mentioned in section 30 of The Act.

78. Section 30 enumerates the grounds for setting aside an award. Section 30 reads as follows:

"30. Grounds for setting aside award—An award shall not be set aside except on one or more of the following grounds, namely:

  1. that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings; that an award has been made after the issue of an order by the Court superseding the arbitration or after arbitration proceedings have become invalid under section 35;
  2. that an award has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid."

79. Ground (b) is not relevant for our purpose. Ground (a) i.e. Misconduct has been dealt with exhaustively and it has been held that there had not been any misconduct on the part of arbitrator in delivering award.

80. Expression expressed in clause (c) is an award which has been improperly procured or is otherwise invalid. In re Whitely and Roberts Arbitration (1891) 1 Ch 558 it has been held that an award is improperly made when it is made by collusion or in consequence of a bribe. In Amarnath vs Echhal, AIR 1932 Lahore 378=137 IC 846 it has been held that the words "an arbitration has been improperly procured" include the case of an arbitrator who has been illegally and improperly appointed.

81. No allegation had been mounted against the arbitrator that award had been obtained by collusion or in consequence of a bribe. It cannot be, also, said that arbitrator had been illegally and improperly appointed inasmuch as with consent and on the joint application of the parties arbitrator had been appointed.

82. The words or "otherwise invalid" were introduced for the first time in Para 15 of the Second Schedule of The Code of Civil Procedure of 1908 on which this is based, according to the recommendation of their Lordships of Privy Council in the case of Ghulam Khan vs Muhammad Hassan, 29 Cal 167 29 1 A 51= 6 CWN 22. An award made otherwise than in accordance with law and authority conferred upon arbitrator is an award which is "otherwise invalid" and may, accordingly, be set aside by the Court. Award made by arbitrator cannot be characterised to be an invalid award. Corollary thereof is that no grounds existed for setting aside award.

83. Arbitrator, in awarding award, took into stock factual matrix and documents by way of Annexures produced by both parties. Arbitrator found that First party-appellant stored cement, rod, stone, chips, etc. at the place of construction. Arbitrator found that the work stood delayed substantially for supply of work order after a lapse of 24 days and, also, for the delay caused in supplying work drawing after three months from the date of delivery of work order and in supplying physical layout after about 7 months and by the acts Second party-respondent jointly and severally violated contract conditions contained in contract. Arbitrator went through Audit Report and Balance Sheet of First party-appellant. Reasonableness of the reasons assigned by the arbitrator cannot be challenged. Appraisement of evidences by arbitrator can never be a matter which court can question. The arbitrator is the sole judge of the quality as well as quantity of evidence and it will not be for the Court to take upon itself the task of being a Judge on evidences before arbitrator. In the case in hand, Court sat as a Judge on evidences and decision of arbitrator and virtually sat as a Court of appeal which is impermissible in law. Learned Subordinate Judge misdirected himself in his approach on the legal debate and committed substantial error in the decision and the decision became unsustainable warranting interference by this Court in exercise of its appellate authority.

84. Arbitrator passed an award of Taka six crore as damage for loss of goodwill and reputation of business noted in Item No. 1 of schedule of claim. Arbitrator, also, delivered award of Taka 92,55,140 in respect of arrear contract money excluding first running bill recorded in Item No. 2 and, also, Taka 14,80,822.40 i.e. 16% simple interest of Taka 92,55,140 as compensatory cost listed in Item No. 3 of the schedule of claim put forward.

85. Bestowal of award amount of Taka six (6) crore as damage for loss of goodwill and reputation of business does neither appear to be proper nor have any legal foundation and award of Taka six (6) crore as damage for loss of goodwill and reputation of business got no leg to stand and the award of the said amount of Taka six (6) crore is set aside. But award of Taka 92,55,140 in respect of arrear contract money and, also, Taka 14,80,822.40 i.e. 16% simple interest on the said Taka 92,55,140 as compensatory cost, transpires to be proper and legal and the award in respect of those amount i.e. Taka 92,55,140 + 14,80,822.40 = Taka 1,07,35,962.40 is maintained. Award in respect of above stated Taka i.e. 92, 55,140 and Taka 14, 80,822.40 in all Taka 1, 07, 35,962.40 is made Rule of Court.

86. Points formulated stand disposed of accordingly.

87. Corollary thereof is that the appeal stands allowed in part in the terms stated above.

Parties shall bear their respective costs.

 End.

parties:
Abdur Rahman Mia (Md) ------ Petitioner
Vs
Md Saber Ali Mia ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 22-8-1990 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Pabna in OC Appeal No. 25 of 1986 affirming the judgment and decree dated 23-12-1985 passed by the learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Santhia Upazila in OC Suit No. 403 of 1984 (OC Suit No. 211/82, Pabna) decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. Opposite party No. 1 Md Saber Ali Mia as plaintiff instituted the instant suit for declaration of title in 4 suit plots claiming that he purchased the same from the owner Md Abdul Kader on 14-7-1978. Since the defendant petitioner disturbed the possession of the plaintiff he instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of title. The present petitioner Md Abdur Rahman Mia contested the suit by filing written statement contending inter alia, that on 26-5-1965 the vendor Abdul Kader sold 6 plots including the suit plots to him. On the same day he was put to possession of the suit plots along with two plots and mutated his name in respect of the suit plots and had been possessing the same for a long period. The vendor Abdul Kader fraudulently sold the land to opposite party No. 2 plaintiff Md Saber Ali Mia in order to deprive the defendant for some ulterior purpose. In fact, he purchased the lands covered by 6 plots which belonged to Abdul Kader Mia, the vendor. So, the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff is a fraudulent one and on the basis of the same the plaintiff is not entitled to any decree.

3. Both the Courts below after considering the material evidence on record decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff holding that he has got the right and title over the 4 suit plots.

4. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the lower Appellate Court the defendant preferred this revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

5. The facts appearing from the records are that one Abdul Kader was the owner of SA Plots Nos. 167, 223, 222, 234, 250 and 235. By a registered sale deed that Abdul Kader sold his aforesaid lands showing plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221, 233, 250 and 235, plots Nos. 250 and 235 are correct but plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221 and 233 was incorrectly written in the deed of sale dated 26-5-1965 instead of plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234. That Abdul Kader was not the owner of plots Nos. 1805, 222, 221 and 233. So, it appears that out of 6 plots, plot number is correct in respect of SA plots Nos. 250 and 235 and incorrect plots numbers were given as plots Nos. 1805, 224, 221 and 233 in the registered document dated 26-5-1965. The selfsame vendor Abdul Kader sold 4 plots showing plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 in the sale deed dated 14-7-1978 in favour of Md Saber Ali Mia namely, the present plaintiff. Being embodied with the aforesaid sale deed dated 14-7-1978 he instituted the present suit namely, OC Suit No. 211 of 1982 on 29-7-1982. Now both the Courts held that since the deed of Abdur Rahman Mia did not contain the correct plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 no title of the aforesaid plots passed to Abdur Rahman Mia and since the sale deed of Md Saber Ali Mia contained plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234, the title passed to this Md Saber Ali Mia by a deed dated 14-7-1978 and as such, the title of the plaintiff has been declared.

6. Mr Abdul Majid, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has referred to section 95 of the Evidence Act and tried to show that though mistaken plots number were given in the deed as regards 4 plots, yet the vender Abdul Kader actually delivered possession of plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 in favour of the present petitioner by a registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965. Since that date the present petitioner had been possessing the lands of the aforesaid 4 plots together with lands of plots Nos. 250 and 235. The defendant petitioner mutated his name in the record of rights and have been paying rents to the Government and in this way he has been enjoying the suit properties along with 2 other plots. With regard to plots Nos. 250 and 235 there was no dispute and Abdul Kader was the owner of these two plots. By the selfsame document Abdul Kader sold plots Nos. 187, 223, 222 and 234 showing wrongly plot Nos. as 1805, 224, 221 and 233. This transaction of 6 plots was made by one and same registered document.

7. Mr MG Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that since both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff acquired right and title in respect of 4 suit plots, the plaintiff acquired the right and title in the suit properties. He further submits that having wrong plots number in the sale deed the present defendant petitioner cannot claim any right and title over the suit plots.

<u>8. Mr Abdul Majid submits that admittedly the vender Abdul Kader sold 6 plots having the respective areas therein to the defendant petitioner. There is no dispute about plot Nos. 250 and 235. If by mistake different plot numbers of other 4 plots were given in the deed of sale then the mistake should be omitted and correct number of plots should be taken into consideration in view of the fact that possession of the selfsame lands which belonged to Abdul Kader were given to the defendant petitioner who has been enjoying the same till to-day. He ultimately submitted that if by fraudulent means the vendor Abdul Kader intentionally and fraudulently had given different plot numbers of his own lands but he handed over possession of the same to the defendant by virtue of registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965 in that case also the defendant is entitled to the aforesaid lands which belonged to Abdul Kader. In this connection he has referred to section 95 of the. Evidence Act which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"When language used in a document is plain in itself, but is unmeaning in reference to existing facts, evidence may be given to show that it was used in a peculiar sense."</u>

<u>9. In Sarkar's Law of Evidence an illustration has been given in the way that A sells by deed a house in Calcutta. A had no house in Calcutta but it appears that he had a house at Howrah of which he had been in possession since the execution of the deed. This sale shows that the deed in fact related to the house of A at Howrah. Mr Majid has also referred to the case of Mahabir Singh vs Jag M Mohan Lal, 57 IC page 569 and the case of Naraindas vs Tekchand, 84 IC page 137. The principle laid down in those decisions supported the submission of Mr Abdul Majid.</u>

<u>10. Vender Abdul Kader was not the owner of plot Nos. 1805, 224, 221 and 233 but he was the owner of plot Nos. 187, 223, 224 and 234. Though mistaken plot numbers were given in respect of 4 plots but the vender Abdul Kader had delivered physical possession to the defendant petitioner by virtue of registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965 of the vender''s own plots namely, 187, 223, 222 and 234. So, it appears that Abdul Kader was the owner of the lands of those 4 plots and though wrong numbers of plots were given yet he put the defendant petitioner in actual possession of his own plots namely, 187, 223, 224, and 234 along with plot Nos. 250 and 235. The defendant petitioner purchased the aforesaid lands for valuable consideration with bonafide belief that vendor Abdul Kader was the owner and he had delivered possession of his own lands giving correct plot numbers in the deed of sale. But numbers of two plots out of 6 plots were given correctly but numbers of 4 plots were given wrongly.</u>

<u>11. Now let us see whether this was done by mistake or it was done with malafide intention to defraud the defendant petitioner Abdur Rahman Mia. From the evidence on record it appears that it was done by vender Abdul Kader not out of any bonafide mistake but it was deliberately done by vender Abdul Kader with malafide motive and intention to defraud the vendee Abdur Rahman Mia. It is clear from the fact that by a separate registered sale deed this Abdul Kader sold the aforesaid 4 plots to opposite party plaintiff Md Saber Ali Mia giving correct number of plots in the document dated 14-7-1978. Had Abdul Kader no malafide intention to defraud Abdul Rahman Mia, he would not sell the disputed 4 plots of lands to Md Saber Ali Mia the plaintiff by a registered sale deed in the year 1978. It shows that with clear malafide motive and intention Abdul Kader gave incorrect numbers of 4 plots and after a long time he sold the selfsame lands giving correct plot numbers to plaintiff Md Saber Ali Mia. So, it appears that this transaction vide registered sale deed dated 14-7-1978 was absolutely a malafide one in order to deprive and defraud Abdur Rahman Mia. So, the person committed fraud should not be allowed to enjoy the fruits of his own fraud. So, I hold that the plaintiff Saber Ali Mia had not acquired any right and title in the suit properties out of such a fraudulent transaction by a deed of sale dated 14-7-1978. As such, the plaintiff has not acquired any right and title in the suit properties. I further hold that right and title in respect of the 4 plots of lands which belonged to Abdul Kader passed to the defendant petitioner by virtue of the registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965.</u>

12. Mr Abdul Majid submits that on 26-5-1965 by registered sale deed Abdul Kader sold the lands of the aforesaid plots to Abdur Rahman Mia and possession of the aforesaid 6 plots were delivered to him. Since then this Abdur Rahman Mia had been possessing the suit lands by mutating his name but the other deed was executed and registered by Abdul Kader in favour of Saber Ali Mia on 14-7-1978 i.e. about 13 years after and thereafter the suit was filed by the present plaintiff on 29-7-1982 i.e. after about 17 years. Since the defendant petitioner was in possession although such a suit after 17 years is barred by limitation . I find substance in the contention of Mr Abdul Majid.

<u>13. Mr Majid further submits that since possession was with the defendant petitioner since 26-5-1965, the suit of the plaintiff is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act inasmuch as the plaintiff prayed for declaration of title and not the recovery of possession. After selling the lands to Abdur Rahman Mia in the year 1965 Abdur Kader did not possess the lands. When Abdul Kader sold the lands with the present plaintiff in 1978 the possession could not be delivered to this plaintiff Saber Ali Mia inasmuch as the defendant petitioner was in possession. So, it appears that since 1965 till the filing of the suit in the year 1982 neither Abdul Kader nor the plaintiff Saber Ali Mia was in possession of the suit lands. So, I hold that the present suit of the plaintiff is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.</u>

14. I have gone through the judgments of both the Courts below. It appears that they considered the whole case from a wrong angle and misconstrued the material evidence on record and as a result they committed an error of law occasioning failure of justice and, as such, the judgments and decrees passed by the Courts below are liable to be set aside. The Courts below just considered the facial value of the two sale deeds executed and registered by Abdul Kader but the intention of the vender could not be gathered by them out of these two sale deeds since the intention of the vendor Abdul Kader was to sell his 6 plots of lands, though wrong numbers were given in respect of 4 plots, yet actual possession of his own lands were given to the purchaser Abdur Rahman Mia by virtue of a registered sale deed dated 26-5-1965. On good faith and honest belief he purchased the lands on 26-5-65 at a valuable consideration and got possession on 26-5-65.

In the result, this Rule is made absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the lower Appellate Court affirming those of the trial Court are hereby set aside and the suit of the present plaintiff is hereby dismissed.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case I pass no order as to costs.

Send down the LC records immediately.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 10th day of August, 2009 and the 31st day of July, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.2452 of 2009 with Writ Petition No.58 of 2008)
full_judgment:
Md Abdul Wahhab Miah J: These three civil petitions for leave to appeal (CP) have been heard together and are disposed of by this common judgment.

CP No. 2515 of 2010:

2. Delay in filing the CP is condoned. This CP has been filed by the Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha (RAJUK) against the judgment and order dated the 10th day of August, 2009 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 2452 of 2009 making the Rule absolute. Respondent No. 1, herein, as petitioner (hereinafter referred to as the writ-petitioner) filed the writ petition before the High Court Division for a direction .upon the petitioners herein (respondent Nos.1-3 in the writ petition and the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works) to approve the building construction plan submitted by him on 23-5-2007 under RAJUK File No. 3C-21/07 and accordingly, the Rule was issued.

3. The case of the writ-petitioner as stated in the writ petition, inter-alia, was that he is a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and is also a citizen of Canada and resides there with his family. He purchased a plot measuring three kathas of land being Plot No. 19, at Road No. 22, Sector-14, Uttara Model Town, Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as the plot in question) from original lessees, Khaliqur Rahman and Mohibur Rahman with permission of RAJUK dated 21-12-2006. The sale deed was executed and registered on 26-12-2006. The writ-petitioner received clearance certificate from RAJUK on 28-3-2007 for submitting plan. Accordingly, he submitted the plan with RAJUK on 23-5-2007 along with plan fee receipt dated 26-4-2007 under RAJUK File No. 3C-21/07. RAJUK did not take any step to approve the plan submitted almost two years back nor informed anything about such delay causing harassment to the writ-petitioner. The writ-petitioner, time to time, held conversations with RAJUK's authority and also met its Chairman who kept silent on the issue. Earlier RAJUK illegally issued Memo No. Rajuk /Estate 69(2) stha dated 23-7-2007 (Plot ID 14-22-19) to harass the writ-petitioner with malafide intention which was challenged in Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008. Upon hearing the parties, the High Court Division by judgment and order dated 31-7-2008 declared the said Memo without jurisdiction. The High Could Division held that:

"For the reasons aforesaid, there is no escape from the conclusion that respondent No. 1 by misuse and abuse of his office as Director (Estate) of RAJUK wrote the impugned letter to achieve certain illegal gains, which was clearly unauthorized, uncalled for and without jurisdiction."

4. In spite of the above finding, RAJUK did not take any step to approve the plan submitted almost two years back nor informed anything about the delay although the writ-petitioner met the authority several times. The writ-petitioner resides in Canada with family and was compelled to come to Dhaka several times at huge cost and harassment for the matter. In the circumstances, the writ-petitioner in March, 2009 met the Chairman, RAJUK, but he kept absolute silence on the issue. On 30-3-2009, the writ-petitioner served a demand justice notice upon the writ-respondents calling upon them to approve the plan submitted by him 2(two) years back and inform his compliance thereof within 7(seven) days from the date of receipt of the notice. The writ-respondents duly received the notice, but they neither did anything nor responded to it, since the plan was submitted as per the Building Construction Rules, 2006, 2007 RAJUK was bound to approve the same within 45 days of the submission thereof, i.e. within 45 days from 23-5-2007, but till the filing of the writ petition, they did not approve the plan nor informed anything to the writ-petitioner. In the above circumstances, he was compelled to file the writ petition.

5. It appears that the writ petition was heard ex-parte and the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute directing the writ-respondents to consider and approve the construction plan submitted by the writ-petitioner for approval in accordance with law as expeditiously as possible "preferably within 1 (one) month from receipt of this order positively"; hence this petition for leave to appeal.

CP No. 864 of 2010:

6. This CP has been filed by RAJUK against the judgment and order dated the 31st day of July, 2008 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008 making the Rule absolute with a cost of Taka 25,000 (twenty five thousand) to be realized from the pocket of writ-respondent No.1, Director (Estate), RAJUK.

7. This writ petition was filed by respondent No. 1 herein, (hereinafter refer-red to as the writ-petitioner) challenging Memo No. RAJUK /Estate 69(2) stha dated 23-7-2007 (Plot ID 14-22-019) issued by RAJUK under the signature of writ-respondent No. 1 to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect and also for a direction to approve the plan submitted by the writ-petitioner on 28-3-2007.

8. The case of the writ-petitioner as made out in the writ petition was that he, in order to purchase a plot of land, caused an advertisement published in the "Daily Janakantha" dated 30-11-2006. In pursuance of the said advertisement, writ-respondent No. 4, Md Khaliqur Rahman entered into a contract with him for sale of a plot of land measuring about three khatas of land in sector 14, Uttara Model Town at Dhaka (hereinafter referred to as the plot in question) which writ-respondent No. 4 and his full brother, writ-respondent No. 5, Md Mahibur Rahman, got as affected persons by way of a lease for 99 (ninety nine) years from RAJUK. Writ-respondent No. 5 was staying abroad, he appointed writ-respondent No.4 as his attorney by a registered power of attorney being No. 21432 dated 7-12-2005. Attorney (writ-respondent No.4) was empowered, amongst others, to execute and register the deed of transfer in respect of the plot in question or any another agreement with RAJUK. On 3-1-2006, writ-respondent No. 5 submitted the aforesaid power of attorney before RAJUK for approval. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Counsel, appearing for the writ-respondent-petitioners in respect of CP No. 2515 of 2010, has also submitted that the matter of approving the construction plan was under official process, the writ-petitioner without final decision of RAJUK's authorities filed the writ petition which was premature and so was not maintainable, but the High Court Division failed to consider this aspect of the case. 26. We find no substance in the submission of Mr Mahbubey Alam in view of the facts and the circumstances under which the writ-petitioner was compelled to file the writ petition. We fail to understand how the writ petition could be said to be premature when the Building Construction Rules was prevalent at the relevant time and as amended by promulgating new Rules in 2008 provided that the plan has to be approved within 45 (forty five) days from the date of receipt of application for approving the plan and till filing of the writ petition in spite of almost long period of two years (plan was submitted on 23-5-2007 and the writ petition was filed on 12-4-2009) elapsed, the plan was neither approved by RAJUK nor was anything intimated to the writ-petitioner. And by the time, judgment was delivered in the writ petition more than 2(two) years and 3 (three) months elapsed. If we give countenance to the submission of Mr Mahbubey Alam, we shall be giving premium to RAJUK and its officials in not acting as per the Rules and to allow them to act as per their own sweet will and in that case, we will be pushing the people of Dhaka City Corporation just at their mercy and thus to show a big thumb to the Building Construction Rules. RAJUK being a statutory body must act promptly and quickly according to the Rules.

27. We also find the submission of Mr Mahbubey Alam that by giving direction to RAJUK and its officials to consider and approve the construction plan submitted by the writ-petitioner for approval, no chance was given to them to verify the "legality and proprietiness" of the deed and the other papers of the writ-petitioner, irrational as admittedly the writ-petitioner purchased the plot in question with the permission of RAJUK and he was delivered possession thereof, after purchase, RAJUK mutated his name and also gave clearance certificate to submit the plan for the construction of the building. Further, when in Writ Petition No.58 of 2008, the letter dated 23-7-2007 issued by the Director (Estate) to the writ-petitioner by which he was asked to appear before him with the original deed and the other papers in support of his ownership, was declared to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect.

The High Court Division made the Rule absolute with a cost of Taka 25,000 with the direction to realize the same from the pocket of writ-respondent No. 1 declaring the impugned letter to have been passed without lawful authority and was of no legal effect. In making the Rule absolute, the High Court Division took into consideration the following facts.

30. It is not disputed that RAJUK transferred the plot in question to writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5, by way of a lease, for 99(ninety nine) years by a registered deed of agreement dated 21-12-2006; writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 entered into an agreement with the writ-petitioner for sale of the plot in question at a fixed price of Taka 46,00,000 (it would be Taka 48,00,000, in the writ petition, the figure has been correctly mentioned) together with cost to be borne by the writ-petitioner; pursuant to such agreement, RAJUK accorded necessary permission to writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 to transfer the plot in question and on the basis of such permission, writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 transferred the plot in question to the writ-petitioner by a registered deed of sale dated 24-12-2006(the correct date is 26-12-2006 and in the writ petition the date has been correctly mentioned) and delivered possession thereof to him; with the approval of RAJUK, writ-respondent No.4 executed the deed of sale for himself and on behalf of writ-respondent No.5 on the basis of a registered power of attorney. Thus, being the owner in possession, the writ-petitioner got the plot in question mutated in his name with RAJUK and obtained necessary approval of a plan for the construction thereon; when the writ-petitioner had undertaken the construction work, he came to know about the existence of the impugned letter, copy of which was not sent to him. By the impugned letter, writ-respondent No. 1 asked the writ-petitioner to appear before him with the original deed and the other papers for hearing and determination of title in the plot in question.

31. The High Court Division observed that after transfer of the plot in question by way of lease for 99(ninety nine) years and further transfer and delivery of possession thereof by the lessees to the writ-petitioner, respondent No. 1 definitely knew that RAJUK had no right, title or possession or any interest therein. Neither writ-respondent No. 1 nor RAJUK had any authority or power to settle any question of title in any land in Bangladesh. When writ-respondent No. 1 issued the impugned letter, he was definitely actuated by certain ulterior motives, which was clear from the fact that he sent a copy of the letter to the Officer-in-Charge of Uttara Police Station, Dhaka for stopping the construction on the plot in question. Respondent No. 1 was definitely aware of the fact that he was not doing the right thing in writing the letter "What such letter could create any impact upon the petitioner, who is living in Canada, is easily understood."

32. In respect of CP No. 864 of 2010, Mr Mahbubey Alam has submitted that writ-respondent No. 1 on receipt of the complaint regarding title of the plot in question simply issued a letter on 23-7-2007 asking the writ-petitioner to appear before him on 15-8-2007 with the original documents for examination and till that date, request was made to post-pone the construction work, the writ-petitioner had no cause of action to file the writ petition. Moreso, RAJUK was quite authorized to ask any one claiming title to any of its leasehold plot to prove the ownership to such plot by producing document, in case any dispute is raised as to the title or ownership to such plot, the High Court Division, while making the Rule absolute, failed to consider these factual and legal aspects of the case. He has further submitted that the writ-petitioner was not authorized to construct the building on the plot in question inasmuch as he was merely issued a 'No objection certificate' upon his submission of plan for the construction of the building, but no order of approval of the plan was issued to him, but before approval of such plan, which is mandatorily required, started the construction works and, as such, the letter dated 23-7-2007 postponing the construction' was not illegal, the High Court Division erred in law in making the Rule absolute declaring the impugned letter to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect.

33. Mr Tobarak Hossain, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioners in CP No. 3033 of 2012, has tried to impress us by submitting that the writ-petitioner appeared at the hearing before writ-respondent No. 1 on 15-8-2007 followed by another hearing on 21-8-2007 and thus complied with the letter dated 23-7-2007 (impugned in the writ petition) and after such compliance, filed Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008 impugning the said letter and then obtained the impugned judgment and order upon suppression of facts and thus practised fraud upon the Court. He has submitted that the registered power of attorney, on the basis of which, the transfer of the plot in question was made in favour of the writ-petitioner, was allegedly executed on 7-12-2005 in Dhaka mentioning the address of executant- Mohibur Rahman (writ-respondent No. 5) at Sylhet though the plot in question situates at Uttara, clearly shows that the power of attorney was created and registered in the office of the Sub-Registrar, Gulshan having no jurisdiction. He has further submitted that the executant of the power of attorney is a resident of UK, who had come to Bangladesh on 9-12-2004 and left for UK on 11-4-2005; thereafter, he never came back to Bangladesh till date; it is apparent that the registered power of attorney, the basis of the alleged deed of transfer, was forged, false, fabricated and illegal and by that transfer, the writ-petitioner did not acquire any right, title or interest whatsoever in the plot in question and consequently he had no locus standi to file the writ petition challenging the impugned letter. He has further submitted that the notices of the Rule issued in the writ petition were not served upon writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 and thus they did not get any chance to contest the Rule and to place their case and could not point out the fact of forgery committed by the writ-petitioner in getting the registered deed of transfer in his favour in respect of the plot in question and as such, the matter may be sent back on remand to the High Court Division for hearing afresh giving them chance to place their case by setting aside the impugned judgment and order.

34. On behalf of RAJUK, an additional paper book has been filed and relying upon the documents incorporated therein, Mr. Mahbubey Alam has also tried to show that the writ-petitioner became the owner of the plot in question by resorting forgery. Therefore, writ-respondent No. 1 did not commit any illegality in issuing the letter impugned in the writ petition.

35. In the context, the pertinent question, that arises for consideration in these two CPs (864 of 2010 and 3033 of 2012), is whether writ-respondent No. 1 was legally authorized to issue the impugned letter dated 23-7-2006 to the writ-petitioner asking him to appear before him (writ-respondent No. 1 ) on 15-8-2007 with the original deed in respect of the plot in question and the other papers for attending a hearing to decide its true ownership and to stop all the construction works thereon till disposal of the matter.

37. From a reading of the impugned letter, it appears that the same was issued on a complaint made by writ-respondent No.4, Md Khaliqur Rahman (leave petitioner No. 1 of CP No. 3033 of 2012) that the writ-petitioner became the owner of the plot in question by virtue of his purchase by forging the signature of one of the lessees, Md Mohibur Rahman (writ-respondent No.5 and leave petitioner No. 2 of CP No. 3033 of 2012). Writ-respondent No. 4 made further complaint that writ-respondent No.5 lives abroad and he did not give any power of attorney to transfer the plot in question, but by using his fake photograph and forging his signature, the act of selling and buying (ক্রয়-বিক্রয়) was completed and then construction of the building was going on the plot in question. Writ-respondent No. 5 gave a power of attorney to him (writ-respondent No.4) from abroad, but he did not submit the same to RAJUK.

38. In the leave petition of writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 (CP No. 3033 of 2012), the same allegations as made before writ-respondent No. 1 have been alleged. The gist of the allegations of the writ-respondents is that the writ-petitioner got the deed of sale in respect of the plot in question in his favour executed and registered by creating a forged power of attorney in the name of writ-respondent No. 5. On the other hand, the case of writ-petitioner as stated in the writ petition was that pursuant to an advertisement made by him in the "Daily Janakatha" dated 30-11-2006, writ-respondent No.4 (petitioner No. 1 of CP No. 3033 of 2012) entered into a contract with him to sell the plot in question at taka 48,00,000 (forty eight lakh) which he and his full brother, writ-respondent No. 5 got as affected persons by way of lease for 99 (ninety nine) years from RAJUK and that as writ-respondent No. 5 was staying abroad, he appointed writ-respondent No. 4 as his attorney by a registered power of attorney dated 7-12-2005 giving him power to execute and register the deed of transfer in respect of the plot in question or any other agreement with RAJUK and on 3-1-2006, writ-respondent No.4 submitted the said power of attorney before RAJUK for approval and RAJUK by its letter dated 28-5-2006 accorded approval to the said power of attorney. On the basis of an application filed by writ-respondent No.4 for himself and for writ-respondent No.5 to RAJUK for according permission to them to transfer the plot in question to the writ-petitioner; RAJUK by its letter dated 20-12-2006 asked them to deposit the transfer fee and the other charges within 1 (one) month and accordingly, the writ-petitioner deposited the transfer fee and the other charges on their behalf as per terms of the agreement; that upon receipt of the transfer fee and the other charges, RAJUK informed writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 about its approval to transfer the plot in question by them by letter dated 21-12-2006; then writ-respondent No.4 for self and on behalf of writ-respondent No.5 as his attorney on receipt of Taka 48,00,000 (46,00,000 through two pay orders and Taka 2,00,000 in cash) executed and registered the deed of sale on 26-12-2006; after purchase, the writ-petitioner got possession of the plot in question and mutated his name with RAJUK and submitted a plan to it for the construction of a 2(two) storied building on the plot in question and RAJUK issued clearance certificate by its letter dated 28-3-2007 with the endorsement of writ-respondent No. 1 that the plan would be approved if submitted as per the Rules.

39. In the leave petition filed by writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5, nothing has been stated as to the assertion made by the writ-petitioner in respect of the agreement entered into by writ-respondent No.4 with him for selling the plot in question and payment of money to the respondents by the writ-petitioner to the tune of Taka 48, 00,000. They have also not denied the assertions made by the writ-petitioner that writ-respondent No.4 filed the power of attorney given in his favour by writ-respondent No. 5 to RAJUK on 3-1-2006 and the same was accepted by RAJUK and that RAJUK gave them permission to sell the plot in question to the writ-petitioner and that after purchase, RAJUK mutated the name of the writ-petitioner. The writ-respondents have not also denied the fact of execution of the sale deed by writ-respondent No.4 and the delivery of possession of the plot in question to the writ-petitioner. The very fact that by the impugned letter, RAJUK asked the writ-petitioner not to make the construction on the plot in question till the decision by it on the complaint lodged by writ-respondent No.4 as to the true ownership of the plot in question, prima-facie prove that after the sale deed was registered on 26-12-2006 possession thereof was delivered to the writ-petitioner. In the leave petition (CP No. 864 of 2010) filed by RAJUK, it has not denied any of the assertions of the writ-petitioner as noted down herein before.

40. It is an admitted fact that RAJUK is the owner of the plot in question and writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 got the allotment thereof as the affected  persons; RAJUK executed and registered the lease deed in favour of writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 for 99(ninety nine) years in respect of the plot in question and thus they became its permanent lessees. Therefore, writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 had the absolute legal right to deal with the plot in question according to their best choices including transferring the same to anyone subject to the approval by RAJUK.

41. Whether the power of attorney executed by writ-respondent No. 5 in favour of writ-respondent No.4 was the act of forgery, whether the deed of sale executed and registered by writ-respondent No.4 for self and on behalf of his brother (writ-respondent No.5) on the basis of the said power of attorney was valid or not; whether, by the sale deed dated 26-12-2006, the writ-petitioner acquired title to the plot in question and whether writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 transferred the plot in question to the writ-petitioner on receipt of valuable consideration of Taka 48,00,000 are the matters between writ-respondent Nos .4 and 5 and the writ-petitioner and such dispute or controversy cannot be decided by RAJUK. After the plot in question was transferred by the lessees to the writ-petitioner by a registered deed of sale with due permission from RAJUK, possession thereof was delivered to the transferee (the writ-petitioner) and his name was mutated with RAJUK, it lost all its grip on the question of ownership and it had no authority or locus standi to sit in an adjudication to decide the true ownership of the plot in question at the instance of writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 as was ventured by it by the impugned letter dated 23-7-2006. Therefore, the High Court Division rightly held that "After transfer of the land by way of lease for ninety nine years, and further transfer and delivery of possession of said land by the leasees(sic) to the petitioner, respondent No. 1 definitely know that RAJUK had no right, title or possession or any interest of such land. Neither respondent No. 1 nor RAJUK had any authority or power to settle any question of title in any land in Bangladesh."

<u>42. Question of practising fraud in executing and registering a sale deed in respect of a plot of land is a serious question of fact which can only be thrashed out on evidence to be produced by the contending parties in a properly constituted suit and it is definitely the domain of the civil Court to decide such fact but not RAJUK or its officials. In the context, it will not be out of place to state the law that the onus to prove fraud is squarely upon the party who alleges it and a registered document has a presumption of correctness under clause (e) of section 114 of the Evidence Act and it needs judicial decision. And RAJUK has not been vested with such judicial power. Neither Mr Mahbubey Alam nor Mr Tobarak Hossain, could show any provision of law which authorized RAJUK or writ-respondent No. 1 to venture upon to decide the dispute as to the true ownership of a plot of land between the lessees (writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5) and the transferee (the writ-petitioner) as sought by the impugned letter. Only because the writ-petitioner appeared before writ-respondent No. 1 pursuant to the impugned letter, he could not be debarred from challenging the propriety or legality of the same before the High Court Division by filing the writ petition in question when the impugned letter was issued without having any legal backing. In the context, the High Court Division rightly declared the same to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect and, as such, no interference is called for with the judgment and order passed by it in Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008, we find no merit in CP No. 864 of 2010.</u>

43. We record our strong disapproval of the action of RAJUK in cancelling the mutation of the plot in question in the name of the writ-petitioner and the other actions relating thereto (নামজারীসহ অন্যান্য সকল কার্যক্রম) on the plea “উল্লেখিত প্লটের মূল মালিক (১) জনাব মহিবুর রহমান ও (২) জনাব খালিকুর রহমান সর্ব পিতা-মরম হাজী আকমল আলী গ্রাম ও পোঃ বানিগ্রাম খানা-গোলাপগজ্ঞ, জেলা-সিলেট কর্তৃক প্লটটির আম-মোক্তার নিয়োগ দখল গ্রহণ লীজ দলিল সম্পাদন হস্তান্তর সম্পাদন ও হস্তান্তর দলিল রেজিষ্ট্রি কার্যক্রমসহ অন্যান্য কার্যাদি সম্পন্ন কর হয়নি বিধায়” as quoted in CP No. 3033 of 2012. In the additional paper book filed in CP No. 864 of 2010, the letter dated 4-3-2009 issued by the Deputy Director (Estate-2), RAJUK Uttara, Dhaka, has been incorporated and it appears that writ-respondent Nos.4 and 5 have quoted the above portion from the said letter. 44. By the decision as contained in the letter, in fact, RAJUK has sought to cancel the registered sale deed executed and registered by writ-respondent No.4 for himself and for writ-respondent No. 5 in favour of the writ-petitioner transferring the plot in question, as it is apparent from the letter that copy of the same was given to the Sub-Registrar Complex, Tejgaon and the Assistant Land Officer, Tahsil Office, Uttara, Dhaka. We wonder how RAJUK could take such a decision and under what legal authority. It is to be further noted that the letter dated 23-7-2007 impugned in Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008 was also issued at the instance of writ-respondent No. 4 on the complaint that the sale deed dated 26-12-2006 was obtained through forgery, but RAJUK chose not to contest the Rule issued in the writ petition and the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order (judgment was passed on 31-7-2008) declared the same to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect with the clear finding that "After transfer of the land by way of lease for ninety-nine years, and further transfer and delivery of possession of said land by the leases(sic) to the petitioner, respondent No. 1 definitely know that RAJUK had no right, title or possession or any interest in such land. Neither respondent No. 1 nor RAJUK had any authority or power to settle any question of title in any hand in Bangladesh." The action taken by RAJUK also appears to us outrageous inasmuch as they cancelled the mutation of the writ-petitioner's name after the letter dated 23-7-2007 issued by writ-respondent No. 1 was declared to have been issued without lawful authority and was of no legal effect by the High Court Division. We are compelled to make the above observations as we could not shut our eyes when such a disturbing fact was brought to our notice by the writ-respondents, i.e. the petitioners of both the CPs, though the letter dated 4-3-2009 is not the subject matter of the leave petitions.

<u>45. In CP No. 3033 of 2012 as well as in the application for condoning the delay in filing the same, the allegation of forgery has been brought against the writ-petitioner in obtaining the registered sale deed dated 26-12-2006 in respect of the plot in question, but as already held hereinbefore, forgery being a serious question of fact cannot be decided in a summary proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution. Moreso, since we have found no legal and factual infirmity in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division, we are not inclined to condone the delay in filing the CP filed out of time by 1594 days. However, since fraud vitiates everything and basically is a question of fact and requires strict proof on the production of proper evidence and such exercise can only be done by the Civil Court, if so advised, the leave petitioners (writ-respondent Nos. 4 and 5 of Writ Petition No. 58 of 2008) may take shelter of civil Court regarding the deed of sale dated 26-12-2006 executed and registered by writ-respondent No. 4 for self and on behalf of writ-respondent No. 5 on the basis of the power of attorney executed and registered by writ-respondent No. 5 appointing writ-respondent No. 4 as his attorney in respect of the plot in question.</u>

46. For the discussions made above:

CP Nos. 864 of 2010 and 2515 of 2010 are dismissed there being no merit.

CP No. 3033 of 2012 is dismissed as being barred by limitation.

End.
