full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 29-5-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 63 of 1993 disallowing the aforesaid Miscellaneous Appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 30-1-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1988 allowing the same should not be set aside and or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court might seem fit and proper.

2. Facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of the rule in short, are that the pre-emptor-respondent-opposite party No. 1 instituted pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1988 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, 1st. Court, Dhaka for getting pre-emption order in the case land.

3. That the case of the petitioner in short is that, the owner of the case land was Syed Mohammad Ali, father of the opposite party No. 4 and after the death of the aforesaid Syed Mohammad Ali, the opposite party No. 4 inherited the case land and they did not possess the suit land, for last 60 years; that the petitioner and his predecessors have been possessing the same; that on 29-10-1987 the opposite party No. 4 sold out the case land to the opposite party Nos. 1-3 for a consideration of Taka 30,000; that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 are neither co-sharers nor contagious land holders of the case land; that the petitioner is the owner of the case land; that the petitioner is the owner of contiguous land situated to the southern side of the case land; that the petitioner being contiguous land holder is entitled to get pre-emption of the case land; that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 are strangers; that on 20-12-1987 while the opposite party Nos. 1-3 expressed that they are the owners by purchase of the case land tried to possess the case land the petitioner came to know that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 have purchased the case land; that on 24-12-1987 the petitioner obtained the certified copy of the aforesaid sale deed; that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 purchased 20 decimals of land at Plot No. 951, 1½, decimals of land at Plot No. 985 and 6 decimals of land at Plot No. 1383 in all 27½ decimals of land from opposite party No. 4 on consideration of Taka 30,000; that the petitioner filed the pre-emption Miscellaneous Case for getting pre-emption order of 20 decimals of land at Plot No. 951 along with order for getting back Taka 9000 out of Taka 30,000 and also for order of confirmation of possession of the aforesaid case land.

4. That the instant petitioners as opposite party Nos. 1-3 contested the said case by filing written objection stating inter-alia that the case is not maintainable in the present form and manner as alleged and also barred by law of limitation and bad for defect of parties etc and also stating that Syed Ahsan Ali inherited the case land along with other property after the death of his father Syed Mohammad Ali; that on 29-10-1987 he transferred the case land to the preempted by way of registered deed being No. 10857 for consideration of Taka 30,000 on condition that if the vendor returns back the said consideration money of Taka 30,000 to the vendee within 3 years of the date of the said transfer the vendee will get back the said property otherwise the said sale deed will remain valid and that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 have been owning and possession the case land by cultivating thereon; that the opposite party Nos. 1-3 are co-sharers by inheritance and the opposite party Nos. 1-3 are the contiguous land holder and that they got the land mutated and have been paying rents etc. That in view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances the present false pre-emption case of the petitioner is liable to be dismissed with cost.

5. That the learned trial Judge on the basis of the pleadings of the parties framed as many as 5 issues for effectual disposal of the case and both the parties in support of their respective case adduced both oral and documentary evidence.

6. The pre-emptor petitioner i.e. the present opposite party No. 1 adduce 3 witnesses and exhibited certain documents in support of his case and the preempted present petitioner adduce 4 witnesses and exhibited certain document in support of their case. The learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka after hearing both the parties and on perusal of the evidences on record both oral and documentary was pleased to allow the aforesaid Miscellaneous Case by his judgment and order dated 30-1-1993. On being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the learned trial Judge he pre-emptees as appellant preferred Miscellaneous Appeal being No. 63 of 1993 in the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka which was on transfer heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, who after hearing both the parties was pleased to disallow the appeal on contest against the respondent No. 1 and co-partner against the rest without any order as to costs and affirmed the judgment and order dated 30-1-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1988 by his judgment and order dated 25-9-2000. The pre-emptee appellant being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the aforesaid judgment and order of affirmance passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 63 of 1993 affirming the judgment and order passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka, the pre-emptee appellant as petitioner preferred this revisional application before this Court under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, hence this rule.

7. Mr Md Kalim Ullah Mazumder, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner first of all submitted that the impugned judgment is neither a proper judgment nor it is in according with law in view of the evidences on record and facts and circumstance and law involved in the case and, as such, the impugned judgment is not sustainable in law as the learned appellate Judge has committed error of law which has resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr Mazumder further submits that the impugned judgment suffers from misreading and non-reading of evidence as it is evident from judgment of both the Courts below that the learned trial Judge as well as the appellate Court did not consider and evaluate the evidences of the witnesses adduced by the opposite parties. Thus the judgment suffers from error of law leading to error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. As such the same is not sustainable in law and it is liable to be set aside.

8. Mr Mazumder next submits that the case of the pre-emptor suffer from non joiner of parties and the opposite parties pre-empties stated this fact in their written objection, but both the Courts below did not take proper cognizance in respect of this matter rather decided the case illegally. Mr Mazumder also submits that the learned appellate Judge committed error of law apparent on the face of the record by disallowing the appeal and affirming the judgment of the trial Court without considering the fact that the pre-emptor had no locus standi to file the aforesaid pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1988.

9. Mr Mazumder next submits that the pre-emptor while claiming the ownership and possession of the adjacent land appertaining to Plot No. 951/1425. Whereas the father of the pre-emptor namely Abdul Aziz transferred the aforesaid contiguous land and sold out the said land to one Shamsuddin by registered deed being No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 as such SA record was prepared in the name of other persons according to Mr Mazumder this fact was brought to the notice of the learned appellate Judge by filing an application on 3-6-1999 by the appellant preemptee and the Court on receipt of this application fixed several date for hearing of the said petition but ultimately without hearing the same or passing any order on the said application pronounced his judgment affirming the judgment of the learned trial Judge. That the learned appellate Judge from 3-6-1999 vide Order No. 41 to Order No. 46 fixed the matter for hearing of the appeal and the petition filed by the appellant but without passing any order or hearing the parties in respect of this petition on 25-5-2000 heard the appeal and thereafter on 29-5-2000 pronounced his judgment and disallowed the appeal by affirming the judgment of the trial Court. Mr Mazumder has filed a supplementary affidavit on 10-2-2009 annexing certified copy of a deed being No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 of which Abdul Aziz son of late Usman that is father of the present opposite party pre-emptor was the vendor and one Shamsuddin Ahmed son of Lal Mia was the purchaser has been marked as Annexure A. And in this respect Mr Majumder submits that this is the deed about which the preempted appellant mentioned before the appellate Court by filing an application dated 3-6-1999 and now he has produced the same before this Court to take cognizance of the same to show that the father of the present pre-emptor opposite party sold out the said property i.e. the land appertaining to Plot No. 951/1425. Thus he exhausted himself and present pre-emptor having to right, title and interest in the said plot as contiguous plot owner of the pre-empted land.

10. The opposite party pre-emptor has filed a counter affidavit against the aforesaid supplementary affidavit filed by the rule petitioner on 10-2-2009 and wherein he has annexed a registered deed of agreement being No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 annexing the same as Annexure X and he has also annexed a sa f kabala deed of reconveyance executed by aforesaid Shamsuddin in favour of Abdul Aziz. on 21-9-1959 being saf kabala deed No. 17697 dated 26-12-1963 and annexed the same marking the same as Annexure Y. And the opposite party has also annexed copies of a series of survey Khatian No. 91 RS No.3087 and RS No. 3280 present Dhaka city settlement Plot Nos. 2311, 2839, 2840 and 2838 within Mouza Kadamtali under Police Station Shyampur now Kadamtali, Dhaka Photostat copy of Khatian being No. 91 having been annexed and marked as Annexure Z, Z1, Z3 and Z4. Thereafter today while I was going to deliver the judgment, Mr Mazumder has again come up with an affidavit in reply on behalf of the petitioner to the counter affidavit filed by the opposite party No. 1 on 11-2-2009. Mr Mazumder on 16-2-2009 filed an affidavit in reply to the counter affidavit filed by the opposite party No. 1 on 11-2-2009 wherein he has annexed the application of 3-6-1999 filed before the appellate Court by the appellant marking the same as Annexure B and he has also filed certified copy of the written objection filed by the respondent opposing the said petition dated 3-6-1999 marking the same as Annexure B1 wherein according to Mr Mazumder the respondent stated in the said written objection that is father of the respondent Abdul Aziz got the said Plot No. 951/1425 together with some other land measuring in all 1.26 acre of land by way of reconveyance from Shamsuddin to whom earlier the father of the respondent sold out the said property by a Saf Kabala deed dated 21-9-1959 followed by a registered agreement, registered on the same date between the same parties for reconveyance of the said land on receiving the consideration money and this money was returned. But the father of pre-emptor respondent because of the simplicity did not get the Saf Kabala (reconveyance deed) registered which has been annexed has Annexure B1 and Mr. Mazumder has also annexed Photostat copy of plaint and written objection etc. of Title Suit No.245 of 2007 marking the same as Annexure C. wherein one Mst. Happy Begum filed this suit as plaintiff against the present pre-emptor opposite party No. 1 Helal Uddin and 29 others imp leading them as defendant marking the same as Annexure C. Today while I have taken the case for delivering the judgment Mr. Majumder has filed another supplementary affidavit today serving copy on the other side at 11.10 am on 22-2-2009 wherein he has annexed a copy of the petition filed by the appellant before the appellate Court on 3-6-1999 marking the same as Annexure B 7 and certified copy of written objection filed by pre-emptor respondent on 28-3-2000 marking the same as B and B1 and he has also filed the certified copy of the order sheet of the learned appellate Judge in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 63 of 1993 starting from order at serial No. 41 dated 3-6-1999 to 29-5-2002 the date on which the learned appellate Judge deliver the judgment marking the same as Annexure C to show that the learned appellate Judge did not pass any order on the said application of the appellant dated 3-6-1999 and Mr. Majumder in this respect submits that after filing of this application the Court ought to have passed an order either accepting or rejecting the said application but without passing any order on the said application the learned appellate Judge delivered his judgment without deciding the said application whereas if this application would have been properly considered would have helped the learned appellate Judge to set aside the judgment and order passed by the learned trial Judge because in this application the appellant has mentioned about the disposal of the property appertaining to Plot No. 951/1425 by the pre-emptor and by this sale he has lost right, title and character of a adjoining owner thus if the petition would have been considered it would have changed the fate of the case.

11. Mr. Mazumder thus submits that the learned appellate Judge committed error in its decision leading to error in law and fact for which this impugned judgment is not sustainable in law. In support of his argument specially on the point of filing the same document here in this Court regarding the misreading and non-reading of evidences on record Mr. Maunder has referred to a decision of our appellate Division in the case of Aliment Hussain Chozvdhury vs Md. Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162. He submits and prays that the rule be made absolute.

12. Mr. Moulovi Md Wahidullah the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party has submitted that the impugned judgment being a judgment of affirmance and well reasoned and well evaluated judgment after proper discussion and evaluation of the evidences on record both oral and documentary and the judgment passed by the learned trial Judge being a well discussed and well evaluated judgment on the basis of the evidence on record both oral and documentary having been affirmed by the learned appellate Judge with proper reasoning and delusion this Court in its revisional jurisdiction has got very limited scope to interfere with such a well reasoned and well discussed judgment of affirmance passed by the learned appellate Judge and in support of his argument Mr Wahidullah has referred to a decision of our appellate Division in the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Chanel Mia, reported in 12 BLD (AD) 48 = 44 DLR (AD) 98.

13. Mr Wahidullah has drawn my attention to his counter affidavit dated 11-2-2009 and he has submitted that the point on which the learned Advocate for the petitioner have been stressing very much that the father of the pre-emptor opposite party has sold the property of Plot No. 951/1425 to one Shamsuddin and thus in 1959 the pre-emptor petitioner has lost the right of adjacent ownership and cannot file petition for pre-emption. Mr Wahidullah has next drawn my attention to annexure Y that is the registered deed of resonance dated 26-12-1963 by which the aforesaid purchaser Shamsuddin reconvened the purchased land to the father of the pre-emptor petitioner Abdul Aziz and this fact having been very much mentioned in the sale deed of his father Abdul Aziz dated 21-9-1959 and he has also drawn my attention to annexure X which is registered agreement being No. 9771 dated 21-9-1959 by the which the parties i.e. the purchaser and seller of the deed No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 i.e. the deed by which the father of the present pre-emptor petitioner mortgaged the said property by way of Saf Kabala followed by a registered agreement of reconvance and this fact is very much mentioned in the Saf Kabala No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 as well as this registered agreement also clearly indicates that the same has been registered on that very day in the same setting which bears No. 9771 and the original deed of mortgaged (Saf Kabala) bears the said deed No. 9770 and both the deed contains the fact of reconvance by the agreement and it is evidence from Annexure Y the registered deed No. 17697 dated 26-12-1963 that father of the pre-emptor petitioner Abdul Aziz got back the said property appertaining to Plot No. 951/ 1425 by way of reconveyance in pursuance of aforesaid Saf Kabala deed No. 17697 Annexure Y filed with the counter affidavit.

14. Mr Wahidullah has also drawn my attention to Annexure Z series which are the attested RS Khatian No. 2488 dated 6-8-1999 of revisional survey operation which contain the name of present pre-emptor petitioner together with other legal heirs of said Abdul Aziz. He has also submitted as he mentioned in paragraph 4 of the counter affidavit stating that the pre-emptor possessed the contiguous land being Khatian No. 91, RS No. 3087 and RS No. 3280 present Dhaka city settlement Plot Nos. 2311, 2839, 2840 and 2838 within Mouza Kadamtali under Police Station Shyampur now Kadamtali Dhaka and in support of his statement he has annexed all copies of the said Khatian. He submits that this Khatian has got presumptive value and which lends support to the possession of the pre-emptor in the adjacent plot of the preempted land. Mr. Wahidullah submits that this documents filed by way of Annexure with the counter affidavit in replay to the rule petition and supplementary affidavit filed by the rule petitioner may kindly be taken into consideration as the pre-emptor as respondent in the appeal filed written objection in response to the petition filed by the appellant in respect of this fact of sale by the father of the pre-emptor petitioner respondent and this pre-emptor opposite parties as respondent in the said written objection clearly mentioned that his father mortgaged the said property with Shamsuddin by registered deed No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 property being in total 1.26 acres of land appertaining to plot No. 951/1425 being 83 decimals and plot No. 1086 land measuring 43 decimals which appertains to Khatian No. 143 and it is specifically mention that the said deed was a deed of mortgage though it was registered as Saf Kabala it was deed of mortgage for an amount of Taka 700 followed by registered agreement, registered on the same date that is 21-9-1959 and it is also stated in the same written objection that the father of the pre-emptor opposite party subsequently return the said Taka 700 to the mortgagee (purchaser Shamsuddin) within the stipulated time and got back the said property in his ownership and possession. But inadvertently it was mention in the petition that the father of the pre-emptor petitioner because of his simplicity did not get the reconvened Saf Kabala registered but Mr. Wahidullah submits that through inadvertence though the pre-emptor respondent could not produce the said deed of reconvene as well as deed of agreement which he has been able to collect subsequently in the year 2007 after vigorous searching and he got certified copy on 19-3-2007 which has been annexed as annexed to the counter affidavit. Mr. Wahidullah submits that since this point at least having been stated before the appellate Court by filing written objection and now it is submitted before this Court by way of counter affidavit by swearing affidavit and annexing those with the counter affidavit this Court for ends of justice can taken into consideration these documents which is most vital point for determination of the status of the pre-emptor as owner of the contiguous plot of land of the case land. He prays that in view of the facts and circumstances of the present case the rule be discharged.

<u>15. I have given my anxious consideration to the submission made at the Bar. I have gone through the rule petition, the impugned judgment and judgment of the trial Court as well. After going through the impugned judgment, I find that the learned appellate Judge has framed as many as five independent issues by himself while disposing of the appeal and after proper and meticulous discussion of the issues and on proper evaluation and discussion of each and every point of issues that has been disposed of by the learned trial Judge. The learned appellate Judge came to his finding and decision and affirmed the judgment of the learned trial Judge and after going through the impugned judgment I do not find material substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment as per provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil procedure and it suffers from misreading and non-reading of evidences on record. Regarding the fact of misreading and non-reading of evidences on record as it is submitted by the learned Advocate of the petitioner, I am unable to discuss and reassess those because of the fact that the learned Advocate for the petitioner a t the time of issuance of the rule did not obtain order calling for the lower Courts record. So since the lower Courts record is not before me I am not in a position to go through the evidences on record as the lower Courts record is not before me. But after going through the judgment of the trial Court I find that the learned trial Judge has very meticulously and vividly discussed each and every point and fact in issue and came to his finding and decision deciding all the 5 issues in favour of the pre-emptor petitioner including the issues of maintainability and the point of conjoined of parties and means defect of parties. The learned trial Judge has very clearly and distinctly after discussing the evidences on record reached a t his decision to decide those issues in favour of the plaintiff. Inasmuch as the learned trial Judge has also very candidly and clearly discuss about the legal position of the pre-emptor to have the right to file the pre-emption case and very clearly found that the pre-emptor is in possession of the adjacent southern plot of the case plot (pre-empted plot) by giving his reasoning and with reference to evidences on record specially he gave reference to CS Map that has been produced by the opposite party before the Court and which clearly shows that Plot No. 951/1425 is adjacent southern plot of the case Plot No. 951/1425. And it is also avail-able from the CS Khatian i.e. Exhibit 1 that Hasan Ali the predecessor of Md Ahsan Ali who is the vendor of the pre-emptor opposite party has been shown in the northern boundary of the said Plot No. 951/1425 of the pre-mentor’s grandfather late Usman. So I find that the learned trial Judge has very meticulously and very carefully discussed each and every piece of evidence while he was deciding the issue in favour of the plaintiff and the learned appellate Judge being the last Court of fact has framed independent issue and discussed all this very important issues like maintainability of the suit and defect of parties and question of limitation and also the point of part pre-emption as prayed for. And after meticulous discussion and proper evaluation of the evidences on record and with reference to the judgment of the learned trial Judge and findings given by the learned trial Judge while allow the pre-emption the learned appellate Judge was pleased to affirmed the judgment of the learned trial Judge by disallowing the appeal. In my opinion while the learned appellate judge is affirming the judgment of the trial Court he need not discussion each and every point and he can even deliver a judgment by discussing each and every point that has been discussed and found by the learned trial Judge.</u>

<u>16. In respect of submission of Mr Mazumder to the effect that the pre-emptor had no locus standi to filed the pre-emption case this point has also been very categorically and candidly dismissed by the learned trial Judge after discussing the evidences on record and the learned appellate Judge also has discussed the same point and affirm the same as the first issue as to whether the suit is maintainable or not. So, I find that this point that has been raised by Mr Mazumder also not being substantiated by sufficient papers and document on record. The next point of submission that has been made by Mr Mazumder that the pre-emptes appellate filed an application on 3-6-1999 stating therein some facts specially the fact that the father of the pre-emptor namely Abdul Aziz sold out the said plot of land i.e. 951/1425 to one Shamsuddin and since he has sold out the property the pre-emptor had no locus standi to file the pre-emption case. And this petition was filed before the learned appellate Judge on 3-6-1999 the learned appellate Judge on receipt of this application kept few days as many as 4 days for hearing of the same but he did not dispose of the same rather with-out disposing the same he has heard the appeal and delivered the judgment without disposing the said petition in the negative or positive. Mr Mazumder has filed a certified copy the said petition and the written objection against that filed by the pre-emptor opposite party in the appellate Court as respondent. I have gone through the said petition which has been marked as annexure as well as the written objection, filed by the pre-emptor respondent dated 28-3-2000 and he order sheet of the Court which has been marked as Annexures B, B1 and C with the supplementary affidavit dated 22-2-2009. After going through the aforesaid petition of the pre-emptee appellant dated 3-6-1999, I find that the said application did not contain as annexure. any copy of the alleged said to be deed No. 9770 dated 21-9-1959 by which the father of the pre-emptor sold out his property appertaining to Plot No. 951/1425 only this number has been mentioned but no copy of the said deed was submitted before the Court nor any petition for allowing the appellant to adduce additional evidence in this respect was filed before the Court. By merely filing a petition and only stating the Saf Kabala number of the father of the pre-emptor disposed of the property without brining any formal prove or evidence before the Court as per provision of law the appellant made a prayer that this fact be made a ground in the Memo of appeal. So after going through this petition as well as order sheet, I find that the learned Appellant judge was right in not considering this application as it was not filed nor any prayer was made as per relevant provision of the Code of Civil Procedure. So the learned appellate Judge did not consider this application as it did not call for any interference by the learned appellate Judge in the appellate forum beyond the legal procedure. But Mr Mazumder the learned Advocate by filing a supplementary affidavit dated 10-2-2009 has filed a certified copy of the said deed of conveyance i.e. the deed No. 9770 by which the father of the pre-emptor sold out his said property to one Shamsuddin Ahmed, make the same Annexure A with the supplementary affidavit and he has very candidly submitted that in view of this Saf Kabala deed the pre-emptor opposite party had no right, title or interest of file Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case and he Courts below committed error of law by allowing the pre-emption case. But I find that this document had neither been placed before the trial Court nor before the appellate Court but only mere statement was made before the appellate Court by tiling an application which the learned appellate Judge did not consider and it was not filed in accordance with law and I further find that by filing a counter affidavit dated 11-2-2009 the pre-emptor opposite party his filed a certified copy of an agreement being deed No. 9771 wherein it has been decided and agreed upon by the parties to the sale deed No. 9770 i.e. the sale deed about which Mr Mazumder has been stressing that in view of this deed all right, title and interest of pre-emptor has been exhausted and have no right to file pre-emption miscellaneous case. But from this annexure X, I find that on the same day an agreement was executed by said Shamsuddin Ahmed under taking to recovery the said purchased land of Kabala No. 9770 to the said vendor within four years of the date of Kabala and the agreement was registered of the same date and within four years time which evident from exhibit Y being a Saf Kabala deed being No. 17697 dated 26-12-1963 it appears that the same self property has been reconveyed to the father of the pre-emptor by said Shamsuddin on receiving back the said consideration money of Taka 700 and in this respect I would like to mention further that the learned trial Judge found possession of the pre-emptor in pursuance of CS record (Khatian) as well as draft publication Khatian of the SA record which stands in the name of the pre-emptor and now I find from the Annexure Z series which has been marked as annexed which the counter affidavit by the pre-emptor opposite party and this Z series shows that the RS Khatian as well as the Dhaka city survey Khatian has been published in the name of the pre-emptor and his other co-sharer which a t least bears presumptive value in respect of possession of the pre-emptor opposite party which he has claimed as per his petition of pre-emption that means all along possession of the suit land as well as his own plot of land being plot No. 951/1425 and the learned trial Judge after vivid discussion of all the evidences on record arrived at his finding that the pre-emptor is owner in possession of the adjacent plot No. 951/1425 and it is more clarified in view of the Annexure filed by Mr Wahidullah by filing the counter affidavit and annexure those document for this reason. In rebutting this counter affidavit Mr Mazumder has filed an affidavit in reply annexing the aforesaid petition dated 3-6-1999 filed by the appellant before the appellate Court and the written objection that has been filed by the pre-emptor respondent wherein as it is submitted by Mr Mazumder and after going the same I find there was line at page 6 of the certified copy of the said written objection that “কিন্তু মজহরের পিতা সরলতা কারণে ইহা রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া নেন নাই। But he has also annexed Photostat copy of certified copy of a Title Suit being No. 245 of 2007 pending in the Court of Joint District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka being Annexure C wherein one Mst Happy Begum being the plaintiff has filed the suit against the pre-emptor Helal Uddin and others claiming ownership of the said land against them. But I do not find any justification or reason to take into consideration this case filed a 3rd party against the pre-emptor where-in the plaintiff claims to have purchase this property from the legal heirs of said Shamsuddin whereas from Annexure Y as filed by the pre-emptor opposite party with his counter affidavit the right, title and possession of the said Shamsuddin had been exhausted with the execution and registration of the said deed of reconveyance in favour of his seller Abdul Aziz. So, this case of Mst. Happy Begum is coming in no way to any help to the pre-emptee petitioner although Mr Mazumder very strenuously tried to argued on all this point but I do not find any cogent reason to accept all this things and I do not find much material force in the argument of Mr Mazumder on this point and in revisional jurisdiction I have taken into consideration the counter affidavit as well as the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner as well as the counter affidavit filed by the opposite party. Only because since the petitioner at the final stage of the case have come with some new facts and filed certain document praying for consideration of the same by this Court. So, I have to take into consideration the counter affidavit as well as the document that been filed by way of Annexure with the counter affidavit by the opposite party and the citation that has been referred to by Mr Mazumder the learned Advocate for the petitioner being case reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein our lordships decided and found that "If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case." This finding of our lordship's in the appellate Division is not coming to very much assistance to the argument advanced by Mr Mazumder because after going through the judgment of both the Courts below, I do not find any omission or material irregularities to have been committed by the Courts below calling for interference by this Court. Moreover, the point of misreading and non-reading of evidences on record being agitated by Mr Mazumder but unfortunately at the time of issuance of the rule the petitioner did not obtain order calling for the lower Court record and since the lower Court record is not before me, I cannot go through the evidences on record and I have to bend upon the veracity of the judgment of both the Court below and after going through both the judgment of the Courts below, I find that both the judgment are well discussed and well founded judgment wherein interference of the revisional Court is not call for in any way or manner as such I am unable to accept the contention of Mr Mazumder. Rather I find substances in the submission of Mr Wahidullah and the citation referred to by him being 12 BLD (AD) 48 = 44 DLR (AD) 98 which is in agreement with his submission and the case of the opposite party No. 1.</u>

17. In view of my discussion made above, I do not find any merit in the rule.

18. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 29-5-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 63 of 1993 disallowing the aforesaid Miscellaneous Appeal and affirming the judgment and order dated 30-1-1993 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 1st. Court, Dhaka in pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 8 of 1988 allowing the same is hereby maintained and upheld.

Let copy of the judgment be sent to the Courts below expeditiously.

End.

lawyer:
Raisuddin Ahmad with Md Aktaruzzaman, Advocates—For the Petitioners.

parties:
HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd and another ------ Petitioners
Vs
Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA) and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Naima Haider J : In this application under Article 102(2)(a)(i) and (ii) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo under reference No.00.314.014.01.00.057.1991-1187 (1) dated September 27, 2011 (Annexure-J to the writ petition) refusing to withdraw the cancellation of No Objection Certificate and cancellation of No Objection Certificate vide Memo No. 1P:0-57/660 dated May 3, 2009 (Annexure-H to the petition) to transfer assets etc. of the company named HKD (BD) Ltd to petitioner No.1 company as was granted earlier under Memo No. IP: 0-57/1643 dated August 26, 2008 (Annexure-C to the petition) as already been acted upon shall not be declared as have been issued and made without any lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The brief facts necessary for the disposal of the writ petition are that petitioner No. 1 is a private limited Test Manufacturing and Exporter Company named HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. and the petitioner No.2 is the Managing Director. A Company named HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd set up an export oriented industry in Chittagong Export Processing Zone, an Export Processing Zone (EPZ) under respondent No. 1. The said Company decided to voluntarily wind up their company and sell all its assets and liabilities to the petitioners Company. Accordingly, petitioners and HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. signed a Deed of Agreement on 14-7-2008 to sell and purchase machinery etc. of HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. by the petitioners.

3. While HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. have been carrying out its business within Chittagong EPZ area, they applied to respondents by their letter dated 14-7-2008 to wind up their company voluntarily and also to sell all their assets and liabilities to petitioners. They have also prayed to respondent No.4 for issuance of 'No Objection Certificate' (NOC) in this regard. The respondent No. 3 by its Memo No. IP: 0-57/1643 dated August 26, 2008 conveyed to Managing Director, HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. that the authority of respondent No.1 BEPZA was pleased to issue NOC in favour of them subject to fulfillment of ten conditions thereby consenting to selling of assets and liabilities covering building machinery, equipment’s and materials of HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd to petitioners HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd.

4. Accordingly, the company HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. was wound up in accordance with the provisions of Companies Act, 1994 and such winding up was duly published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23-9-2008 and Certificate of filing No. 516 dated 24-3-2009 was issued from the Office of Assistant Registrar of the Joint Stock Companies and Firms consequently the company HKD International (Bangladesh) Ltd. stood dissolved in the eye of law.

5. All on a sudden BEPZA by their letter date May 03, 2009 cancelled its NOC dated August 26, 2008 issued by General Manager (investment Promotion) BEPZA which was earlier granted in favour of HKD International (BD) Ltd. primarily alleging that HKD International (BD) Ltd. transferred its assets, liabilities etc. to HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. "for availing the tax holiday facility". Though the cancellation letter was issued in May 03,2009 but BEPZA has been asking the petitioners to run business in the name of HKD International (BD) Ltd, whereas said company was wound up with the permission of Registrar of Joint Stock Companies, who had already issued certificate of winding up on March 24, 2009. In the eye of law HKD International (BD) Ltd ceased to exist with effect from March 24, 2009 so there is no scope to restart any business under that name. Further, according to BEPZA web page under the heading "EPZ Benefits and Incentives," 10 years tax holidays is one of the inbuilt incentives granted to any investor for investing in EPZs and availing of tax holiday facilities are itself inbuilt in the process of process of investments in EPZs which cannot be termed as an offence and that cannot be a ground for cancellation of NOC. Further, no basis of BEPZA's coming to a decision "that it seems to the Authority" has been explained in their cancellation of NOC letter dated May 03, 2009. It is further stated that no authority has been conferred upon the Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority Act, 1980 to cancel a NOC granted in favour of any entity and which has already been acted upon on grounds of "it seems to the Authority" as no reference of taking any of such decision by competent authority of BEPZA as to its seeming has been cited and no decision of Authority to support cancelling the NOC for alleged "availing the tax holiday facility" which is inbuilt incentive for investment in EPZs, has been cited in the letter of cancellation of NOC, which is nothing but colourable exercise of power not vested in the BEPZA. It is further stated that the respondents have retracted from their own promises made to petitioners and actions against which promise have already been taken by petitioners as well as respondents and even Custom Authorities on the basis of BEPZA issued NOC, that is, in the light of their promise made, well before illegal cancellation of NOC. The petitioners company having facing serious difficulties in running their business, under anomalous situation created by respondents in course of business, made series of representations to respondents to withdraw their cancellation of NOC letter dated May 03, 2009 and made last representation to that effect on August 27, 2011. But the respondent No.3 by his letter dated September 27, 2011 finally refused to reconsider their decision and conveyed their unwillingness to withdraw cancellation of NOC dated August 26, 2008.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the cancellation of NOC dated May 3, 2009 the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the Rule Nisi.

7. The case of the respondent Nos. 1 & 2 is that the HKD International (BD) Ltd. had started commercial operation on 1-1-1991 and HKD international (CEPZ) Ltd started operation on 01-01-2005. HKD International (BD) Ltd enjoyed 10 years of tax holiday. But the company tried to enjoy the same facility again by selling all assets and liabilities to newly formed sister concern HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd, upto 1-1-2014. So, as and when the authority identified their intention of selling all its assets and liabilities in order to evade tax, the authority cancelled the NOC for protecting financial loss of the Government before final permission. The further case of the respondents is that as per clause No.(g) of NOC the company did not propose for cancellation of plots from the account of HKD International (BD) Ltd. and allot the same plot in favour of HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. The cancellation of plots from transferee and alloting the same plots to transferor is the 3rd phase activity and it will be completed as and when the transferee gets final permission from the authority.

8. Mr Rais Uddin Ahmad, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that HKD International (BD) Ltd. ceased to exist with effect from March 24, 2009 in the eye of law after having been wound up and there is no scope to restart any business under that name. He next submits that according to Board of Investment web page under the heading "EPZ" Benefits and Incentives", 10 years tax holidays is one of the inbuilt incentives granted to any investor for investing in EPZs and hence as availing of tax holiday facilities is itself inbuilt in the process of investments in the EPZs which cannot be termed as an offence. Mr Rais Uddin Ahmad next submits that the cancellation of NOC is ex facie, illegal and void ab initio as BEPZA's coming to a decision "that it seems to the Authority" has not been explained in their cancellation of NOC letter dated May 03, 2009. Further, Foreign Private Investment (Promotion and Protection) Act, 1980 also provides for granting tax holiday subject to NBR approval. So, availing of tax holiday by any investor in EPZ cannot be termed to be a wrong doing warranting cancellation of NOC on that ground. He further submits that two plots of wound up Company HKD International (BD) Ltd. has already been transferred in the name of petitioner HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. by respondent No. 4 by its letter dated 26-1-2009.

9. Mr Ahmed Sohel, learned Advocate on behalf of the respondent Nos. 1 & 2, submits that the respondents did not violate any provision of BEPZA Act, 1980 or Foreign Private Investment (Promotion and Protection) Act, 1980. They acted in accordance with law for greater public interest. Mr Sohel further con-tends that the company failed to submit necessary documents for final permission in favour of sale/transfer as per the clauses of NOC, so the company has the existence in the eye of law and as per the terms of the land lease agreement they were requested to commence commercial operation.

10. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates of respective parties and perused the application, affidavit-in-opposition and annexure appended thereto.

11. The question which arises for our consideration is whether the memo under challenge cancelling the NOC dated August 26, 2008 issued by the respondent can be sustained.

12. It transpires from record that HKD International (BD) Ltd. by its letter dated July 14, 2008 requested the Chittagong Export Processing Zone Limited to issue them No Objection Certificate (NOC) to wind up their company. Accordingly, BEPZA Dhaka Office by its letter dated August 26, 2008 granted permission to sell assets etc. of HKD International (BD) Ltd. to HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. The NOC was granted subject to the fulfillment of some conditions. The conditions were met and in the process BEPZA by its letter dated November 18, 2008 granted permission to transfer some vehicles of HKD International (BD) Ltd. to HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. Thereafter, BEPZA on January 25, 2009 allowed insertion of name of HKD International (CEPZA) Ltd. against Plot Nos. 10-12, Sector-4 of CEPZ in place of HKD International (BD) Ltd.

13. For facility of reference the letter dated January 26, 2009 as it appears from Annexure-G is reproduced below:

BEPZA/CEPZ/SEE/91

26/01/2009

M/s I-IKD International (CEPZ) Ltd.

Plot 10-12, Sector-4

Chittagong EPZ Chittagong

Subject : Regarding name of M/s HKD International (CEPZ) M/s HKD International (BD) Ltd.

Ref: (1) Our letter reference No. IP:0- 51 /1643 dated 26-8-2008.

(2) Your letter reference No. nil dated 4-12-2008.

Please refer to above This is to inform you that the Authority has accorded your factory name M/s HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. instead of M/s HKD International (BD) Ltd. at Plot No. 10-12, sector-4, of CEPZ according to your prayer. All utilities bills like Electricity, Water and Land rent shall be issued with effect from 04-1-2009 in the name of M/s HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd.

Thanking and assuring you of our best co-operation at all time.

Bd/-

27-1-2009

(Abdul Alim)

Superintending Engineer

Chittagong EPZ

Phone: 741441

14. This Court notes that when the said NOC was already acted upon, BEPZA by their subsequent letter dated May 3, 2009 cancelled its NOC granted earlier on August 26, 2008 alleging that HKD International (BD) Ltd.transferred its assets and liabilities etc. to HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. "for availing the tax holiday facility:"

15. It appears that HKD International (BD) Ltd. was wound up and the Registrar of Join Stock Companies issued Certificate of Winding up on March 24, 2009. The said company ceased to exist in the eye of law and it was not possible to restart any business in the name of a wound up company. Further, the impugned memo cancelling the NOC does not narrate as to why it has taken such a step when BEPZA itself had given the NOC. BEPZA's coming to a decision "that it seems to the authority" is very vague and does not reflect any ground for cancelling the NOC.

<u>16. By issuing the NOC in favour of HKD International (CEPZ) Ltd. the respondents are now estopped from coming with the different plea that the company earlier in the name of HKD International (BD) Ltd. has not been wound up. BEPZA in view of the earlier stand cannot resile from the same and, thus, its action would be barred by the principle of promissory estoppel. There is another aspect of the matter. Should the Court allow the parties to take a stand and then resile on the stand taken? The principles of approbate and reprobate envisage that once a party takes a stand which ends in some kind of compromise and also acts on the compromise, such a party cannot be allowed to take a contrary stand unless the earlier stand is against all known principles of law. Reverting back to the case in hand, we find that the respondents earlier have treated the petitioner's company to be wound up and now they cannot take a different stand and are stopped to resile from their earlier stand on their own action.</u>

17. In view of the discussions made herein-above, we are of the view that the Rule deserves to succeed.

18. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute.

The impugned cancellation of No Objection Certificate vide Memo No. IP: 0- 57/660 dated May 3, 2009 (Annexure-H to the petition) is hereby set-aside and declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

No order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated the 30th day of August, 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.3019 of 2001).
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Wahhab Miah J: This appeal, by leave, is from the judgment and order dated 30-8-2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil. Revision No. 3019 of 2001 making the Rule absolute.

2. Facts giving rise to this appeal are as follows:

The respondent as plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 84 of 1993 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Shingra, Natore against the defendant-appellant for cancellation of the registered deed of exchange being No. 7659 dated 19-8-1990 of the office of Sub-registrar, Shingra described in schedule-'Gha' to the plaint (hereinafter referred to as the impugned deed).

3. The plaint case was that the defendant is the paternal uncle of the plaintiff who brought him up after his father's death in his childhood. The plaintiff used to respect the defendant like his father. The land described in schedule-'Kha' which is a part of schedule-'Ka' land belongs to the plaintiff. 'Ga' scheduled land is owned and possessed in ejmali by the plaintiff and the defendant. The defendant proposed to exchange-'Ga' scheduled land with 'Kha' scheduled land to which the plaintiff agreed. But the defendant in collusion with the scribe fraudulently created the impugned deed showing exchange of 'Ga' scheduled land with 'Ka' scheduled land instead of 'Kha' scheduled land. On 3-5-1993, the plaintiff for the first time came to know about this fact when the defendant demanded rest of 'Ka' scheduled land from him giving out that the entire 'Ka' scheduled land had been transferred to him by the impugned deed of exchange. Then the plaintiff obtained the certified copy of the impugned deed and came to know definitely about the fraud practised by the defendant in executing and registering the same in collusion with the scribe. The plaintiff requested the defendant to rectify the impugned deed, but he refused and hence he was compelled to file the suit.

4. The defendant contested the suit by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and was barred by limitation. The suit was also not maintainable for want of cause of action. The positive case of the defendant was that the plaintiff proposed to sell 'Ka' scheduled land to him to which he agreed. The consideration for the land was fixed at Taka 70,000 (taka seventy thousand) only and the parties being closely related to each other, no bainapatra was executed. The defendant paid Taka 60,000 (taka sixty thousand) to the plaintiff in two installments and in lieu of the remaining amount of Taka 10,000 (taka ten thousand) only, the plaintiff demanded 'Ga' scheduled land to which he .agreed and at the advice of the scribe instead of sale deed, a deed of exchange was executed and registered on 19-8-1990. The suit was filed on false pleas with a view to harassing the defendant. After the filing of the suit, there was a village salish wherein it was decided that the defendant would transfer 0.13½ acre of land to the plaintiff by a registered deed in order to avoid future problem and as per terms of the salishnama dated 26-10-1991, the plaintiff was supposed to file solenama in the suit, but he killed time on this or that plea and ultimately refused to file the solenama and hence, the suit was liable to be dismissed with costs.

5. The learned Assistant Judge, on consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties by his judgment and decree dated 29-9-1999 decreed the suit. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the learned Assistant Judge, the defendant filed Title Appeal No.  202 of 1999 before the District Judge, Natore. The learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) who heard the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 15-1-2001 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit. Against the said judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the plaintiff filed Civil Revision No. 3019 of 2001 before the High Court Division. A single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the Rule absolute, set-aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court. Against the judgment and order of the High Court Division, the defendant-appellant filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1038 of 2006 before this Division and leave was granted to consider the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellants as follows:

"Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel, appearing for the petitioner submitted that the High Court Division committed error in law in passing the impugned judgment without reversing the finding of law as arrived at by the lower appellate Court to the effect that in view of the allegations made and evidence on record as adduced by the plaintiff-respondent the suit was not maintainable in the present form and manner under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act but a suit fore rectification of the instrument under Section 31 of the said Act should have been filed."

6. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, learned Counsel, appearing for the appellant, made his submissions in the light of the leave granting order. He further submitted that in view of the fact that the plaintiff himself admitted in the plaint as well as in his deposition that he wanted to exchange his 'Kha' scheduled land with the 'Ga' scheduled land of the defendant, instead the defendant by the impugned deed showed to have exchanged the 'Ka' scheduled land with the 'Ga' scheduled land, he ought to have filed the suit under section 31 of the Specific Relief Act (in short, the Act) for rectification of the deed and not under section 39 thereof for its cancellation, the Appellate Court rightly found the suit not maintainable, the High Court Division committed an error of law in interfering with the decision of the Appellate Court. In support of his contention, he has relied upon the case of Messrs Siddique and Co vs Messrs Utoomal and Assudamal Co., AIR 1946 (PC) 42.

7. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Advocate, appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, on the other hand, contended that in the plaint, the plaintiff alleged fraud in executing and registering the impugned deed which he proved by adducing evidence, the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record also came to the clear finding that fraud was practised by the defendant in executing and registering the impugned deed. The High Court Division rightly interfered with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court and restored those of the trial Court. He further contended that since the deed was void vitiated by fraud practised by the defendant, the suit for cancellation of the same under section 39 of the Act was very much maintainable; the Appellate Court wrongly found that the suit was not maintainable. Mr Neogi further contended that in view of the provisions of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure (the Code), there is no bar to granting relief under section 31 of the Act in a suit framed under section 39 thereof and that, even if, for argument's sake, it is conceded that the plaintiff ought to have filed the suit for rectification of the impugned deed and there-fore, in no way, the suit was liable to be dismissed. Mr Neogi lastly contended that admittedly the impugned deed was out and out a deed of exchange, leading to oral evidence in support of the defendant's case that in fact, he purchased the 'Ka' scheduled land by paying Taka 60,000 out of the total price of Taka 70,000 and that for the balance of Taka 10,000 the impugned deed executed and registered was inadmissible in evidence in view of the provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, but the Appellate Court failed to consider this legal aspect of the case in dismissing the suit; the High Court Division rightly interfered with the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court and, as such, no interference is called for with the impugned judgment and order.

8. In support of his contentions Mr Neogi relied on the cases of Firoza Majid vs Jiban Bima Corporation, 39 DLR (AD) 78; Maico Jute and Bag Corporation vs Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporatioh, 55 DLR(AD)23; Lalbanu Bibi and others vs Nurjan Banu, 41 DLR 519; Rajendra Tiwari vs Basudeo Prasad, AIR 2002 SC 136; (Mahant) Shantha Nand Gir Chela and Mahant Gayanand Gir vs (Mahant) Basudevanand, AIR 1930, Allahabad, 225 and Shankri vs Milkha Singh, AIR 1941 (Lahore) 407.

9. The trial Court decreed the suit on the clear finding that exhibit-'Ka', the impugned deed, was created by the defendant in collusion with the deed writer showing the exchange of 'Ka' scheduled land of the plaintiff with the 'Ga' scheduled land of the defendant. In coming to the said finding, the trial Court observed that it was simply impossible to exchange 1.41¼ acres of land, i.e. the 'Ka' scheduled land with 0.16½ acre of land, i.e. the 'Ga' scheduled land. The trial Court came to the further finding that there was no talk of sale of the 'Ka' scheduled land at Taka 70,000 as claimed by the defendant and that the defendant did not pay any money to the plaintiff at all. The trial Court found the suit maintainable in its present form. The Appellate Court did not reverse the above findings of fact of the trial Court and in a cumbersome way came to the finding that the terms of the salishnama proved that the plaintiff executed and registered the impugned deed, exhibit-'Ka' within his full knowledge “(স্বজ্ঞানে) Sound mind (সুস্থ মস্তিকে) The Appellate Court relying on the salishnama came to the further finding that since the plaintiff agreed to exchange 'Kha' scheduled land (out of his 'Ka' scheduled land) with the 'Ga' scheduled land of the defendant, but the defendant in collusion with the deed writer created the impugned deed (exhibit 'Ka') showing exchange of the 'Ka' scheduled land with the 'Ca' scheduled land and that he ought to have filed a suit for rectification of the deed under section 31 of the Act and that his present suit under section 39 of the Act was not maintainable. In coming to the said finding, the Appellate Court relied upon one of the terms of the salishnama (exhibit-'Uma') that the defendant would transfer 0.13½ acre of land from 3(three) plots to the plaintiff. Relying upon the salishnama, the Appellate Court failed to consider that it was not given effect to either by filing solenama in the suit or by transferring 0.13½ acre of land in favour of the plaintiff pursuant to term No.  4 thereof which reads as follows:

৪। নিম্ন তপশিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তি ১ম পক্ষ তাহার সুবিধা মোতাবেক সোলেনামা অথবা রেজিঃ ২য় পক্ষ গনের নিকট হইতে সম্পাদন করিয়া লইবেন এবং ২য় পক্ষ সোলে/রেজিঃতে বাধ্য থাকিব।

10. The Appellate Court also failed to consider the evidence adduced by the plaintiff in support of his case of practising fraud upon him by the defendant in executing and registering the impugned deed and the finding given by the trial Court in that respect, salishnama lost its factual and legal impact, if there be any, on the void or voidability of the impugned deed. It may be stated that the salishnama (exhibit-'Uma') was allegedly written in a village salish held on 26-10-1993, i. e. after filing of the suit.

11. From the impugned judgment, it appears that the High Court Division did not give any finding as to the maintainability of the suit although, in fact, the Appellate Court dismissed the suit on the ground of its maintainability The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding that "It has come out from the evidence of DW (Neither number of the DW nor his name has been mentioned. The defendant examined 5 D.Ws) that an amount of Taka 60,000 was paid to the petitioner (the plaintiff) for excess tatio (sic, it would be ratio) of land which has not been written in the exchange deed. The payment of Taka 60,000 has vitiated the exchange deed. The appellate Court neither considered the payment of Taka 60,000 nor the unreasonable difference in the ratio of lands as mentioned in the exchange deed."

12. In view of the leave granting order and the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the respective party, the questions to be decided in this appeal are: (i) whether the plaintiff's suit for cancellation of the impugned deed under section 39 of the Act was maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence adduced by the parties and (ii) whether, in view of the provisions of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code, relief under section 31 of the Act could be given in the suit framed under section 39 thereof.

13. Before deciding the questions as formulated hereinbefore, it is necessary to see the bare case of the respective party as made out in their pleadings though it may sound repetition.

14. The case of the plaintiff was very simple. His case was that the defendant is his own paternal uncle who reared him up since childhood with the affection of his father after his death and he used to respect the defendant like his father; that the defendant wanted to exchange his 'Ga' scheduled land with the 'Kha' scheduled land (out of 'Ka' scheduled land) of the plaintiff to which he agreed and accordingly, on good faith, he executed and registered the impugned deed, but subsequently, when on 3-5-1993, the defendant demanded the rest of the 'Ka' scheduled land (minus the 'Kha' scheduled land), he obtained the certified copy of the deed and found that the entire 'Ka' scheduled land was shown to have been exchanged which compelled him to file the suit. The defendant set up a completely different story in his written statement. His case was that the plaintiff proposed to sell the entire 'Ka' scheduled land to which he agreed and the price was fixed at Taka 70,000. The parties being closely related to each other, no bainapatra was executed; that out of the total consideration, the plaintiff paid Taka 60,000 in two installments and for the rest amount of Taka 10,000, he sold the 'Ga' scheduled land to the plaintiff, but on the advice of the deed writer instead of sale deed, a deed of exchange was written.

15. In the context, we feel it necessary to consider the provisions of sections 31 and 39 of the Act which are as follows: "

"31. When instrument may be rectified—When, through fraud or a mutual mistake of the parties, a contract or other instrument in writing does not truly express their intention, either party, or his representative in interest, may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified; and if the Court finds it clearly proved that there has been fraud or mistake in framing the instrument, and ascertain the real intention of the parties in executing the same, the Court may in its discretion rectify the instrument so as to express that intention, so far as this can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value.

39. When cancellation may be ordered—Any person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury, may sue to have it adjudged void or voidable; and the Court, in its discretion, may, adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled.

If the instrument has been registered under the Registration Act, 1908, the Court shall also send a copy of its decree to the officer in whose office the instrument has been so registered; and such officer shall note on the copy of the instrument contained in his books the fact of its cancellation."

16. A reading of section 31 shows that if a contract or other instrument in writing, here the impugned deed of exchange (exhibit-'Ka') does not truly express their intention, either party, or his representative in interest, may institute a suit to have the instrument rectified. From the section, it further appears that before passing the decree for rectification of a contract or other, instrument, it must be proved by the party who seeks such contract or instrument to be rectified that there had been fraud or mutual mistake of the parties in framing the instrument, the Court also to ascertain the real intention of the parties in executing the same. From a reading of the section, it further appears that rectification of an instrument is the discretion of the Court and so far as it can be done without prejudice to rights acquired by third persons in good faith and for value.

17. In the case of Messrs Siddique and Co. vs Messrs Utoomal and Assudamal Co., (supra) as relied upon by MR AJ Mohammad Ali, their Lordships of the Privy Council held that in order to obtain rectification of an instrument under section 31 of the Act, it must be proved that it was through a mutual mistake of the parties that the instrument in question did not truly express the intention of the parties; and the duty of the Court, before it can rectify, is to find it clearly proved that there has been mistake in framing the instrument, and it must ascertain the real intention of the parties in executing the instrument. On being satisfied of those two elements, it is in the discretion of the Court to grant rectification. In that case, their Lordships held that the plaintiffs seeking rectification of the written contract, had failed to prove that which it was necessary for them to prove, namely: that the word "Shipment" was used by them for "delivery" through mistake and that necessarily negatived any case of mutual mistake.

18. In the case of Lal Banu Bibi vs Nourjan Banu (supra), a learned Single Judge held that in order to rectify a deed, four conditions as contemplated in section 31 of the Act, have to be satisfied. The conditions being: (i) the agreement, be it oral or in writing, must express the final intention of the parties, (ii) both parties must have contended that exact term of prior agreement should be reduced to writing and this intention should remain unchanged up to the moment of actual execution of the circumstances, (iii) mistake or fraud should be obvious and not mere probability. In other words, it must be proved by unimpeachable evidence to show that intention of the parties, i.e. intention of the parties at the time of prior agreement was different from that expressed in the written instrument, (iv) rectification of literal mistake occurred though fraud or mistake as to enable the parties to act according to their intention already revealed in that prior agreement. In holding so, the learned Single judge correctly appreciated the provisions of section 31 of the Act.

19. In the instant case, from the contradictory pleadings of the parties and the findings of the Courts below, it is apparent that fraud was practised by the defendant upon the plaintiff in executing and registering the impugned deed and the real intention of the parties in framing the same was not same. And none of the parties pleaded mutual mistake in framing the impugned deed.

20. A reading of section 39 of the Act shows that it is the option of the person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable, who has reasonable apprehension that such instrument, if left outstanding, may cause him serious injury to sue or not to sue to have the written instrument adjudged void or voidable and the Court in its discretion may, adjudge it and order it to be delivered up and cancelled. The difference between the two sections is that section 31 speaks about rectification of the instrument, i. e. the instrument remains, whereas section 39 speaks about its cancellation, i. e. the instrument does not remain. Now, the question is whether a person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable is entitled to file a suit under section 39 of the Act to cancel the same on the ground of fraud or he should be compelled to file a suit for rectification of the same under section 31 thereof.

21. A cohesive reading of section 39 shows that a person against whom a written instrument is void or voidable can very well file a suit for its cancellation and filing of such suit shall depend upon his apprehension that the deed, if left outstanding, may cause serious injury to him. In the instant case, we have already found that the plaintiff wanted to exchange his `Kha' scheduled land out of the 'Ka' scheduled land with the 'Ga' scheduled land of the defendant, but the defendant in collusion with the scribe executed and registered the impugned deed showing exchange of the said 'Ga' scheduled land measuring only 0.16½ acre of land with 'Ka' scheduled land measuring 1.41¼ acres of land. Besides the evidence adduced by the plaintiff in support of his case, the very disproportion of the two areas of land exchanged prima facie shows that fraud was practised upon the plaintiff in executing and registering the impugned deed. The trial Court also gave finding to the effect

“ নথি পর্যাবেক্ষন আমি বাদি পক্ষের সাক্ষীদের সাক্ষ্য নিরপেক্ষ ও নির্ভরযোগ্য মনে করি। তাহাদের সাক্ষ-বিশ্বাস করিয়া আমি মনে করি যে, সাধারনভাবে ১.৪১½ একর জমির সহিত ১৬½ শতক জমির বিনিময় আদৌ সম্ভব নয়। জমির মূল্য ও পরিমানের এই ব্যাপক ব্যবধান লইয়া ক তপশিলের সহিত গ তপশিলের আদৌ বিনিময় হওয়া সম্ভব নয়।”

But the Appellate Court totally failed to consider this apparent factual aspect of the case in dismissing the suit on the ground of its non-maintainability.

22. In the plaint, the plaintiff categorically stated to the effect .

“এইরুপে ‘গ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত ভুমির সহিত ‘ক’ তপশিল বর্ণিত ভূমি বাবদ নালিশি ‘ঘ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত দলিল লিখা হইয়াছে জানিতে ও বুঝিতে পারিলে বাদি কখনই নালিশি দলিল সম্পাদন ও রেজিঃ করিয়া দিতেন না। এইরুপে নালিশি ‘ঘ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত দলিল সম্পূর্নরুপে জাল, যোগসাজশী তঞ্চকতা পূর্ব ফলবলহীন ও শঠতা পূর্ন দলিল হইতেছে। এইরুপে নালিশি ‘খ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত দলিলে বাদীর অপুরনীয় ক্ষতির কারন হইয়াছে এবং উক্ত দলিল বহাল থাকিলে বাদির অপুরনীয় ক্ষতি হইবে হেতু নালিশি ‘ঘ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত দলিল বাতিল হওয়া আবশ্যক। এ কারনেই বাদি বাধ্য হইয়া নালিশি দলিল বাতিলের প্রার্থনায় বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে অত্র মোকদ্দমা আনয়ন করিলেন।

23. From the above, it is clear that the plaintiff apprehended that if the impugned deed of exchange left outstanding without being adjudged as void that would cause him "serious injury."

24. The defendant took the plea that he purchased the `Ka' scheduled land from the plaintiff at Taka 70,000 out of which he paid Taka 60,000 and for the remaining amount of Taka 10,000, the 'Ga' scheduled land was transferred to the plaintiff, but on the advice of the deed writer instead of sale deed, the impugned deed of exchange was executed and registered. But the defendants totally failed to prove his said case including the payment of Taka 60,000 and the trial Court on consideration of the evidence of the DWs disbelieved the case of the defendant. And the defendant was also not permitted to take such a plea in view of the provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act, as the impugned document itself showed that it was out and out a deed of exchange. In this regard, Mr Probir Neogi rightly relied upon the case of Firoza Majid vs Jiban Bima Corporation (supra)

25. The conduct of the defendant is deplorable. Even after filing of the suit, he wanted to perpetuate with his fraudulent activities by taking a plea of purchase of the 'Ka' scheduled land from the plaintiff as stated above, which he failed to prove. From the con-duct of the defendant, it is clear that his intention was not to exchange his 'Ga' scheduled land with the 'Kha' scheduled land of the plaintiff, but to grab the 'Ka' scheduled land by practising fraud upon the plaintiff in collusion with the scribe in the name of framing a deed of exchange. In the plaint, the plaintiff categorically asserted that after the fraud became known to him, he requested the defendant to rectify the deed, but he refused. So the plaintiff had no other option but to file the suit for cancellation of the impugned deed vide exhibit-'Ka'. The Appellate Court, in holding that the plaintiff ought to have filed the suit under section 31 of the Act for rectification of the impugned deed instead of section 39 thereof totally failed to comprehend the case of the plaintiff and also failed to consider that the intention of the defendant was not to rectify the deed but to perpetuate with his fraud and that there was no mutual mistake within the meaning of section 31. Moreso, when the defendant resorted to fraud and the plaintiff apprehended that if the impugned deed was left outstanding that would cause him serious harm so why the plaintiff should be compelled to file a suit for rectification of the same instead of its cancellation. To us it does not appear that the facts and circumstances of the case and the evidence on record at all attract the provisions of section 31 of the Act and the plaintiff rightly filed the suit for cancellation of the impugned deed. Therefore, the Appellate Court was absolutely wrong in holding that the plaintiff's suit for cancellation filed under section 39 of the Act was not maintainable. Accordingly, the first question is answered in the affirmative.

26. Now the second question:

"A reading of the provisions of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code shows that in the plaint, the plaintiff must state specifically the relief which he claims either simply or in the alternative and a general or other relief need not be specifically prayed in the plaint as such general or other relief may always be granted by the Court, if it thinks just to the same extent, as if it had been asked for.

27. This Division in the case of Maico Jute and Bag Corporation vs Bangladesh Jute Mills Corporation (supra) held that "It is absolutely the domain and the discretion of the Court to grant the relief sought for or to grant any other general or other relief that may be thought fit and proper."

28. In the case of Rajendra Tiwary vs Basudeo Prasad (supra), the Indian Supreme Court held that "Where the relief prayed for in the suit for a larger relief and if no case is made out for granting the same but the facts, as established, justify granting of smaller relief, Order VII, rule 7 permits granting of such a relief to the parties. However, under the said provisions a relief larger than the one claimed by the plaintiff in the suit cannot be granted."

29. In the case of Kedar Lal Seal vs Harilal Seal, AIR 1952, SC 47, Bose, J who spoke for the Court observed that—

"I would be slow to throw out a claim on a mere technicality of pleading when the substances of the thing is there and no prejudice is caused to the other side, however clumsily or inartistically the plaint may be worded. In any event, it is always open to a Court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for, provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in cost."

(The two other cases relied upon by Mr Neogi not being relevant in the context are not considered.)

<u>30. The suit for cancellation of an instrument filed under section 39 of the Act, is in a larger compass than a suit for rectification of an instrument under section 31 thereof. And the relief of cancellation of an instrument (here the impugned deed of exchange) is surely larger than the relief of rectification of an instrument. Therefore, if a written instrument sought to be adjudged void or voidable, cannot be so adjudged for the failure on the part of the plaintiff to make out such a case, but the facts, as proved, warrant granting a relief within the scope of section 31 of the Act, can very well be given. In other words, framing of a suit cannot stand as a bar to the applicability of the provisions of section 31 of the Act in a suit under section 39 thereof if the facts proved warrant giving of such relief. Therefore, our answer to the second question is also in the affirmative.</u>

31. However, in the instant case, it was not at all necessary to fall back upon the provisions of section 31 of the Act and to take the aid of Order VII, rule 7 of the Code. The plaintiff clearly couched his prayer within the full ambit of section 39 of the Act. The principal prayers were as follows:

(ক) আরজির বর্ণিত কারন ও ঘটনাধীনে নিম্ন ‘ক’ তপশিল বর্ণিত ভূমি বাবদ নালিশি ‘ঘ’ তপশিল বর্ণিত দলিল বাতিলের ডিক্রী বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে বাদির অনুকুলে দিতে।

(খ) উক্ত ডিক্রীর এক প্রা্ন্ত সংশ্লিষ্ট রেজিঃ অফিসে প্রেরন করতঃ নালিশি দলিল বাবদ সংশ্লিষ্ট ভলিউমের সংশ্লিষ্ট পাতায় একটি নোট লিপিবদ্ধ করিবার আদেশ দিতে।

<u>32. Fraud vitiates everything. Since the plaintiff succeeded to prove that fraud was practised upon him by the defendant in executing and registering the impugned deed, it vitiated the entire transaction and therefore, the defendant was liable to be punished by way of its cancellation as a whole. As already stated earlier, even in contesting the suit, the defendant took a false plea that in fact, he purchased the 'Ka' scheduled land at Taka 70,000 but as he paid Taka 60,000 only out of the total price for the rest amount, he sold the 'Ga' scheduled land to the plaintiff, but instead of sale deed the deed of exchange was framed and this totally showed that the defendant had no intention to exchange his `Ga' scheduled land with the 'Kha' scheduled land of the plaintiff, the question of rectification of the impugned deed does not arise at all. The High Court Division rightly held that the plea of payment of Taka 60,000 vitiated "the exchange deed." We do not also see any prejudice caused to the defendant in cancelling the impugned deed of exchange, as with its cancellation the right, title of the respective party to his respective land revived.</u>

33. In conclusion, we hold that the High Court Division did not commit any error of law in setting aside the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court and thus, in passing the impugned judgment and order making the Rule absolute. There is no merit in the appeal.

Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed. There will be no order as to costs.

End.
