full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 17-4-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 14/2006 affirming those dated 31-1-2006 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Lakshmipur in Miscellaneous Case No. 102/2000 should not be set aside.

2. The relevant facts, for disposal of this Rule, in short, are that the petitioners as pre-emptors instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 102 of 2000 in the Court of the learned Assistant Judge, Lakshmipur for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act alleging that the land as described in the Schedule of the application for pre-emption belonged to Manzuma Khatun, the vendor-opposite party No. 2 who transferred the said land by a deed executed on 16-4-1998 to the pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 Abu Hanif Howlader. The said deed was presented for registration on 24-4-1998 and ultimately the same was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 10-3-1999. The said deed was executed and registered in the form of a deed of exchange. The pre-emptors knew the said deed as deed of exchange. But the vendor Manzuma Khatun went to the house of her father in the middle of September 2000 and at the time of talking the pre-emptor No. 1 asked her as to whether she had constructed any structure in the land at Mohammadpur, Dhaka, which she got in lieu of exchange, or not. Then she replied that she did not exchange the disputed land and she had sold the same. The said deed was executed and registered in the form of deed of exchange, only to avoid pre-emption. After execution of the deed of exchange she had returned the land. The pre-emptor knowing about it, at first, collected the certified copy of the deed of exchange. Thereafter on 19-10-2000 he collected the certified copy of deed of retransfer as executed by the vendor Manzuma to the pre-emptee in respect of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza, under Police Station Mohammadpur, Dhaka and confirmed that the instant transaction was, in fact, out and out a sale, but the pre-emptee and the vendor, in collusion with each other, made the same in the form of deed of exchange only to avoid pre-emption. Thereafter, the pre-emptors instituted the instant application for pre-emption on 30-11-2000. The pre-emptors also collected the certified copy of another Kabala deed in respect of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza, where from it is detected that the pre-emptee, after taking return of the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza from the vendor Manjuma Khatun, had transferred the said land to one Anwara Khatun by executing Kabala deed dated 13-11-1999. In such view of the matter, the pre-emptors are entitled to get the disputed land by way of pre-emption.

3. The pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 contested the application for pre-emption by filing written objection denying all the material allegations contending that the instant application for pre-emption was not maintainable and the same was barred by section 96(10)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. His specific case, in short, was that he exchanged his land measuring 0.04 acre of Ramchandrapur Mouza under Police Station Mohammadpur, Dhaka in lieu of the disputed land. After so exchange, possession was delivered accordingly. The market price of the disputed land is more than Taka 16,00,000 (Taka Sixteen lacs). Earlier, admitting the deed of exchange the pre-emptors executed a Nadabipatra in favour of the pre-emptee when it was detected that some portion of the disputed land had been erroneously recorded in the names of the pre-emptors. After admitting the impugned deed as deed of exchange the pre-emptors cannot say that the same was a sale deed. It has further been staled that the pre-emptor had knowledge about the instant deed from the time of its execution. Subsequent story regarding the date of knowledge as mentioned by the pre-emptors is false. The instant application is barred by limitation. It has further been stated that the vendor Manzuma never executed and registered the sale deed dated 19-4-1998 in favour of the pre-emptee and the pre-emptee had not executed and registered any deed in favour of Anwara Khatun. In such view of the matter, the instant application for pre-emption was not maintainable so the same should be dismissed.

4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge by his judgment and order dated 31-1-2006 dis-missed the application for pre-emption. Thereafter, the pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 14/2006 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Lakshmipur which was ultimately heard by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur who by the impugned judgment and order dated 17-4-2007 dismissed the appeal affirming the judgment and order of the trial Court. Then the pre-emptors moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

5. Mr Khair Ezaz Maswood, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the Ext’s. 4, 4(ka) and 5 clearly proved that the instant transaction was out and out sale but in order to avoid pre-emption the vendor and vendee, in collusion with each other, created the same in the form of deed of exchange. Subsequent after execution of Ext. 4 vendor Manjuma Khatun who allegedly got .04 acre of land in lieu of exchange had retransferred the same to the pre-emptee vide Ext. 4(ka). Thereafter, by executing Ext. 5 the pre-emptee transferred the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza to Anwara Khatun. He further submits that although the pre-emptors had initial knowledge about Ext. 4 but they knew such transaction as exchange not sale. In the middle of September, 2000 the vendor-opposite party No. 2 Manzuma disclosed that she had sold the disputed land to the pre-emptee and collecting Ext. 4(ka) he confirmed that, in fact, she had sold the disputed land to the pre-emptee and deed was made in the form of exchange collusively, only to avoid pre-emption. The date of knowledge of sale is the date when they came to know from Monzuma in middle of September 2000. The pre-emptors are entitled to get benefit of section 18 of the Limitation Act.

6. Mr. Quamrul Haque Siddiqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, while assailing the submission of Mr. Maswood, submits that Ext. 4(ka), is secondary evidence and the same has not been admitted in evidence on due compliance of sections 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act. He further submits that from plain reading of Ext.4 it appears that the same is a deed of exchange. So, the instant application for pre-emption is barred under section 96(10)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He further submits that sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act will operate as a bar to admit any oral evidence to contradict the contents of the register instruments. He further submits that as the pre-emptors failed to prove Ext’s. 4(ka) and 5 in accordance with law and there is no other direct or circumstantial evidence to prove that the instant transaction was out and out a sale and allegation of fraud as made by Mr. Maswood has not been established so the Courts below rightly disbelieved the story of fraud and the finding of the Courts below regarding fraud is finding of fact which cannot be interfered with by exercising power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure by this Court.

7. It appears from Ext. 4, the impugned deed that the pre-emptee-opposite party No.1 Abu Hanif Howlader is the first party and vendor-opposite party No.2 Manzuma is the second party and the same was executed and registered in the form of deed of exchange. Abu Hanif Howlader was the owner of land covering 0.04 acre of Ramchandrapur Mouza under the Police Station Mohammadpur, Dhaka and the land under pre-emption covering an area of 2.48 acres of mouza Bijoy Nagar, Police Station Lakshmipur, District Lakshmipur belonged to vendor-opposite party No.2 Manjuma Khatun. The said deed was executed on 16-4-1998 and presented for registration before the Sub Registrar on 24-4-1998. The same was registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 10-3-1999. The pre-emptor instituted the pre-emption case on 30-11-2000. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, submits that although Ext.4 was executed and registered in the form of exchange deed but the same was, in fact, a sale deed and in order to avoid pre-emption the vendor and pre-emptee fraudulently created the said deed of exchange only to avoid pre-emption. He further submits that although apparently the instant application was barred by the provisions of limitation, but the said limitation will run from the date when the fraud is detected.

<u>8. As the pre-emptors allege the fraud so onus lies upon them to prove so. Since fraud is a secret in its origin and inception; the fraudulent motive or design, and even fraud cannot be proved to the very hilt. Fraud must necessarily be inferred from the circumstances. Fraud is so various in form and colour that it is difficult if not impossible to confine it within the limits of any precise definition Concealment of facts amount to fraud. There must have been some intentional imposition or some deliberate concealment of facts by which ignorance of the pre-emptor was brought about. There must be some evidence to establish affirmative that the pre-emptee had designed to prevent the discovery of cause of action of the pre-emptor.</u>

9. Now we shall see as to whether the pre-emptor has been able to prove fraud or not.

10. In the application for pre-emption the pre-emptors specifically pleaded that in the middle of September, 2000 the pre-emptors asked the vendor as to whether she had made any construction in the land of Ramchandrapur Mouza, PS Mohammadpur, Dhaka or not then the vendor disclosed that she did not get the land from Mohammadpur. She had sold the disputed land and subsequent after execution of the deed of exchange she had retransferred the land of Mohammadpur, Dhaka to the pre-emptee. Then the pre-emptors collected the certified copy of the deed Ext. 4. Thereafter collecting the certified copy of the subsequent deed 4(Ka) they confirmed that the instant transaction was, in fact, out and out a sale. In support of such pleadings the pre-emptors produced the certified copy of the Kabala deed as executed by vendor Manjuma Khatun in favour of the pre-emptee as executed on 19-41-998 Ext. 4 (Ka) and they also produced the certified copy of the Kabala deed dated 13-1-1999 (Ext. 5). These two documents clearly established that within 4 days from the date of execution of Ext. 4, the vendor transferred the land of Mohammadpur to the pre-emptee which she got in lieu of exchange from the pre-emptee. Thereafter the pre emptee again transferred the said land to Anwara Khatun. From plain reading of Exts. 4 (ka), and 5 together it is apparent that with an intention to avoid pre-emption deed of exchange Ext. 4 was executed and with in 4 days exchanged property was retransferred to pre-emptee by Ext. 4 (Ka) and he transferred the same Anwara by Ext 5.

11. Mr. Siddique candidly submits the Exts. 4(ka) and 5 are secondary evidence and those are not admitted in evidence due compliance of the provisions of sections 63, 65 and 66 of the Evidence Act, Accordingly to Mr. Siddique Ext. 4 is a registered instrument. From its contents it appears that the same was a deed of exchange. Any oral evidence contradict, vary and subtracting from' its term is barred by under section 92 of the Evidence Act.

12. Section 63 of the Evidence Act mentions 5 kinds of secondary evidence, clause (1), (2) and (3) refer to copies of the documents; clause (4) refers to counter parts of documents and clause (5) refers to oral accounts of the contents of documents. Correctness of the certified copies referred to in clause (1) of section 63 is presumed under section 79 of the Evidence Act. Certified of a registered sale deed may be produced as secondary evidence in the absence of the original. Section 63 declares certified copies to be a permissible form of secondary evidence; section 65, clause (e) and section 77 of the Evidence Act make the certified copies of the public documents admissible in proof of the contents of such documents; and section 79 requires every document purporting to be a certified copy to be presumed to be genuine. In the case of Shishir Kanti Pal vs Nur Muhammad, reported in 55 DLR (AD) 39, their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed:

"A registered document carries presumption of correctness of the endorsement made therein and that one who disputes the said presumption is under the law required to dislodge the correctness of the endorsement in the registered document. Exhibit 1 has been registered by the Munsif-Cum-Magistrate of Udaypur, Tripura State, India. Since defendant No.5 was disputing the genuineness of the registered document Exhibitl it was his duty to establish that there was nothing like Munsif; Magistrate, Official or Office in Udaypur in the Tripura State who was authorised to register irrevocable power of attorney. But the said defendant totally failed to bring on record any material where form it can be said Munsif/ Magistrate, Udaypur, Tripura State, India was not competent to register Exhibit 1. The fact is that exhibit 1 was revalidated and re-stamped by the Office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Comilla. Official act has the presumption of correctness and that one who challenges or disputes that presumption of correctness is required to establish that by legal evidence."

13. In the case of Tambia Khatun vs Rafiquullah, reported in 2 ADC 838 it appears that in similar circumstances the High Court Division observed that "Section 92 will operate as a bar in respect of admissibility of oral evidence." In that case a certified copy of deed of retransfer was produced. The impugned deed was a deed of exchange, pre-emptor producing the certified copy of the deed of retransfer claimed that the instant transaction was colourable one and made only to avoid pre-emption. The High Court Division accepting the argument as advanced on behalf of the pre-emptee that the oral evidence contradicting the contents of the registered document will not be admissible in evidence as the impugned deed was a deed of exchange. So the application for pre-emption will also be barred under section 96(1)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Thereafter Appeal was preferred and their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed:

"It appears from the judgment and order of the learned Single Judge that he held, "No oral evidence contrary to the facts recorded in the deed in question is admissible in evidence" and the evidence adduced by the .witnesses of the appellant being contrary to the averments recorded in the deed of exchange. The lower appellate Court wrongly held that the pre-emption case was not barred under section 96(10)(b) of the Act."

14. Section 96 (10) (b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 reads as follows:

"96(10) Nothing in this section shall apply to

(a) transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase; or

(b) a transfer by exchange or partition."

<u>15. From the aforesaid provision we are unable to read that no oral evidence can be adduced for determining the nature of transfer of a holding or a portion thereof which is effected by an exchange deed. The learned Single Judge, it seems to us, made a mistake in holding that no oral evidence can be adduced to decide the nature of transfer in the pre-emption proceeding presumably in view of sections 91 and 92 of the Evidence Act, 1872. Section 91 of the Evidence Act is about the manner of proof of a document which has been reduced to the forms of a document. The document itself has to be proved, or where secondary evidence is admissible, secondary evidence of its contents may be proved. The terms of document cannot be proved by any other mode of proof. The impugned Kabala has been proved under section 91.</u>

16. Section 92 of the Evidence Act provides that when a document described in section 91 has been proved according to section 91, "no evidence of any oral agreement or statement shall be admitted, as between the parties to any such instrument or their representatives in interest, for the purpose of contradicting, varying, adding to, or subtracting from, its terms.

17. In this case, the contest is between the pre-emptor and the pre-emptee as to whether the Kabala in question was a sale or an Ewaz. The pre-emptor was not a party to the document. She is perfectly at liberty to question the nature of the transaction and the pre-emption Court has full jurisdiction to entertain the pre-emptee's challenge."

18. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division further observed:

"In view of the legal position we hold that the learned Singe Judge fell in serious error of law in holding that no oral evidence can be adduced to decide the nature of a transfer sought to be pre-empted."

19. In view of the aforesaid decision as referred above of the apex Court, I am of the view that the submission as made by Mr. Siddique has got no force.

20. In the case of Monwara Begum vs Anwarul Islam reported in 5 ADC 649 it appears that a deed of exchange was made. Subsequently, the vendor retransferred his land, which she got in lieu of exchange, in favour of the son of the pre-emptee. Their Lordships of the Appellate Division, taking into consideration of the certified copy of the deed of retransfer, concurred the findings of the Courts below and held that the instant transaction was out and out sale but in order to avoid pre-emption the said transfer was made in the form of deed of exchange which was a colourable one and accordingly allowed the application for pre-emption.

<u>21. In view of the aforesaid facts and circumstances of the case and the decisions as referred above, I am of the view that the pre-emptee and vendor collusively created Ext. 4 in the form of deed of exchange. Ext’s. 4(ka) and 5 clearly proved that the impugned transfer was out and out a sale and in order to avoid pre-emption it was made in the form of deed of exchange. I do not find any reasons to disbelieve Ext. 4 (ka) and 5, only for the reasons that original copies of those deeds have not been produced before the Court which are presumed to be either in the custody of the pre-emptee Abu Hanif Howlader or subsequent purchaser Anwara Khatun. After producing the certified copy the pre-emptor has discharged his initial onus because those are the certified copies of a registered instrument and it is to be presumed that those are genuine documents. But the pre-emptee did not take any steps to establish that those documents are forged one.</u>

22. Mr. Siddique, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party submits that prior to admitting the certified copies Exts.4(ka) and 5 no notice under section 66 of the Evidence Act was issued. Mr. Khair Ezaz Maswood, the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that as the original was lying either in custody of the pre-emptee or the subsequent purchaser Anwara Begum, so the notice was not at all necessary. In support of his submission he cited the decision in the case of Mst. Lalan Bibi vs Muhammad Ashfaq, reported in PLD 1951 (Lahore) 457, wherein it was observed:

"The first contention was based on two grounds: Firstly, it was contended that, since no formal notice under section 66 of the Evidence Act was given by the plaintiff to the defendant, secondary evidence of the contents of the divorce deed could not be legally received. This objection is easily met for clause (2) of the proviso to section 66 dispenses with notice when, from the nature of the case, the adverse party must know, he will be required to produce the document in question. It cannot be seriously denied that, from the nature of the present case, the defendants must have known that she would be required to produce the divorce deed. It is, therefore, obvious that the objection 'to the reception of secondary evidence to prove the contents of divorce deed is without substance."

23. In the case of Asanullah Fakir vs Jogendra Nath Sarkar, reported in PLD (1961) 703 = 13 DLR 470 as cited by Mr. Maswood, it appears that his Lordship Mr. Siddiqui, J. observed:

"It is, therefore, found from the decisions of the cases referred to above, which is consistent for a period of more than 70 years, that when a party alleges fraud and invokes the aid of section 18 of the Limitation Act, he must first establish the fraud committed by the other side, and once he has done so, it will be for the other side, to prove that the party injured had the knowledge of fraud at a point of time beyond the period of limitation calculated from the time the application is filed. It has also been held that the mere knowledge of the sale will not be sufficient to put the petitioner out of Court on grounds of limitation."

24. His Lordship further held:

"The knowledge of the sale and the knowledge of the fraud are two different things. The knowledge of the facts constituting the fraud may include the knowledge of the sale but the mere knowledge of the sale does not include the knowledge of the facts of the fraud. The distinction no doubt, is subtle, but it is clear and understandable. I, therefore, hold that the mere knowledge of the sale which may be ascribed to the petitioner which may relates back to 7-11-57 does not constitute his knowledge of the facts of the fraud committed upon him by the decree-holder- auction-purchaser in the present case and therefore he was not out of time on 20-6-58 in view of the fact that he invoked the aid of section 18 of the Limitation Act. The courts below definitely fell into an error on this point."

<u>25. In this case it appears that the pre-emptors admitted that they had knowledge about the deed of exchange but they had no knowledge, regarding the sale and fraud. Knowing about the fraud they, collecting the certified copy of the subsequent deed, that is, Ext’s. 4(ka), filed the application for pre-emption. From the date of knowledge of sale the application was within time.</u>

26. In view of such circumstances and the decisions referred above, I am of the view that the instant application for pre-emption was filed within time from the date of knowledge of sale. It is not disputed that the petitioners are not co-sharers of the disputed holdings. Considering the facts and circumstances of the same I am of the view that the Courts below failed to consider the Ext’s. 4(ka) and 5 property and other circumstantial evidence thereby erroneously held that the pre-emptors have failed to prove the fraud inasmuch as the Ext’s. 4(ka) and 5 and the circumstances as mentioned above it is clear that the pre-emptee and vendor in collusion with each other executed and registered the impugned deed in form of exchange (Ext.4) in order to avoid pre-emption.

27. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case mentioned above, I am of the view that both the Courts below committed an error of law in not allowing the application for pre-emption. I find substance in the Rule.

28. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The judgments and orders of the Courts below are hereby set aside.

29. The application for pre-emption is hereby allowed.

30. The order of injunction granted while issuing the Rule is hereby vacated.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Ashfaqul Islam J: All the writ petitions are taken up together for hearing and disposed of by a single judgment as there involved common question of facts and laws.

2. At the instance of the petitioners The Westin Dhaka, Sena Hotel Developments Limited (Radisson Water Garden Hotel), Pan Pacific Sonargoan Hotel and Bangladesh Services Limited (Dhaka Sheraton Hotel) the Rules were issued almost in common terms. For the convenience of disposal we want to quote the Rule issued in Writ Petition No.3910 of 2009 which is in following terms:-

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Memo No.4/LTU (Musak) 25/The Westin Dhaka/Demand/Circle-3/09/2111 dated 20-4-2009 issued by the Respondent No. 3 under section 55(1) of the VAT Act, 1991 making demand of Taka 7,12,95,948 as supplementary duty and VAT on the said supplementary duty (Annexure-A); shall not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect."

3. In all the petitions the parties are at dispute on imposition of supplementary duty as it has been claimed/demanded by impugned notices under section 55 of the VAT Act. For the acquaintance with the factual aspect of the case it would be worthwhile to reproduce the impugned order in Writ Petition No. 3910 of 2009 which is as under:

গণপ্ৰজাতন্তী বালাদেশ সরকার

বৃহৎ করদাতা ইউনিট-মূল্য সংযোজন কর

২য় ১২ তলা সরকারী অফিস ভবন (৬ষ্ঠতলা)

সেগুনবাগিচা, ঢাকা৷

নথি নং-৪ এলটিইউ (মুসক) ২৫/দি ওয়েস্টিন ঢাকা/দাবীনামা/

সার্কেল ৩/০৯

“প্রেরকঃ কমিশনার

প্রাপকঃ ব্যবস্থাপনা পরিচালক

দি ওয়েস্টিন ঢাকা

9. The VAT Act was introduced by the Act 22 of 1991 pursuant to a Gazette dated 10-7-1991. In the original VAT Act 'Hotel and Restaurant' though broadly categorized under service Code No. 5001.00 but the Hotel was categorized under a distinct service Code No. S001.10 and the Restaurant under service Code No. 5001.20 and for both the hotel and restaurant 10% supplementary duty was imposed. By SRO No. 338/Ain/003/397 Musak dated 3-12-2003 supplementary duty imposed on 'hotel and restaurant' under service Code 001.10 was exempted under section 14 of the Act. Thereafter SRO No.166 Ain/2004/412 Musak dated 10-6-2004 repealed the earlier SRO No.338 dated 3-12-2003 and the 'Hotel' under service Code No. 001.10 as mentioned in Column 3 in table -2 was given exemption from paying supplementary duty under section 14 of the Act. হোটেলঃ-অর্থ কোন ক্লাব সহ, এমন কোন প্রতিষ্ঠান, সংখ্যা বা স্থান যেখানে সাময়িকভাবে অবস্থানের জন্য কোন কক্ষ বা কক্ষসমূহের স্যুট বা অন্য কোন ধরনের আবাসন, উহাতে ক্যাটারিং এর ব্যবস্থা অথবা যে কোনো নামে অভিহিত অন্য কোন সেবা, সুবিধা বা উপযোগিতার ব্যবস্থা থাকুক বা না থাকুক ভাড়া দেওয়া হয় এবং ফ্লোর শো প্রদর্শনকারী কোন প্রতিষ্ঠানও এই সজ্ঞার অর্ন্তভুক্ত হইবে ৷

ব্যাখ্যা-রেস্তোরাঁ অর্থ, কোন ক্লাব সহ এমন কোন প্রতিষ্ঠান, সংজ্ঞা বা স্থান যেখানে অথবা যে কোনো নামে অভিহিত অন্য কোন সেবা, সুবিধা বা উপযোগিতা প্রদান করা হউক, ইহাতে বা অন্যত্র ভোগের উদ্দেশ্যে কোন খাদ্য বা পানীয় বিক্রয় করা হয়, এবং ফ্লোর শো প্রদর্শনকারী প্রতিষ্ঠানসহ যান্ত্রিকযানে পরিচালিত মোবাইল রেন্তোরাঁও ইহাতে অন্তর্ভুক্ত হইবে ৷

12. This definition of Hotel and Restaurant has been continuing till date. Even in SRO No. 168/Ain/2013/672 Musak dated 6-6-2013 the definition of the two establishments stands the same. In the original Act we have found that for imposition of supplementary duty Hotel and Restaurant have been further explained as under :—

আবাসন, খাদ্য বা পানীয় সরবরাহকালে যদি হোটেল বা রেস্তোরাঁয় মদ জাতীয় পানীয় সরবরাহ করা হয় বা যে কোন ধরনের ফ্লোর শো এর আয়োজন করা হয় (বছরে একদিনের জন্য হইলেও) I

13. That being the background the learned counsel representing different petitioners almost unequivocally argued that after exemption of imposition of supplementary duty both on hotel and restaurant by SRO No.338 dated 3-12-2003, the subsequent exemption of supplementary duty only on 'hotel' by SRO No.166 dated 10-6-2004 by superseding SRO 338 as mentioned above would also apply upon the restaurants inside those hotels. Therefore, the supplementary duty upon the restaurants inside those hotels can not be claimed by the order impugned against being not sustainable in law as the said exemption of supplementary duty on hotel also equally applies in case of the restaurants inside the hotels.

14. Mr. Omar Sadat, Mr. Md. Asaduzzaman and Mr. Sk. Awsafur Rahman the learned counsels appearing for the petitioners submits that section 7(1) of the VAT Act contains the provisions for imposition of supplementary duty. It provides that supplementary duty shall be imposed on the items and services listed in the Third Schedule of the Act. Hotel, under Heading S001.10 was included in the Third Schedule of the originally enacted Act as one of the services charged with supplementary duty.

15. He submits that the Internal Resource Division of the Ministry of Finance ("IRD") exercising its power under section 14 of the VAT Act published SRO No. 338/Ain/2003/ 397-Mushak dated 3-12-2003 and through the said SRO exempted "Hotel and Restaurant" under Heading S001.10 from paying supplementary duty. Thereafter SRO No. 166-Ain/ 2004/412-Mushak dated 10-6-2004 was published by IRD repealing SRO No. 338/Ain/ 2003/397-Mushak, wherein "Hotel was continued to be exempted from paying supplementary duty Afterwards, IRD issued another SRO No. 152-Ain/2005/443-Mushak dated 9-6-2005 repealing SRO No.166-Ain/2004/412 Mushak, wherein hotels were exempted from paying supplementary duty under section 14 of the Act. Then IRD issued SRO No. 205-Ain/ 2010554-Mushak dated 10-6-2010 wherein hotels once again have been listed as being exempted from paying supplementary duty. Thereafter, the said SRO No.205-Ain/2010/554- Mushak was repealed by another SRO No.176- Ain/2011/599-Mushak dated 9-6-2011 published by IRD continuing the exemption of hotels from paying supplementary duty IRD later, publishing SRO No. 184-A in/2012/ 642- Mushak dated 7-6-2012 repealed by SRO No. 176-Ain/2011/566-Mushak and imposed supplementary duty on hotels.

16. It has been specifically mentioned in the said SRO that other than the services listed in Table-3 of the said SRO, all other services listed in the Third Schedule of the Act shall be exempted from paying any supplementary duty and hotel was listed as a service in Table-3 of SRO No. 184-Ain /2012 /642-Mushak. Therefore, it is clear that the Ministry of Finance had been, since 2003 till 7-6-2012, continuing to exempt hotels from paying supplementary duty IRD later on repealed the said SRO No.184-Ain/2012/642-Mushak vide SRO No. 171-Ain/ 2013 /675-Mushak dated 6-6-2013 which did not change the status of 'hotel' in terms of supplementary duty Recently, IRD published SRO No. 109-Ain/2014/704-Mushak dated 5-6-2014 repealing SRO No. 171Ain/2013 /675-Mushak, under which 'hotel' are still required to pay supplementary duty.

17. He finally submits that the SROs as discussed above abundantly make it clear that the hotels and restaurants in general have been exempted from paying supplementary duty with the publication of SRO No.338/Ain/ 2003/397-Mushak on 3-12-2003 which continued till publication of SRO No. 184-Ain/2012/ 642-Mushak on 7-6-2012 when supplementary duty on restaurant was imposed and therefore, the petitioner is not liable to pay any supplementary duty on restaurant inside the hotels demanded by the impugned notices. Omar Sadat justifies that otherwise it would not have been required to impose supplementary duty upon restaurant in the year 2012 by the said SRO No. 184, and, as such, the impugned demands of supplementary duties upon restaurants inside the hotels are not sustainable in law.

18. Sheikh Awsafur Rahman, the learned counsel in Writ Petition Nos. 4317 and Writ Petition No. 3880 of 2009 also reiterates the same argument.

19. Mr. Md. Asaduzzaman, the learned counsel appearing for the petitioner in writ petition No. 8051 of 2011 and writ petition No.5430 of 2009 also adopted the same argument as advanced by Mr Omar Sadat with only exception in case of writ petition No. 5430 of 2009 where he submits that the impugned claim is also barred by limitation. He contends that demand was made by impugned order in 2009 claiming supplementary duty on restaurant for the year 2005 to 2009, which is barred under law.

20. Mr. Md. Asaduzzaman clarifies that even if the impugned Nothi is considered to have been issued within the purview of section 55(1) of the said Act, it is barred by limitation as it has alleged that supplementary duty and VAT has been evaded from January 2005 to February 2009 but the impugned notice has been issued on 23-4-2009 and hence the impugned Nothi has been issued for a period beyond three years from the date of nonpayment as under section 55(1) of the Act a notice can be issued within three years from date of nonpayment, or less payment of VAT and supplementary duty or evasion of the same. Since in the instant case the demand notice was issued on 23-4-2009 the demand of entire period before 30-3-2006 is barred by limitation, the alleged evasion of supplementary duty and VAT thereon having made for the period from January 2005 to February 2009 as a consolidated amount for over three years, the impugned Nothi is illegal and has been issued without lawful authority as it suffers from inherent lack of jurisdiction.

21. We have heard the learned counsel representing different hotels on the issue and considered their valued arguments with utmost care and precision. In our anxiety we have carefully perused almost all the relevant SROs construing and explaining of the periphery of hotel and restaurant and also the extent of exemption given by the SROs as discussed above.

22. The moot question that falls for consideration by this Division in all these petitions is whether the imposition of supplementary duty on the restaurants inside the hotels in question in terms of the argument advanced by the parties should be held unsustainable.

23. The learned Additional Attorney General Mr. Murad Reza appearing with the learned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Moniruz-zaman, Assistant Attorney General Mrs. Shuchira Hussain by submitting affidavit -in-opposition on behalf of the respondents opposes the Rules vehemently. Mr. Murad Reza raised question of maintainability of the writ petitions at the very outset. His bone of contention is that subject in issue is merely the notice under section 55 of the VAT Act pursuant to which in some of the cases parties also negotiated and asked for explanation whether they are required to give supplementary duty under the given situation and therefore, as he submits the writ petition itself is a premature one and any decision in compliance of section 55(1)(3) could be resorted and in furtherance thereto by filing an appeal under section 42 of the Act. In paragraph 4 and 6 of the affidavit in opposition the reasons have been given by the respondents explaining why supplementary duty as claimed by the VAT authority was justified. On the question of maintainability Additional Attorney-General cited several decisions.

24. Before addressing the issue in question let us first discuss the ratio decided of two of our decisions where one of us was a party reported in Zastat Limited, vs Customs Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal 64 DLR 33 and Bangladesh Intending Agent Association vs Bangladesh 64 DLR 389 having bearing on the point at issue. In the Case of Zastat our discussion though focused on imposition of VAT on hotel and restaurant but the main ratio was that "nothing short of waiver, exemption or by operation of law the rate of Vat can be fixed." In the second case of Bangladesh Indenting Agent Association as referred to above the Indenters were given exemption by different SROs time to time from payment of Vat but subsequently the exemption of payment of vat was lifted by the authority. Writ Petition was moved where Mr. AF Hasan Arif, the learned Senior Advocate contending different provisions of VAT Act tried to impress upon this Division that Indenters are not required to pay any VAT. That being the situation this Division came down as under:

"We are in full agreement with the submissions of the learned Senior Counsel that by legal fiction as it has been already discussed, the service rendered abroad by the petitioner i.e. outside the territory of Bangladesh is subject to/zero/nil rate of VAT if section 3(2) of the Act is read in conjunction with 2(Fa) and 2(La) of the VAT Act. But this can only be done by the Government. It lies indeed within the domain of Government."

25. With these decisions of ours in juxtaposition we want to cite the decision of Director of Taxation & Excise Govt. of E. Pak (new Bangladesh) vs Mehedi Ali Khan Panni 32 DLR (AD) 1980 P-138 wherein Chief Justice Kamal Uddin Hossain (As his Lordship then was) very succinctly made some observations which are relevant on the issue: :—

"Interpretation of taxing statutes-Doctrine of Laissez faire and welfare economy.

In interpreting a taxing statute a controversy often arises and learned authorities are cited are cited in support of the proposition that a taxing statute is to be construed strictly in favour of the subject. But this view though not abandoned in case of unresolved ambiguity, does no longer get the one-sided support from the judicial authorities. The view of strict construction prevailed at a time when the doctrine of laissez faire was the ruling principle of economy of a State, but almost all the leading States of the world have long abandoned the doctrine, and adopted the welfare doctrine of economy. Even a country like England where the doctrine of laissez faire originated has abandoned it in favour of welfare economy. The newly emerging nations like ours have mostly adopted the welfare doctrine."

<u>26. Now, coming back to our cases we have found that exemption of paying supplementary duty was there on the hotel but no exemption was given upon the service Code S001.20 which is the 'restaurant'. This goes without saying as on the basis of ratio decided of the 32 DLR and 64 DLR as referred to above that the restaurants inside the hotels having different service Code are separate entity rendering different services altogether upon which there was no exemption of supplementary duty whatsoever. Section 7 of the Act enjoins supplementary duty to be paid referring third schedule of the Act and we have made elaborate discussion on those aspects already. It has been rightly observed in 32 DLR (AD) that:</u>

<u>"In a fiscal or taxing statute one has to look merely at what is clearly said therein, for there is no room for any intendment nor for any equity or for any presumption. In case of unresolved ambiguity, it may be interpreted favorably to the citizen but nothing more. The attempt of the Court in case of ambiguity is to be guided by the principle of justice and fairness and to try to arrive at a true meaning of word."</u>

<u>27. We have found no ambiguity of any kind to hold that the restaurants inside the hotels in question at the relevant time were not exempted from paying supplementary duty. The exemption of Supplementary duty upon 'Hotel' & 'Restaurant' was given under section 14 of the VAT Act by SRO No. 338 dated 3-12-2003. In the year 2004 SRO No. 166 dated 10-6-2004 repealed the earlier SRO-338 which exempted supplementary duty only upon the hotel but restaurant was not allowed such exemption. Now by any legal fiction or by bringing any analogy it cannot be inferred since the hotels under service Code No. S001.10 were given exemption from paying supplementary duty time to time, the restaurants inside those hotels were also given the same exemption. Law does not allow something to achieve indirectly which cannot be achieved directly. Nothing short of waiver, exemption or by operation of law that can be done. There is no gain-saying the fact that the 'Restaurant' under service Code No. S001.20 was never given any exemption under section 14 of VAT Act 1991 from paying supplementary duty. All the submissions to justify the same fall apart being fallacious having no substance.</u>

28. In Writ Petition No.4317 of 2009 in the ordering part of Annexure-A dated 10-6-2009 it has been observed:—

“সার্বিক পর্যালোচনার প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, বিদ্যমান আইনের বিষয়ে অজ্ঞতাহেতৃ বিপুল পরিমাণ সম্পূরক শুল্ক অনাদায়ী রয়েছে। মূল্য সংযোজন কর আইন, ১৯৯১ এর তৃতীয় তফসিল বর্ণিত সেবার কোড অর্থাৎ রেস্তোরাঁ এর উপর সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপিত রয়েছে। বিন্দু এস আর ও নং-১৫২- আইন/২০০৫/8৪৩-মুসক, তারিখ ৯-৬-২০০৫ এর মাধ্যমে সেবার কোড ----- অর্থাৎ হোটেলকে সম্পূরক শুল্ক হতে অব্যাহতি প্রদান করা হয়েছে। হোটেল ও রেস্তোরাঁর ব্যাখ্যায় বলা আছে আবাসন, খাদ্য বা পানীয় সরবরাহকালে যদি হোটেল বা রেস্তোরাঁয় মদ জাতীয় পানীয় সরবরাহ করা হয় বা কোন ধরনের ফ্লোর শো এর আয়োজন করা হয়, তবে সেক্ষেত্রে সম্পূক শুল্ক আরোপিত হবে (বৎসরে একদিনের জন্য করা হলেও)৷ যেহেতু বিদ্যমান আইন অনুসারে রেস্তোরাঁ (মদ জাতীয় পানীয় সরবরাহ করা হয় বা ফ্লোর শো এর আয়োজন করা হয় এরূপ রেস্তোরাঁ) এর উপর সম্পূরক শুল্ক আরোপিত রয়েছে সেহেতু কোন প্রতিষ্ঠান কর্তৃক হোটেল ও রেস্তোরাঁ উভয় ধরনের সেবা প্ৰদত্ত হলে অর্থাৎ কোন হোটেলের অভ্যন্তরে রেস্তোরাঁ সেবাও প্রদত্ত হলে সেক্ষেত্রে রেস্তোরাঁ সেবার বিনিময়ে প্রাপ্ত পণ্যেও ক্ষেত্রে সম্পূরক শুল্ক আদায় ও পরিশোদযোগ্য হবে।”

29. The observations seems to be sound and perfect which has also been reflected in the arguments of the learned Additional Attorney General and learned Deputy Attorney General Mr. SM Moniruzzaman and also on our meticulous perusal of the materials on record specially the SROs and above all our elaborate discussion on the same. Fortified with all the decisions, observations, perusal of all the materials on record and the arguments pressed into service by both sides, we are of the view that all these Rule should be discharged being devoid of any substance.

<u>30. In respect of the submissions by the learned counsel Mr. Asaduzzaman on the question of limitation in writ petition No. 5430 of 2009 we are of the view that the submissions have merit and the same should be considered positively by the VAT authority after hearing the parties in strict compliance of the provisions under section 55(3) & (4) of the VAT Act together with the point of limitation as raised.</u>

31. In the result, all the Rules are discharged without any order as to cost. The order of stay in all the petitions stands vacated.
